components.detail: Rum infused with lime zest, ginger, clove and almond

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: An infusion and blend — nothing is redistilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; made and bottled fresh

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 11% ABV

composition.process: Lime zest rather than juice is what keeps it aromatic instead of sour.

name: Irish Cream
description: A silky truce between Irish whiskey and fresh dairy cream, with chocolate playing peacemaker. It appears wherever coffee, dessert, or holidays are found.
funFact: When Baileys was being invented in the early 1970s, its creators fixed the harsh-tasting first whiskey-and-cream prototype by stirring in powdered drinking chocolate.

serve.how: Keep the bottle in the fridge and pour it well chilled over ice in a rocks glass, or spike your coffee and crown it with whipped cream. Steer clear of citrus-heavy mixers — the cream will curdle — and refrigerate after opening. Sip slowly and notice the order of arrival: silky cream, then chocolate and vanilla, with the whiskey warmth surfacing only at the finish.

composition.summary: Irish whiskey emulsified with fresh dairy cream, sugar and chocolate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Irish whiskey, fresh dairy cream, sugar and cocoa

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Not distilled as a liqueur — the whiskey is blended in

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; the cream sets a real shelf life

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 17% ABV

composition.process: Homogenising the cream with the spirit is the trick that stops it curdling or separating.

name: Limoncello
description: Bottled Amalfi sunshine, made by steeping lemon zest in spirit until it glows. Served glacially cold after dinner, it is Italy's brightest digestivo.
funFact: Traditional limoncello uses only the fragrant zest of the lemons, never the juice, which is why it is sweet and aromatic rather than sour.

serve.how: Store the bottle in the freezer — the high sugar keeps it pourable — and serve small measures in chilled cordial glasses straight after dinner, Amalfi style. Sip it slowly while it is still glacially cold and slightly syrupy, letting it warm on the tongue. Notice that it is all fragrant zest and no sourness: candied lemon and flowers, never lemon juice.

composition.summary: Southern Italian liqueur made by steeping lemon zest in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, lemon zest only, sugar and water

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pure maceration — the zest gives up its oils to the alcohol

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; rested a few days, then bottled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 25–30% ABV

composition.process: Only the zest goes in, never the juice, which is why it's aromatic instead of sour.

name: Maraschino Liqueur
description: A crystal-clear cherry liqueur distilled from marasca cherries, pits and all, giving it a funky almond-and-flowers mystique. The secret handshake of classic cocktails like the Last Word.
funFact: The Luxardo family made maraschino in Zadar for over a century before rebuilding in Italy after World War II, replanting their marasca cherry orchards from scratch.

serve.how: Pour a small measure at cellar temperature into a cordial glass and treat it as a curiosity-sipper: it is drier and funkier than its candied-cherry name suggests. Most bottles earn their keep a quarter ounce at a time in a Last Word, Martinez, or Hemingway Daiquiri. Nose it first for the almond-and-flowers mystique from the distilled pits, then taste for the sour-cherry funk underneath.

composition.summary: A clear liqueur distilled from marasca cherries, their pits, stems and leaves.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Marasca cherries fermented whole, with pits, stems and leaves

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot-distilled to a clear spirit, then sweetened

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in neutral ash-wood vats that don't add colour

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 32% ABV

composition.process: Distilling the pits and leaves along with the fruit builds that funky almond-and-flowers character.

name: Nocino
description: An inky Italian liqueur brewed from unripe green walnuts, bittersweet and mysterious. Farmhouse alchemy passed down through Emilian families for generations.
funFact: Tradition dictates that the green walnuts for nocino be harvested on St. John's Eve, June 23rd to 24th, while they are still soft enough to cut.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve it the Emilian way: a small pour at room temperature in a cordial glass after a heavy meal, though a single small cube or a slight chill suits warmer nights. It is also wonderful drizzled over vanilla gelato or stirred into espresso. Sip slowly and follow the arc from dark walnut and baking spice into coffee-like, bitter-herb depths — farmhouse alchemy in slow motion.

composition.summary: An Italian liqueur made from unripe green walnuts macerated in spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Green walnuts, husks and all, in neutral spirit with sugar and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Maceration only — the walnuts steep for weeks or months

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested months or years, which softens the bitterness

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 24–40% ABV

composition.process: The walnuts go in while still soft enough to cut through, husk included — that's the inky colour.

name: Orange Curaçao
description: A richer, often brandy-based cousin of triple sec born of the Caribbean's most stubborn orange. Its deep candied-peel warmth is a tiki and classic-cocktail essential.
funFact: Curaçao is flavored with the laraha, a bitter orange that evolved from Valencia orange trees the Spanish planted on the island, which turned inedible in the arid soil.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Richer bottlings sip like a gentle orange brandy: pour it neat or over one large cube in a rocks glass and let the candied peel and warm spice unfold. It is also the backbone of a proper Mai Tai and lends classic cocktails a deeper glow than triple sec can. Notice the bitter laraha-peel edge that keeps all that candied-orange sweetness honest.

composition.summary: Orange liqueur flavoured with dried peel from Curaçao's bitter laraha orange.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Brandy or neutral spirit with sun-dried laraha peel and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peels steeped and often redistilled, then sweetened and blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some richer bottlings rest in oak; many do not

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 25–40% ABV

composition.process: Sun-drying the laraha peel concentrates the bitter oils that give curaçao its depth.

name: Peach Schnapps
description: A sweet, sunny peach liqueur that ruled 1980s American bars. Unashamedly fun, it still powers the fuzzy navel and sex on the beach.
funFact: American 'schnapps' is a sweet liqueur, unlike traditional German and Austrian schnaps, which is an unsweetened fruit distillate.

serve.how: Keep it in the fridge and embrace the fun: build a Fuzzy Navel with orange juice over ice in a highball, or lengthen it with soda water and a squeeze of lemon to trim the candy sweetness. A frozen blend with fresh peaches is its summer party trick. Sip and enjoy the unapologetic ripe-peach juiciness — this is sunshine, not subtlety.

composition.summary: A sweet American peach liqueur, flavoured and sugared rather than distilled from fruit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit with peach flavouring and plenty of sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Flavoured after distillation — no fruit brandy involved

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 15–24% ABV

composition.process: Sweetening is the whole point, and it's what separates it from unsweetened German schnaps.

name: Triple Sec
description: The tireless workhorse of the orange liqueur clan, clear and citrus-bright. It quietly powers margaritas, cosmopolitans, and sidecars around the globe.
funFact: No one is entirely sure what the 'triple' in triple sec originally meant; even the historic French producers tell conflicting stories about it.

serve.how: Triple sec is a workhorse, so let it work: keep it cool and reach for it in margaritas, cosmopolitans, and sidecars, where its clean orange brightness does the heavy lifting. To assess a bottle, sip a small chilled pour from a rocks glass — better versions taste of real orange peel, not candy. A splash in chilled prosecco with a twist makes an effortless aperitif.

composition.summary: A clear orange liqueur made by distilling neutral spirit with orange peel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sweet and bitter orange peel, sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with the peels, which keeps it clear and bright

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: A wide 15–40% ABV depending on quality

composition.process: Redistilling with the peel — rather than just infusing — is what makes it clean enough to disappear into a margarita.

name: Umeshu
description: A Japanese liqueur of whole ume fruit steeped in spirit and sugar, balancing honeyed sweetness with almond-tinged tartness. Often homemade and aged like a family heirloom.
funFact: The ume used in umeshu is usually translated as 'plum,' but the fruit is botanically closer to an apricot.

serve.how: Umeshu is flexible: pour it well chilled over ice in a rocks glass (the classic 'rokku' serve), straight from the fridge in a small glass, or lengthened with cold soda water as a highball. In winter, try it gently warmed with hot water, oyuwari-style. Sip and notice the honeyed sweetness balanced by apricot-like tartness, with the almond note from the ume kernel on the finish.

composition.summary: Japanese liqueur of whole ume fruit steeped in spirit with rock sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Unripe ume fruit, shochu or white liquor, and rock sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Not distilled — the whole fruit steeps in finished spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Months to years of maceration; many families age it far longer

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 10–15% ABV

composition.process: Using unripe, still-hard fruit is what gives the tartness and the almond-tinged edge.

name: Clairin
description: Haiti's untamed cane spirit, fermented with wild yeasts and distilled by hundreds of small village stills. No two batches are quite alike, like encountering a shiny variant every time.
funFact: Haiti is home to an estimated 500-plus small clairin distilleries, most using wild fermentation and local heirloom sugarcane varieties.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour a modest ounce and a half neat into a rocks glass and let it sit for a minute — wild-ferment cane spirits open up dramatically with a little air. Sip slowly and hunt for the olive-brine savoriness underneath the fresh cane and tropical fruit; every bottling is different, so taste it blind before deciding whether it needs a cube. If the proof runs hot (many are 50%+), a single large cube or a few drops of water tames the fire without muting the funk.

composition.summary: Haitian cane spirit from fresh juice or syrup, fermented with wild yeast.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh sugarcane juice or syrup from heirloom Haitian cane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: A single pass through small village pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Traditionally unaged and bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–55% ABV

composition.process: Spontaneous fermentation with whatever yeast is in the air makes every village taste different.

name: Dark Rum
description: A brooding, molasses-rich creature that lurks at the bottom of tiki drinks and floats ominously on top of them. Deep aging and dark molasses give it heavyweight flavor.
funFact: Goslings trademarked the Dark 'n' Stormy cocktail, so by the letter of the trademark an authentic one must be made with Goslings Black Seal rum.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve it in a rocks glass over one big cube, which slowly opens the molasses and coffee notes as it melts. Give the glass a gentle swirl and nose it before the first sip — the brown-sugar and dried-fruit aromas are half the pleasure. It also makes a fine simple highball with ginger beer if you want something longer, but resist small ice, which waters it down too fast.

composition.summary: Molasses-based rum aged long in oak, often deepened with caramel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, sometimes from darker, heavier grades

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills, columns, or a blend of both for body

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Extended oak maturation; caramel colouring is common

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–43% ABV

composition.process: Heavier molasses plus long barrel time is what builds that brooding, tiki-anchoring weight.

name: Demerara Rum
description: A dark, smoky-sweet rum from the banks of Guyana's Demerara River. Its burnt-sugar depth is the secret engine of classic tiki recipes.
funFact: Guyana's Diamond Distillery still operates the world's last working wooden Coffey still, along with heritage wooden pot stills that are centuries-old designs.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour it neat at room temperature first to appreciate the burnt-sugar and raisin depth, then add one large cube if the bottling is cask strength. Swirl and let it rest a few minutes — the smoke and licorice notes emerge as it breathes. Notice the almost-savory char on the finish; that's the signature of Guyana's ancient wooden stills.

composition.summary: Guyanese molasses rum distilled on heritage wooden stills by the Demerara River.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses from sugarcane grown along Guyana's Demerara River

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Historic wooden pot stills and the last working wooden Coffey still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Tropical oak maturation, with a fierce angel's share

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–57.5% ABV

composition.process: Those centuries-old wooden stills leave heavy, smoky congeners a modern column would strip away.

name: Gold Rum
description: White rum's sun-kissed evolution, mellowed by time in oak barrels. Rounder and warmer, it bridges the gap between mixable lightness and sipping depth.
funFact: The golden color comes from barrel aging, though many producers also adjust the hue with a small amount of caramel coloring.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: This is an easygoing sipper: pour two fingers into a rocks glass, neat or over a single large cube. Take a small first sip to acclimate, then look for the caramel, vanilla, and ripe banana that the oak has coaxed out of the cane. It is also forgiving in a highball with soda and a lime wedge on hot days.

composition.summary: Molasses rum mellowed by a few years in oak barrels.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, fermented and distilled conventionally

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Usually column stills, sometimes blended with pot still rum

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Several years in oak; colour is often topped up with caramel

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40% ABV

composition.process: Enough barrel time to round the edges, not enough to overwhelm the cane.

name: Jamaican Pot Still Rum
description: The funkiest member of the rum family, famed for its intense fruity 'hogo.' Long wild fermentations and pot stills breed esters that smell like overripe pineapple and banana.
funFact: Some Jamaican distilleries boost esters using 'muck pits,' aged reservoirs of leftover fermentation material that supercharge the rum's signature funk.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour it neat in a rocks glass and give it a good nose before sipping — the famous 'hogo' of overripe banana and pineapple is the whole show. Let it sit on your tongue a beat longer than you would other rums so the ester funk unfolds into allspice on the finish. High-proof bottlings welcome a big cube or a teaspoon of water, which softens the heat and amplifies the fruit.

composition.summary: Jamaican molasses rum from long wild fermentations run through copper pot stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses, fermented for weeks with dunder and wild microbes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, retaining the heavy esters on purpose

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak-aged tropically, though unaged high-ester rums exist

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–63% ABV

composition.process: Long, deliberately dirty fermentations build the esters behind that overripe-pineapple hogo.

name: Overproof Rum
description: The fire-breathing form of rum, bottled well above standard strength. Handle with respect: it powers flaming tiki garnishes and adds a roaring backbone to punches.
funFact: The word 'proof' comes from an old test in which spirit was mixed with gunpowder; if the powder still ignited, the rum was 'proved' strong enough.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: At 57%+ this is not a neat-pour spirit for most people — serve a small measure over one large cube, or better yet lengthen it into a highball with plenty of ice in its natural habitat, a tiki mug. If you do taste it neat, take tiny sips and let the ripe banana and burnt sugar punch through the heat; a splash of water reveals surprising fruit. Keep it well away from open flames unless you actually intend the theatrical float.

composition.summary: Molasses rum bottled far above standard strength.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, as with most Caribbean rum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column stills, simply proofed down much less

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often unaged and clear; some aged versions exist

composition.process: Minimal dilution after distillation keeps both the flavour and the fire intact.

name: Rhum Agricole
description: A grassy, wild-hearted rum distilled from fresh-pressed sugarcane juice instead of molasses. It tastes like a cane field after rain and stars in the Ti' Punch.
funFact: Rhum agricole from Martinique earned a French AOC designation in 1996, a protection more commonly associated with wine and cheese than with spirits.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Drink it the Martinique way: a short pour in a rocks glass at room temperature, ideally as a Ti' Punch — a squeeze of lime disc and a small spoon of cane syrup stirred right in the glass. Neat, swirl gently and breathe in the fresh-cut-grass and green-olive aromas that molasses rums never show. Skip heavy ice on aged expressions; the vegetal character is delicate and fades when over-chilled.

composition.summary: French Caribbean rum distilled from fresh-pressed sugarcane juice, never molasses.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed sugarcane juice, fermented within hours of harvest

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: A single pass through a tall creole column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Blanc rests months in steel; vieux spends at least three years in oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–55% ABV

composition.process: Distilling living cane juice, not molasses, is exactly why it tastes like a wet cane field.

name: Spiced Rum
description: A rum that raided the spice cabinet and never looked back. Vanilla, cinnamon, and clove cling to a sweet cane base, making it the gateway species for many trainers.
funFact: Captain Morgan is named after Henry Morgan, a real 17th-century Welsh privateer who later became lieutenant governor of Jamaica.

serve.how: Spiced rum is happiest long and cold: fill a highball with ice, pour two ounces, and top with cola or ginger beer plus a lime wedge. The vanilla and cinnamon are built to mingle with a mixer rather than stand alone, though a chilled neat pour works as an easy after-dinner nip. Notice how the clove and caramel bloom on the finish once the initial sweetness fades.

composition.summary: Rum flavoured with vanilla, cinnamon, clove and other spices, usually sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses rum, plus spices, vanilla, sugar and colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled as rum, then flavoured after the fact

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Base rum may see brief oak; spices are added afterward

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 35–40% ABV

composition.process: The spice blend and added sugar happen post-distillation, which is why brands taste so different.

name: White Rum
description: The clear, quick-footed starter of the rum family, filtered to a clean gleam. It hides in plain sight inside daiquiris and mojitos, striking with soft sugarcane sweetness.
funFact: Bacardí's bat logo comes from the fruit bats that roosted in the company's first distillery, which Doña Amalia Bacardí considered a sign of good luck.

serve.how: Serve it cold — straight from the freezer door or over fresh ice in a rocks glass — since chill sharpens its clean sugarcane snap. Take a sip and look past the neutrality for soft vanilla and citrus; good white rum is subtle, not empty. At home it shines simplest as rum-and-soda with a fat lime wedge, no shaker required.

composition.summary: Light molasses rum, column-distilled and filtered clear.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, fermented quickly with cultured yeast

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: High-proof continuous column stills for a clean, light spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Briefly rested in oak, then charcoal-filtered back to clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40% ABV

composition.process: Charcoal filtration strips the colour a short barrel rest added, leaving softness without weight.

name: Blended Malt Scotch
description: A marriage of single malts from multiple distilleries with no grain whisky invited. All the malt character, none of the single-distillery ego.
funFact: This style was known as 'vatted malt' until the Scotch Whisky Regulations of 2009 officially renamed it 'blended malt.'

serve.how: Pour a standard dram (about 1.5 oz) into a Glencairn at cool room temperature and give it a couple of minutes to settle in the glass. Nose it with your mouth slightly open, then sip and watch how malts from different distilleries layer honey, orchard fruit, and oak into one voice. A few drops of still water will loosen the texture and lift the fruit if it feels tight.

composition.summary: Single malts from several Scottish distilleries, blended with no grain whisky.

components.label: Base
components.detail: One hundred percent malted barley, from multiple distilleries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills at each contributing distillery

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least three years in oak casks in Scotland

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–46% ABV

composition.process: Vatting malts from different distilleries builds complexity no single house could reach alone.

name: Blended Scotch
description: Malt whisky's charisma married to grain whisky's smoothness, assembled by master blenders chasing perfect consistency. The workhorse that carried Scotch around the globe.
funFact: Blends account for roughly 90% of all Scotch whisky sold worldwide, dwarfing the single malts that get most of the glory.

serve.how: This is the most flexible Scotch on the shelf: sip it neat in a rocks glass at cellar temperature, add a single cube, or stretch it into a highball with chilled soda — all three are legitimate. Neat, look for the honey and vanilla smoothness the grain whisky contributes, with malt and soft smoke peeking through. Don't overthink it; blends were engineered for relaxed drinking, not ceremony.

composition.summary: Malt whisky married to column-distilled grain whisky by a master blender.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley for the malts, wheat or maize for the grain

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills for malt, continuous columns for grain whisky

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Every component at least three years in oak in Scotland

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–43% ABV

composition.process: The blender's job is consistency: the same bottle, year after year, from ever-changing casks.

name: Campbeltown Single Malt
description: Briny, oily, faintly funky malts from a tiny peninsula town that whisky history nearly forgot. What survived is fiercely loved and stubbornly old-fashioned.
funFact: Victorian-era Campbeltown called itself the whisky capital of the world with over 30 distilleries; today it remains a protected Scotch region with only three in operation.

serve.how: Pour a dram into a Glencairn and let it rest five full minutes — Campbeltown's oily, briny character rewards patience. Sip without water first and register the sea salt and machine-shop funk, then add a few drops to unlock hidden fruit beneath the smoke. Never serve it over ice; the famous oily texture that defines the region goes numb when cold.

composition.summary: All-malt Scotch from a single distillery in the tiny Campbeltown region.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, often lightly peated, from one Campbeltown distillery

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills; the surviving distilleries keep old-fashioned methods

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak in Scotland, usually far longer

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 46–56% ABV

composition.process: Old equipment and stubbornly traditional production give the region its oily, briny signature.

name: Highland Single Malt
description: Malts from Scotland's biggest and most varied region, ranging from heathery and floral to muscular and faintly smoky. A region so large it refuses to have one personality.
funFact: The Highlands are geographically the largest of Scotland's legally protected whisky regions, stretching from just north of Glasgow to the far northern coast.

serve.how: Serve a dram at cool room temperature in a Glencairn, swirl gently, and nose for heather and dried fruit before the first sip. Because the Highlands span so many styles, taste it on its own terms — some pours lean floral and honeyed, others muscular with a wisp of smoke. A teaspoon of water is the classic move if the malt feels closed; add it gradually and re-nose each time.

composition.summary: All-malt Scotch from a single distillery in Scotland's largest whisky region.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, peating levels varying enormously across the region

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice through copper pot stills, at one distillery

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least three years in oak in Scotland

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–46% ABV

composition.process: Still shape varies wildly across the region, which is why Highland malts refuse a single personality.

name: Island Single Malt
description: Maritime malts from Skye, Orkney, Jura, Arran, and Mull — salt-licked, honeyed, and often kissed with smoke. Each island argues, convincingly, that it tastes like nowhere else.
funFact: The Islands are not a legally recognized Scotch region — under the official rules, every island distillery except those on Islay is classified as Highland.

serve.how: Pour it into a Glencairn at cellar temperature and take your time nosing — sea spray and heather honey should arrive before the pepper and light peat. Sip slowly and notice the salty edge on your lips; that maritime signature is what you paid for. A drop or two of water softens the pepper and pulls out sweetness, but skip ice, which buries the coastal nuance.

composition.summary: All-malt Scotch from a single distillery on Skye, Orkney, Jura, Arran or Mull.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, often lightly to moderately peated

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, usually twice, at one island distillery

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak, maturing in salt-laden sea air

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–48% ABV

composition.process: Coastal warehouses and local peat give each island its own claim to maritime character.

name: Islay Single Malt
description: The smoke-breathing dragon of Scotch: peat-fired malts from a windswept Hebridean island, tasting of bonfires, sea spray, and old rope. You never forget your first.
funFact: Islay is home to around ten working distilleries despite having a population of only about 3,000 people.

serve.how: Pour a dram neat into a Glencairn and let it breathe for several minutes — peat smoke dominates a fresh pour and settles into iodine, brine, and tar complexity with air. Sip in small doses and exhale slowly through your nose to get the full bonfire effect. A few drops of water famously cracks Islay malts open, trading some smoke for surprising sweetness underneath; ice just puts the fire out.
pair: oysters (even with a drop of whisky in the shell)

composition.summary: All-malt Scotch from a single Islay distillery, usually made with heavily peated barley.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley dried over burning Islay peat

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, typically twice, at one island distillery

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least three years in oak, often in seaside warehouses

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–48% ABV

composition.process: Peat smoke drifting through the drying malt is what puts the bonfire in the glass.

name: Lowland Single Malt
description: Light, grassy, and gently floral malts from Scotland's southern belt, historically triple-distilled into silkiness. The aperitif of the Scotch family.
funFact: Lowland malts were historically nicknamed the 'Lowland Ladies' for their delicate character, and some distilleries there still practice traditional triple distillation.

serve.how: This is the Scotch to serve before dinner: a neat dram in a Glencairn, slightly cool, no water needed at standard proof. Sip gently and look for cut grass, citrus, and a creamy triple-distilled softness — it whispers where Islay shouts. Its delicacy means it drowns easily, so add water a drop at a time if at all.

composition.summary: All-malt Scotch from one distillery in Scotland's southern belt, classically light.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, almost always unpeated

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills; several Lowland distilleries still distil three times

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least three years in oak in Scotland

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–46% ABV

composition.process: A third distillation strips out weight, leaving the grassy, floral delicacy the region is known for.

name: Single Grain Scotch
description: Column-distilled whisky from one distillery using grains beyond malted barley — light, sweet, and long the unseen backbone of every great blend. Increasingly bottled on its own for the curious.
funFact: The 'single' refers to a single distillery, not a single grain — a single grain Scotch can be made from several cereals at once.

serve.how: Pour a dram into a Glencairn at cool room temperature and approach it like a dessert whisky — butterscotch, coconut, and vanilla are the headline acts. It is lighter-bodied than malt, so sip without water first; older grain whiskies in particular can be silky and surprisingly complex. It also makes an elegant highball with soda, a style the light sweetness handles beautifully.

composition.summary: Column-distilled Scotch from one distillery using grains beyond malted barley.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wheat or maize with a small proportion of malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Continuous column stills, distilled high and light

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak in Scotland

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–46% ABV

composition.process: Continuous distillation to high strength makes a light spirit that turns sweet and creamy in oak.

name: Speyside Single Malt
description: Elegant, fruity malts from the valley of the River Spey, where distilleries cluster thicker than anywhere else on Earth. The honeyed diplomat of the Scotch world.
funFact: Speyside packs roughly 50 distilleries into one small river valley, the densest concentration of whisky-making on the planet.

serve.how: Serve a neat dram in a Glencairn at cellar temperature and nose it patiently — apple, honey, and vanilla should rise in sequence, with sherried fruit on richer bottlings. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate; Speyside's elegance is about balance rather than punch. A few drops of water can unfold extra orchard fruit, but many Speysides are perfect exactly as poured.

composition.summary: All-malt Scotch from a single distillery in the River Spey valley.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, typically unpeated

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, twice, at one of roughly fifty distilleries

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak; sherry casks are a regional signature

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–46% ABV

composition.process: Tall stills and generous sherry-cask maturation build the honeyed, orchard-fruit house style.

name: Grain Vodka
description: The stealth specialist of the spirits world, distilled from wheat, rye, or corn to near-silence. Its subtle texture and faint grain sweetness carry countless cocktails without a sound.
funFact: US regulations long defined vodka as being 'without distinctive character, aroma, taste, or color,' wording the TTB finally removed in 2020.

serve.how: Store the bottle in the freezer and pour small measures into chilled shot glasses — the cold thickens the texture to a silky, almost viscous pour. Sip rather than slam it, and pay attention to the finish: good grain vodka shows faint cream, white pepper, and mineral notes instead of burn. Serve it alongside salty little bites, Eastern European style, refilling glasses in rounds.
pair: caviar or salted roe on blini

composition.summary: Vodka distilled from wheat, rye or corn and rectified to near-neutrality.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wheat, rye or corn, fermented into a grain wash

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Continuous column rectification, often to very high proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; filtered, usually through charcoal, then proofed with water

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40% ABV

composition.process: Rectifying to near-pure ethanol is the whole craft — the goal is what's absent, not present.

name: Potato Vodka
description: A fuller-bodied, earthier vodka variant with a creamy weight on the tongue. Despite the stereotype, it is the rarer breed, as potatoes are stubborn to distill.
funFact: Only a small fraction of the world's vodka is actually made from potatoes; they are bulkier, starchier, and more expensive to process than grain.

serve.how: Chill the bottle thoroughly but not to freezer-death — a fridge-cold pour keeps the signature creamy weight on the tongue that hard freezing can dull. Sip it slowly from a chilled shot glass and roll it around; the earthy, buttery body is the whole point of choosing potato over grain. It also anchors an exceptional dirty martini, where its fuller texture stands up to the brine.

composition.summary: Vodka distilled from potatoes, giving a fuller and creamier body.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Potatoes, cooked to convert their starch before fermenting

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column distilled, though often less aggressively rectified

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; filtered and proofed with water

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40% ABV

composition.process: Potatoes must be cooked and enzyme-treated before they'll ferment, which is why they're so much work.

name: Aquavit
description: Scandinavia's caraway-and-dill spirit, sipped ice-cold at feasts with a hearty skål. It tastes like rye bread's spirited ghost.
funFact: Norwegian 'linie' aquavit is aged in sherry casks aboard ships that cross the equator twice, a sea voyage the makers credit with mellowing the spirit.

serve.how: Serve it Scandinavian-style: well chilled in small stemmed glasses, poured at the table for the whole company and drunk with a toast — meet eyes, say skål, sip. The caraway and dill hit first, followed by citrus peel and grain warmth; barrel-aged Norwegian styles can also be enjoyed closer to room temperature to show their oak. Keep pours small and repeat through the meal, as aquavit is a food spirit before all else.

composition.summary: Scandinavian spirit redistilled with caraway or dill as the dominant flavour.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain or potato spirit, caraway or dill leading

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with the spices, like a Nordic cousin of gin

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often unaged; Norwegian linie styles rest in sherry casks at sea

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 37.5–45% ABV

composition.process: Caraway or dill must be the dominant flavour — that requirement is what makes it aquavit.

name: Awamori
description: Okinawa's ancestral rice spirit, fermented with black koji and long-grain Thai rice, sometimes aged for decades in clay pots. Japan's oldest distilled spirit, with island soul.
funFact: Awamori is considered Japan's oldest distilled spirit, born of 15th-century trade between the Ryukyu Kingdom and Siam, which is why it still uses Thai indica rice.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Drink it the Okinawan way: pour into a small clay cup either neat, over a large piece of ice, or diluted roughly 1:1 with cool water (mizuwari), which softens the proof and blooms the earthy rice aromas. Sip slowly and look for mushroom, cream, and mineral depth — aged kusu expressions especially deserve unhurried attention. Warmer service (not hot, just room temperature) shows more aroma; ice makes it a clean, easy dinner companion.

composition.summary: Okinawan spirit distilled from long-grain Thai rice fermented with black koji.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Thai indica long-grain rice, inoculated with black koji mould

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: A single pot distillation from one all-at-once fermentation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often matured in clay pots; kusu means at least three years

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 25–43% ABV

composition.process: Black koji produces protective citric acid, which is how fermentation survives Okinawa's heat.

name: Baijiu
description: China's ancient grain spirit, fermented solid-state in earthen pits with a microbial culture called qu. Ferociously aromatic and nearly mythical to Western drinkers.
funFact: Baijiu is the best-selling spirit category on Earth by volume, yet the overwhelming majority of it is consumed within China.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve it at room temperature in tiny ceramic cups — a pour is barely a mouthful, taken in small sips or a single 'ganbei' toast among friends. Nose it first without fear: the fermented funk, tropical fruit, and soy-sauce savoriness are intentional and grow fascinating with exposure. Always drink it with food rather than alone; the intense aromatics are engineered to cut through rich, oily dishes.

composition.summary: Chinese grain spirit fermented solid-state in earthen pits using a qu starter.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with wheat, rice, corn or glutinous rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Steam distillation of solid fermented grain, not a liquid wash

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Matured in large ceramic jars, sometimes for years

components.label: Strength
components.detail: A wide 38–65% ABV

composition.process: Qu — a brick of moulds, yeasts and bacteria — drives a solid-state ferment found nowhere else.

name: Feni
description: Goa's pungent double-distilled spirit made from cashew apples or coconut palm sap. Wildly aromatic, farmhouse-funky, and fiercely protected as an Indian heritage drink.
funFact: Cashew feni received a Geographical Indication in 2009, making it one of the first Indian spirits legally tied to its home state of Goa.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour it over one large cube in a rocks glass and let the first wave of cashew-fruit pungency settle before sipping — feni announces itself from across the room. Sip slowly and pick out the sea air and wild-yeast funk behind the peppery heat; a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt, Goan-style, turns it into a bracing sundowner. It also stretches happily into a highball with soda or bitter lemon if neat feels like too much spirit.

composition.summary: Goan spirit distilled from cashew apple juice or coconut palm sap.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fermented cashew apple juice, or toddy tapped from coconut palms

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional clay or copper pot stills, run in successive stages

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; some producers rest it in clay or wood

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 42–45% ABV

composition.process: Cashew apples are crushed underfoot in stone troughs, and the juice ferments in earthen pots.

name: Shochu
description: Japan's versatile, gently savory spirit, single-distilled from sweet potato, barley, rice, or buckwheat with the help of koji mold. Subtle where baijiu is loud.
funFact: In 2003, shochu shipments overtook sake within Japan, a milestone in the homeland of both drinks.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Shochu is a shapeshifter: serve it over one large cube (rokku), cut 6:4 with warm water (oyuwari) to bloom the aroma of sweet-potato styles, or with cold water for easy dinner drinking. At its gentle proof you can sip generously — notice the earthy umami and soft grain sweetness that make it such a natural food partner. Barley shochu takes ice best; imo (sweet potato) shochu is transformed by warm water, so try both.

composition.summary: Japanese spirit single-distilled from sweet potato, barley, rice or buckwheat.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sweet potato, barley, rice or buckwheat, plus koji-inoculated rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Honkaku shochu is distilled once, preserving the raw material's character

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually rested briefly in steel or clay; some sees oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 20–35% ABV

composition.process: Koji mould converts the starch first, then a single gentle distillation keeps the ingredient recognisable.

name: Soju
description: Korea's smooth, lightly sweet spirit in its iconic green bottle. Easygoing yet relentless, it accompanies Korean barbecue the way rain accompanies clouds.
funFact: Jinro soju has repeatedly ranked as the world's best-selling spirit brand by volume, outselling every famous vodka and whisky label.

serve.how: Serve the green bottle well chilled and pour for others, never yourself — soju is a communal ritual, received with two hands and returned in kind. Drink it in small shot-glass pours alongside food, noticing the clean grain sweetness and soft mineral finish that make it so dangerously easy. Give the bottle the traditional swirl-and-tap if you like; mostly it just needs cold temperature and good company.

composition.summary: Korean spirit, traditionally rice-distilled, now mostly diluted column spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Historically rice; modern mass-market uses sweet potato or tapioca

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional soju is pot-distilled; the green-bottle kind is column-rectified

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; blended with water and sweeteners before bottling

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 12.5–25% ABV

composition.process: Diluting highly rectified spirit and adding sweeteners is what makes modern soju so easy-drinking.

name: Canadian Whisky
description: Light, smooth blends built grain by grain, where each cereal is often distilled and aged separately before assembly. Canadians call nearly all of it 'rye' out of sheer tradition.
funFact: Canadian rules famously allow up to one-eleventh (9.09%) of other aged spirits or wine to be blended into whisky destined for the U.S. market.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers into a rocks glass neat or over a single large cube — Canadian whisky's light, smooth build is made for low-effort enjoyment. Sip and separate the caramel-vanilla sweetness from the rye spice that flickers on the finish; that interplay is the blender's whole art. It is also a natural highball whisky with ginger ale, the classic 'rye and ginger' of Canadian bars.

composition.summary: Canadian whisky built by blending grains distilled and aged separately.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Corn, rye, wheat and barley, each usually handled on its own

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Mostly continuous column stills, producing light and flavouring whiskies

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least three years in small wood casks in Canada

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–45% ABV

composition.process: Distilling and aging each grain separately, then blending, is the Canadian method in one sentence.

name: Indian Single Malt
description: Malt whisky matured at tropical speed, where the subcontinental heat does in four years what Scotland needs twelve to accomplish. Bold, jammy, and in a hurry.
funFact: India's hot climate can evaporate over 10% of a maturing cask per year — several times the 'angel's share' lost annually in Scotland.

serve.how: Serve a dram in a Glencairn at cool room temperature and expect ripeness beyond its years — tropical heat matured this malt at a sprint. Nose for mango-adjacent tropical fruit and barley sugar, then sip and follow the spice into toasted oak. Bottlings often run 46-50%, so keep water handy and add a few drops if the jammy fruit feels buried under heat.

composition.summary: One hundred percent malted barley from a single Indian distillery, aged fast.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, often India's own six-row varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills at a single distillery

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and sherry casks; tropical heat does years of work quickly

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 46–50% ABV

composition.process: Subcontinental heat drives spirit deep into the wood, compressing maturation into a few years.

name: Japanese Whisky
description: Scotch's meticulous Japanese apprentice that grew into a master: precise, balanced whiskies built for quiet contemplation or the perfect highball. Restraint as a flavor.
funFact: Masataka Taketsuru learned whisky-making in Scotland around 1919, helped build Japan's first whisky distillery for Suntory, then left to found its great rival, Nikka.

serve.how: Honor the highball: fill a tall glass to the brim with clear ice, pour one part whisky, stir a few times to chill, then gently add three to four parts cold soda and stir once. The delicate honey, incense, and orchard-fruit notes stay vivid through the dilution — precision drinking for a precise spirit. Better bottles equally reward a quiet neat pour in a Glencairn at room temperature; either way, restraint is the flavor.

composition.summary: Japanese whisky from malted and other grains, built for balance and precision.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, sometimes with other grains

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot and column stills; distilleries famously make many spirit styles in-house

components.label: Aging
components.detail: The industry's 2021 labelling standard asks for at least three years in wood

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 43–48% ABV

composition.process: Blending many self-made spirit styles, including mizunara-cask whisky, is the Japanese signature.

name: Taiwanese Single Malt
description: Subtropical single malt that ages at a sprint and drinks like a mango orchard met a sherry cask. The upstart that made the old world nervous.
funFact: Taiwan's Kavalan distillery only released its first whisky in 2008, yet by 2015 one of its casks was named the world's best single malt at the World Whiskies Awards.

serve.how: Pour a dram into a Glencairn at cellar temperature and nose it slowly — the mango and sherried-fruit perfume is the calling card of subtropical aging. Sip and let it linger; the vanilla and polished oak arrive fast and rich because the Taiwanese climate compresses decades of maturation into a few years. Cask-strength releases can top 55%, so add water drop by drop until the fruit basket fully opens.

composition.summary: All malted barley from a single Taiwanese distillery, matured at subtropical speed.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Imported malted barley, typically unpeated

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills at one distillery

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Heavy sherry and wine-cask use; maturation runs extremely fast

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–58% ABV

composition.process: Subtropical heat and humidity push huge annual evaporation, forcing intense wood extraction in a few years.

name: Scottish Gin
description: More than two thirds of all British gin is distilled in Scotland, and the country long ago stopped treating it as whisky's side project. Expect heather, sea pink and bog myrtle alongside the juniper.
funFact: Scotland distils roughly 70% of the UK's gin, largely because the whisky industry left the country full of stills, expertise and spare capacity.

serve.how: Build over plenty of ice with a light tonic, two parts to one, and stir once. A heather-forward Scottish gin wants a garnish that echoes it rather than fights it, so reach for grapefruit peel or a sprig of thyme instead of the usual lime.

composition.summary: Neutral grain spirit redistilled with juniper and Scottish botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit, usually wheat

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus heather, bog myrtle, sea pink, milk thistle

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, one-shot or concentrate

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, though barrel-rested bottlings exist

composition.process: Foraged coastal botanicals are what separate a Scottish gin from a London Dry made anywhere else.

name: Plymouth Gin
description: Softer, earthier and rounder than London Dry, with more root and less pine. It is the only English gin tied by protection to a single city, and there is only one distillery left making it.
funFact: Plymouth Gin was the specified gin in the first written Dry Martini recipes, and the Royal Navy carried it worldwide from the Black Friars Distillery, in use since 1793.

serve.how: This is the gin to make a Martini with when you want weight rather than bite. Stir with a dry vermouth at about five to one until the mixing glass frosts, strain, and express a lemon peel over the top. Its lower juniper pitch also makes it the right call in a Gimlet.

composition.summary: Wheat spirit redistilled with seven botanicals, weighted toward roots.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral wheat spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, coriander, angelica, orris root, cardamom, lemon and orange peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single copper pot still at Black Friars, Plymouth

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: A higher proportion of root botanicals gives the earthiness that defines the style.

name: English Whisky
description: England distilled whisky for centuries, stopped entirely around 1905, and started again in 2006. The new distilleries had no house style to inherit, so they invented one: fruit-forward, lightly peated when at all, and unafraid of odd casks.
funFact: English whisky received legally protected status in 2022, more than a century after the last English distillery of the old era fell silent.

serve.how: Pour a generous measure and give it a few minutes in the glass; young whisky opens quickly. A drop or two of water is worth adding at cask strength, where it pulls the orchard fruit forward out of the alcohol.

composition.summary: Malted barley, distilled and matured in England for at least three years.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, much of it Norfolk-grown

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years, often in ex-bourbon and STR casks

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–46%, with cask-strength releases common

composition.process: Warmer English summers push maturation along faster than in Scotland, so young stock tastes older than it is.

name: Pimm's No. 1
description: A gin-based fruit cup at 25%, invented by a London oyster bar owner as a digestive and now inseparable from English summer. On its own it is treacly and odd; drowned in lemonade with a fruit salad in it, it makes sense.
funFact: James Pimm served it in a small tankard called a No. 1 Cup in the 1840s, which is why the bottle still carries a number rather than a name.

serve.how: One part Pimm's to three parts chilled lemonade over a lot of ice. Then the fruit, which is not optional: cucumber ribbon, orange slice, strawberry, and a good handful of mint bruised between your palms first.

composition.summary: Gin sweetened and infused with caramelised fruit and herbal extracts.

components.label: Base
components.detail: London gin

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bitter orange, caramel, herbs and spices to a secret recipe

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: None; the base gin is infused and sweetened

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 25% ABV, built for dilution

composition.process: The recipe has stayed with six people at a time since the 1820s, or so the company says.

name: Welsh Whisky
description: Wales went without a whisky distillery for most of the twentieth century until Penderyn opened in 2004 in the Brecon Beacons. Its unusual single-copper-still design produces a notably light, floral spirit.
funFact: Penderyn uses a Faraday still designed at Surrey University that does in one pass what most distilleries need two or three stills to achieve.

serve.how: Neat first, then a few drops of water. Penderyn's Madeira-finished bottling in particular tightens up with too much dilution, so add water in small increments and stop as soon as the raisin note blooms.

composition.summary: Malted barley wash distilled in a single bespoke still and matured in Wales.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, wash bought in from a Welsh brewery

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single Faraday copper still, one pass to around 92%

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, then finished in Madeira, sherry or port

composition.process: Distilling to a very high strength in one pass makes for a lighter spirit than a conventional double pot still gives.

name: Eau-de-Vie
description: Clear, unaged fruit brandy, and the hardest category in distilling to do well. There is nowhere to hide: no wood, no sugar, no colour, just whatever the fruit gave you and whatever you did to it.
funFact: It can take around thirty kilos of raspberries to make a single bottle of framboise, which is why good eau-de-vie costs what it does.

serve.glass: Small tulip or chilled stemmed glass
serve.how: Chill the glass rather than the bottle, since a freezing spirit shows nothing. Pour about an ounce after a meal and drink it in small sips. The aroma is the entire point, so nose it well before the first taste.

composition.summary: Whole fruit fermented and distilled to preserve aroma, then rested in glass.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Raspberry, pear Williams, mirabelle, quetsch or cherry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot still, low and slow, tight heart cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None in wood; rested in glass or earthenware to soften

composition.process: Distilled to a lower strength than most spirits so that the fruit esters carry over rather than being stripped out.

name: Marc
description: France's answer to grappa, distilled from the skins, pips and stems left in the press after the wine is made. Rustic where grappa aims for finesse, and often aged in wood until it tastes closer to an old brandy.
funFact: Marc de Champagne is used far more often in kitchens than in glasses, where it flavours truffles, sorbets and the odd wedding cake.

serve.how: Serve after dinner at room temperature in a small pour. Aged marc rewards a warmed glass; young marc does not, and heat only sharpens its edges. It also does honourable work poured into an espresso.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and distilled after the wine press.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems from winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still, often mobile and shared between growers

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Frequently oak-aged, sometimes for decades

composition.process: Because the pomace has already given up its juice, everything left is skin and structure, which is where the grip comes from.

name: Grand Marnier
description: Cognac married with bitter Caribbean orange, which puts it a class above the neutral-spirit orange liqueurs. Heavier and rounder than triple sec, and the reason a Sidecar tastes different depending on which bottle you reach for.
funFact: Created in 1880, the name was a joke by César Ritz at a time when fashion demanded everything be called petite; Marnier called his grand instead.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.glass: Snifter, or a coupe in a drink
serve.how: Neat in a snifter after dinner, or over a single large cube. In cocktails it belongs in a Sidecar or a Cadillac Margarita, where its cognac base adds weight that Cointreau deliberately leaves out.

composition.summary: Cognac blended with distilled bitter orange essence and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac, roughly half the blend

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Citrus bigaradia, the bitter orange of the Caribbean

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Orange peel macerated and distilled, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak after blending

composition.process: Using cognac rather than neutral spirit is the whole difference, and it is why the liqueur can be drunk on its own.

name: Suze
description: Yellow gentian root, dug by hand from Alpine and Jura hillsides after several years in the ground, macerated into a pale gold aperitif that is bitter in a way almost nothing else is: floral, earthy and faintly medicinal.
funFact: Picasso painted a bottle of it into a 1912 collage, Verre et bouteille de Suze, which now hangs in a university museum in St Louis.

serve.how: Over ice with tonic or soda and a slice of orange is the French café serve. In a cocktail it is the backbone of a White Negroni, standing in for Campari with gin and Lillet.

composition.summary: Gentian root macerated and distilled, then sweetened and lightly coloured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Gentiana lutea root, aged four years in the ground before harvest

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Part macerated, part distilled, then blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 15–20%, low for a bitter

composition.process: Gentian takes years to mature underground and is dug with a long two-pronged fork, which is why it has never been cheap.

name: Izarra
description: The Basque country's herbal liqueur, made in green and yellow versions like Chartreuse but sweeter, with armagnac underneath and a heavy hand of local plants. Izarra means star in Basque.
funFact: The recipe was assembled in 1906 by a Basque chemist who had spent years cataloguing plants in the Pyrenees before deciding what to do with them.

serve.how: Straight and cold after a meal, or poured over crushed ice as they do in Bayonne. The yellow is the gentler of the two and the better introduction; the green is stronger and more aggressively herbal.

composition.summary: Armagnac and plant distillates blended with honey and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Armagnac

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Reportedly 32 Pyrenean plants for the yellow, 48 for the green

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Plants macerated and distilled, then blended and sweetened with honey

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak

composition.process: Honey rather than sugar syrup gives it the weight that separates it from its Alpine cousins.

name: Pineau des Charentes
description: Unfermented grape must stopped in its tracks with young cognac, so it keeps the sweetness of the fruit and gains the strength of the spirit. Legend says a Charentais grower invented it in 1589 by pouring must into a barrel he thought was empty.
funFact: It must be aged at least a year in oak before sale, and the rosé version is made the same way from red grapes.

serve.how: Serve cold as an aperitif, which is how the region drinks it, rather than after dinner. It works better than most sweet wines with foie gras or melon because the cognac keeps it from cloying.

composition.summary: Fresh grape must fortified with cognac before fermentation can start.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Unfermented must from Charentais grapes

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Cognac eau-de-vie at least one year old

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum 12 months in oak, often far longer

composition.process: Because fermentation never begins, the sugar in the grape stays in the glass.

name: Floc de Gascogne
description: Armagnac country's version of Pineau, and arguably the better drink: grape must fortified with young armagnac, which brings more grip and less polish than cognac does. Floc means bouquet of flowers in Gascon.
funFact: The appellation was only created in 1990, though Gascon farmers had been making it for their own tables for four centuries before anyone wrote it down.

serve.how: Cold, before the meal, in a small pour. The rosé is fuller and stands up to charcuterie; the white is better with melon or a slice of foie gras on toast. Do not let it sit warm, as the sweetness takes over.

composition.summary: Gascon grape must fortified with armagnac from the same estate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Unfermented must, white or red, from the Armagnac region

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Young armagnac, typically from the producer's own stock

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least ten months, in tank or oak

composition.process: Rules require the must and the armagnac to come from the same producer, which keeps it a farmhouse product.

name: Korenwijn
description: The maltiest grade of jenever, at least 51% malt wine and usually cask-rested, which puts it closer to a young whisky than to gin. This is what gin tasted like before anyone thought to strip the grain out of it.
funFact: Tradition demands the tulip glass be filled to the brim and the first sip taken with hands behind your back, bending to the glass rather than lifting it.

serve.how: Keep the bottle in the freezer and fill the glass until it domes. Take the first sip without touching it, then drink the rest slowly. A blond lager alongside makes it a kopstootje, the Dutch boilermaker.

composition.summary: Malt wine and juniper distillate blended and rested in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malt wine from rye, corn and malted barley, at least 51%

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, with restraint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still for the malt wine, then redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, commonly one to three years

composition.process: The malt wine is the point; the juniper is seasoning rather than the main event.

name: Beerenburg
description: A Frisian bitter built on juniper spirit and a fistful of gentian, bay and dried herbs. Invented by an Amsterdam spice merchant, adopted wholesale by the north, and drunk cold against weather.
funFact: Hendrik Beerenburg sold the herb mixture over the counter so people could steep their own jenever at home; the bottled version came much later.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass, taken before or after food rather than with it. In Friesland it is also drunk with hot water and sugar as a cure for whatever is going around.

composition.summary: Jenever or neutral spirit steeped with a fixed herb blend.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Juniper spirit or jenever

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, bay, juniper berry, laurel and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated rather than redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 30%

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation keeps the herbs tasting green and raw instead of polished.

name: Elixir d'Anvers
description: Antwerp's herbal liqueur, made to the same recipe since 1863 by the same family in the same building. Saffron-gold, sweet on the front, and considerably more bitter on the finish than the colour suggests.
funFact: The distillery in Antwerp has never moved and still runs a museum in the same premises where François-Xavier de Beukelaer first made it.

serve.how: Neat after dinner is standard. Belgians also pour it over vanilla ice cream, and in winter mix it with hot water as a grog. It is sweet enough that a small pour goes a long way.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit distilled with 32 plants and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 32 herbs and plants, saffron among them

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then sweetened and rested

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak before bottling

composition.process: The recipe has been held by five generations of the same family and never published.

name: Mandarine Napoléon
description: Cognac infused with Sicilian mandarin peel, softer and more perfumed than an orange liqueur. The story attaches it to Napoleon's personal chemist, which is almost certainly a marketing decision made long after the fact.
funFact: Antoine-François de Fourcroy, the chemist credited with the recipe, was a real member of Napoleon's circle, though the liqueur itself was commercialised in Brussels in 1892.

serve.glass: Snifter, or coupe in a drink
serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or over ice with soda as a long aperitif. It substitutes well for triple sec in a Margarita or Sidecar when you want the drink rounder and more floral.

composition.summary: Cognac macerated with mandarin peel and spice, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sicilian mandarin peel, plus herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and distilled, then blended into aged cognac

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested before bottling

composition.process: Mandarin peel carries a softer, sweeter oil than bitter orange, which is why this reads as perfume rather than marmalade.

name: Korn
description: German grain spirit, unaged and legally forbidden to contain anything but grain, water and yeast. No flavouring, no sweetening, no colouring. What is left is a clean spirit that tastes faintly of bread and nothing else.
funFact: Korn must be at least 32% by law, and Doppelkorn at least 38%; the rules date to a 1789 Prussian decree and have barely changed.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a tiny glass, drunk in one go with a beer to follow. In the north it is called Herrengedeck when paired with a pilsner. Ageing it in oak makes something closer to a light whisky, but that is no longer Korn.

composition.summary: Rye, wheat, barley or oats distilled to a modest strength with nothing added.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rye, wheat, barley or oats, or a blend

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, but not to full neutrality

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None permitted for the Korn designation

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 32% minimum, 38% for Doppelkorn

composition.process: Distilling below neutrality is deliberate: the grain character is the product, so stripping it out would defeat the purpose.

name: Obstler
description: The catch-all orchard brandy of southern Germany and Austria, usually apple and pear together, though the name covers whatever the trees produced. Farm-made versions are rough and honest; the good ones are as precise as any eau-de-vie.
funFact: Germany has tens of thousands of registered small distillers, most of them farms with the right to distil a fixed annual quota from their own fruit.

serve.how: Cool rather than frozen, after a heavy meal, in a small pour. Southern Germans will tell you it settles the stomach after schnitzel, and there is enough of a digestive tradition behind that to take it seriously.

composition.summary: Orchard fruit mashed, fermented and pot-distilled without added sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Apples and pears, sometimes plums or mixed orchard fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot still, usually on the farm

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Normally unaged; some rest in ash or glass

composition.process: Fruit is fermented whole on its own sugars, so a poor harvest shows up directly in the bottle.

name: Steinhäger
description: A Westphalian juniper spirit protected to the town of Steinhagen, and distinct from gin in one important way: the juniper is fermented and distilled itself rather than steeped in finished spirit. Drier, sharper and far less perfumed.
funFact: It is traditionally sold in a grey-brown stoneware crock, which is why the older bottles look more like cough medicine than a spirit.

serve.how: Freezer cold and neat, chased with a pilsner. It is a drink for cutting through fat rather than for sipping, and Westphalians serve it alongside ham rather than after it.

composition.summary: Fermented juniper berry distillate blended with grain spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain spirit plus a separate juniper berry distillate

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper alone, fermented rather than macerated

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Berries fermented and distilled, then blended and redistilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Fermenting the berries produces a rawer, greener juniper note than any maceration can.

name: Jägermeister
description: Fifty-six herbs, roots, fruits and spices macerated, filtered and rested in oak for a year before sweetening. It has spent decades being drunk cold and fast by people who have no idea it is a serious German digestive, which it is.
funFact: The name means master of the hunt, a formal German forestry title, and the stag on the label refers to the legend of Saint Hubertus.

serve.glass: Small shot glass or chilled tumbler
serve.how: The company insists on freezer temperature, and they are right: cold mutes the sweetness and lets the anise and bitter root through. Sip it rather than shoot it and it behaves like the amaro it actually is.

composition.summary: 56 botanicals macerated in alcohol and water, filtered, then oak-rested.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit and water

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 56 herbs, roots, fruits and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated over weeks, not distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: One year in oak vats before sugar and caramel are added

composition.process: Maceration in five separate batches, then a year in wood, is what turns a bitter herbal extract into something drinkable.

name: Weinbrand
description: German brandy, softer and sweeter than cognac and generally aged in smaller casks. Hugo Asbach coined the word Weinbrand in 1907 to replace cognac on German labels after the French objected, and it stuck.
funFact: Asbach also invented the brandy bean, a chocolate filled with liquid Weinbrand, which remains a fixture of German Christmas markets.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature after dinner, or in coffee with cream. German bars also serve it long with cola, which is less of a crime than it sounds given how sweet the base spirit already is.

composition.summary: Wine distillate, mostly imported, aged in Limousin oak in Germany.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine, largely from France and Italy

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum six months, quality grades far longer, in small Limousin casks

composition.process: Smaller casks mean faster wood contact, which is where the vanilla and caramel come from.

name: Danziger Goldwasser
description: A herbal liqueur suspended with flakes of genuine 22-carat gold, first made in Danzig in 1598. The gold does nothing at all to the flavour, which was rather the point when alchemists were selling it as medicine.
funFact: Gold was thought to be medicinal in the sixteenth century, so drinking flakes of it was a health measure rather than a flourish.

serve.how: Roll the bottle gently before pouring to lift the gold back into suspension, then serve cold and neat. It is worth pouring in decent light, since watching the flakes settle is most of the experience.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit distilled with spices and herbs, sweetened, with gold leaf added.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Anise, cinnamon, cardamom, citrus peel and around twenty others

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, sweetened, then gold flakes suspended

composition.process: Gold is chemically inert, so it passes through untouched and contributes nothing but the look.

name: Eierlikör
description: German egg liqueur, thicker and richer than Dutch advocaat, and served often enough with a small spoon that the spoon is sold with it. Christmas markets run on the stuff.
funFact: It is sold at Christmas markets in edible waffle cups, which solves the problem of what to do with the glass once you have drunk it.

serve.glass: Small cup, or poured over ice cream
serve.how: Cold and thick, eaten as much as drunk. Poured over vanilla ice cream it makes a passable dessert, and whisked into cream it becomes the filling for a great many German cakes.

composition.summary: Egg yolk, sugar and brandy emulsified into a thick liqueur.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Brandy or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Egg yolk, sugar, vanilla, sometimes cream

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: None; the base spirit is emulsified with yolk

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 20%, minimum 14% by EU rule

composition.process: EU law sets a minimum egg yolk content, which is what separates it legally from a cream liqueur.

name: Underberg
description: A digestive bitter sold only in single-serve 20ml bottles wrapped in straw paper, made from herbs of 43 countries and rested in Slovenian oak. There is no large bottle, and there never has been.
funFact: The straw paper wrapper was introduced in 1949 to protect the bottle from light, and the company has kept it despite it having no modern purpose.

serve.glass: Its own bottle, or a small glass
serve.how: One bottle, after a large meal, in a single go. Germans drink it straight from the bottle without ceremony. It is emphatically not a sipping amaro; the whole design is a measured dose.

composition.summary: Herbs from 43 countries macerated in neutral spirit and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Herbs and roots sourced from 43 countries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, not distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Several months in Slovenian oak

composition.process: Bottling at a fixed 20ml is a deliberate constraint: the product is a dose, not a measure.

name: Marillenbrand
description: Wachau apricot brandy, and the finest fruit distillate Austria makes. The Klosterneuburger apricots grown along that stretch of the Danube are small, intensely perfumed, and worth the premium the bottles command.
funFact: Wachau apricots have protected designation status, and the trees flower so early that a single bad frost can wipe out a year's production.

serve.how: Cool but not cold, in a glass with a narrow rim to hold the aroma. Nose it for a good while before drinking; a fine Marillenbrand smells more of ripe apricot than the fruit itself does.

composition.summary: Whole Wachau apricots fermented and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Klosterneuburger apricots from the Wachau valley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, narrow heart cut

components.label: Aging
