name: Chilcano
description: Peru's everyday pisco drink: pisco, ginger ale, lime and bitters over ice. Lighter than a Pisco Sour and far easier to make ten of.
funFact: Peru holds a national Semana del Chilcano every January; the drink descends from the 'chilcano de pescado', a fish broth once drunk as a hangover cure in the port of Chilca.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the pisco and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Dash the Angostura over the surface.
Stir once gently and garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Machu Picchu
description: Green, yellow and red in one tall glass, layered to look like the mountain at sunrise. A tourist drink Cusco has fully embraced.
funFact: It exists almost entirely for the photograph — but Cusco's bars have made it well enough for long enough that it has become a genuine local order.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of a tall glass.
Fill the glass carefully with crushed ice to hold the layers apart.
Shake the pisco with the orange juice and pour slowly over the ice.
Float the crème de menthe on top over the back of a spoon.
Serve with a straw and let the drinker mix it themselves.

name: Gin Pom
description: Ginebra San Miguel with powdered pomelo juice and ice. Cheap, sharp and the most-drunk gin serve in the world's biggest gin market.
funFact: The Philippines drinks more gin than any other country on earth, almost all of it Ginebra San Miguel — and most of that is mixed with a sachet of powdered juice costing a few pesos.

steps: Dissolve the powdered drink mix in the cold water in a pitcher.
Add the gin and stir well.
Pour over ice into tall glasses.
Serve with a calamansi wedge if you have one.

name: Weng Weng
description: Every white spirit on the shelf plus whisky, orange juice and grenadine. Named for the noise your head makes afterwards.
funFact: 'Weng weng' is Filipino for dizzy or spinning; the drink is a Boracay beach-bar institution, and most bars cap the order at two per person.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add all five spirits.
Top with orange juice and stir.
Pour the grenadine down the inside of the glass so it sinks to the bottom.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Mad Dog
description: Vodka, raspberry syrup and Tabasco layered into one shot. Sweet, then red, then suddenly very hot. Polish student legend.
funFact: 'Wściekły pies' is a staple of Polish student bars, where the layering matters: the syrup sinks, the Tabasco floats, and the burn arrives a beat after the sweetness.

steps: Pour the raspberry syrup into the bottom of a shot glass.
Layer the vodka carefully over it with a barspoon.
Dash the Tabasco on top so it sits on the surface.
Drink in one — sipping it is a mistake people only make once.

name: Tatanka
description: Bison grass vodka and cloudy apple juice. Tastes like apple pie and freshly cut hay, which is a stranger compliment than it sounds.
funFact: Also called a Szarlotka, after the Polish apple cake. Żubrówka is flavoured with a blade of bison grass from the Białowieża Forest, and each bottle traditionally contains one.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Żubrówka.
Top with cold cloudy apple juice.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice and a light dusting of cinnamon.

name: Nikita
description: Beer, pineapple, white wine and vanilla ice cream, blended. It should be a disaster. Madeira has been proving otherwise since the eighties.
funFact: Named after the Elton John song 'Nikita', which was in the charts when a Câmara de Lobos bar owner first blended it in the mid-1980s.

steps: Put the pineapple, ice cream and white wine into a blender.
Add the beer last, to control the foam.
Blend briefly — just enough to combine, or it will overflow.
Pour into a tall glass and serve with a spoon and a straw.

name: Poncha
description: Madeiran cane spirit muddled with honey and lemon using a wooden 'caralhinho'. Sweet, sharp and much stronger than it lets on.
funFact: The stirring tool — a ridged wooden stick called a caralhinho — is specific to Madeira, and the fishermen's original version was drunk as a cold remedy before going out in the morning.

steps: Put the honey and lemon juice into a small tumbler or a jug.
Work them together with a wooden stick or muddler until the honey fully dissolves.
Add the aguardente and the orange juice if using.
Stir vigorously until frothy and serve at room temperature, without ice.

name: Porto Tónico
description: White port and tonic over ice with mint. Portugal's answer to the Gin and Tonic, and arguably the better summer drink.
funFact: Port houses pushed it hard in the 2010s to sell white port, which had been the least-loved category in the Douro — it worked so well it is now the default aperitif in Porto.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the chilled white port.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once gently and garnish with a mint sprig and an orange slice.

name: Bilí
description: Vieques in a bottle: pitorro steeped for months with quenepas, cinnamon and sugar until the moonshine turns sweet, fruity and deceptively smooth.
funFact: Bilí is a Vieques speciality made with quenepas (Spanish limes) and is traditionally buried or hidden to age — families open bottles at Christmas that were sealed the previous summer.

steps: Put the peeled quenepas, cinnamon, sugar and vanilla into a large sealable jar.
Cover with the pitorro and seal tightly.
Store somewhere dark and cool for at least two months, turning the jar occasionally.
Strain into bottles, leaving the fruit behind.
Serve chilled in small measures.

name: Chichaíto
description: Two ingredients, no mercy: pitorro and anisette, shaken with ice and served cold enough to hide how strong it is.
funFact: A staple of Puerto Rican Christmas parrandas, where it is carried house to house in a bottle kept in the freezer — the sugar content stops it from freezing solid.

steps: Combine the pitorro and anisette in a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds to chill and slightly dilute.
Strain into chilled shot glasses.
Serve immediately, ice cold.

name: Coco Loco
description: Served in the coconut it was made from: rum, coconut cream and whatever tropical juice is closest to hand, blended into holiday shorthand.
funFact: The 'loco' is usually the pour — beach vendors from Luquillo to Loíza free-pour three spirits into the same coconut and stop when it looks about right.

steps: Cut the top off a young coconut and pour the water into a blender.
Add the rums, coconut cream, pineapple juice, lime and crushed ice.
Blend until smooth and slushy.
Pour back into the coconut shell and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Pineapple wedge and a paper umbrella

name: Țuică Fiartă
description: Plum brandy heated with sugar and peppercorns until it steams. Romanian winter, taken standing outside in it.
funFact: The sugar is caramelised in the pan before the țuică goes in, which is what gives it the amber colour; the peppercorns are traditional and genuinely change the finish.

steps: Melt the sugar in a small pan over low heat until it just caramelises.
Add the peppercorns and cinnamon and stir for a few seconds.
Pour in the țuică carefully — it will spit — and warm it through without boiling.
Serve hot in small heatproof glasses.

name: Sbiten
description: Honey, spices and herbs simmered together and spiked — Russia's hot drink of choice for four centuries before tea arrived and took over.
funFact: Sbiten was street food in imperial Russia, sold from insulated copper samovar-like urns carried on the back; it was displaced almost entirely by tea in the nineteenth century.

steps: Bring the water and honey to a simmer, skimming any foam that rises.
Add the ginger, cinnamon, cloves and mint and simmer for 15 minutes.
Strain out the solids.
Stir in the wine or vodka off the heat if you want it alcoholic.
Serve very hot in mugs.

name: Yorsh
description: Vodka poured into beer. Named after a spiny river fish, and about as gentle as one.
funFact: The name comes from the ruffe, a small bristly fish — Russian drinkers use it as a warning label, since the mix is notorious for arriving all at once.

steps: Pour the beer into a mug, leaving room at the top.
Add the vodka directly to the beer.
Stir once, or drop the shot glass in whole for the theatrical version.
Drink promptly.

name: Bambus
description: Red wine and cola, half and half, over ice. Beloved across the Balkans and defended fiercely by everyone who drinks it.
funFact: The Balkan bambus predates Spain's kalimotxo in local memory by decades, and the two regions have never agreed on who got there first.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the red wine.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and add a lemon slice if you want it sharper.

name: Tatratea Hot
description: Slovakia's herbal tea liqueur, served hot with honey and lemon. Comes in strengths from 22% to 72%, colour-coded by how serious you are.
funFact: The bottles are numbered by ABV — 32, 42, 52, 62, 72 — and the 72% 'Outlaw' edition exists mostly so that people can say they have had it.

steps: Put the honey and lemon slice in a warmed glass mug.
Add the hot water and stir until the honey dissolves.
Pour in the Tatratea and stir once.
Serve hot, with the lemon left in.

name: Dom Pedro
description: Vanilla ice cream blended with whisky or Amarula until it pours. On every South African dessert menu, and ordered by adults without embarrassment.
funFact: It appears on South African menus far more often than it does anywhere else on earth, and ordering one 'with Kahlúa' rather than whisky is a legitimate regional variation.

steps: Let the ice cream soften for a few minutes so it blends smoothly.
Put the ice cream, spirit and cream in a blender.
Blend briefly — you want it thick and pourable, not liquid.
Pour into a wine glass and dust with grated chocolate or nutmeg.
Serve with both a spoon and a straw.

name: Klippies en Coke
description: Klipdrift brandy and Coke, poured heavy. South Africa drinks more brandy-and-cola per head than almost anywhere, and this is why.
funFact: South African brandy is legally required to be pot-still aged at least three years for the premium grades — a rigour largely wasted on a drink that is then filled to the top with cola.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the brandy.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and add a lemon wedge if you like.

name: Rock Shandy
description: Soda water, lemonade and a hard shake of Angostura, over ice. Essentially alcohol-free, and the default order at any Southern African clubhouse.
funFact: The bitters are the only alcohol in it, in quantities small enough that it is served to children — and it is the drink that keeps Angostura relevant in a region that otherwise barely mixes cocktails.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in equal parts soda water and lemonade.
Dash the Angostura generously over the top until the drink turns pink.
Stir once and squeeze in a lemon wedge.

name: Springbokkie
description: Green over cream, in the colours of the national rugby jersey: crème de menthe under a float of Amarula. Poured in vast quantities on match day.
funFact: Amarula is made from the fruit of the marula tree, which elephants are famously — and mostly apocryphally — said to get drunk on after eating the fallen fruit.

steps: Pour the crème de menthe into a shot glass.
Float the Amarula over the back of a barspoon so it sits in a clean layer.
Serve immediately, before the layers start to bleed.
Drink in one.

name: Makgeolli
description: Unfiltered rice brew, milky and lightly fizzing, poured from the bottle into a shallow bowl. Korea's oldest drink and its most farmhouse.
funFact: Nuruk — a wild-yeast and mould starter cake — does the work that malting does for beer, breaking down the rice starch; makgeolli is traditionally drunk after farm work, and increasingly after rain, by tradition.

steps: Steam the rice and cool it to room temperature.
Mix the rice with the crumbled nuruk and the water in a clean crock.
Cover with cloth and ferment at room temperature for about a week, stirring daily.
Strain through cloth, pressing lightly — makgeolli is meant to stay cloudy.
Refrigerate, and shake the bottle before pouring into shallow bowls.

name: Somaek
description: Soju dropped into beer, in a ratio people argue about seriously. Korea's most-poured mixed drink, and the engine of the company dinner.
glassware: Beer glass and a soju shot glass
funFact: The golden ratio is contested — three parts beer to one soju is the common baseline, and there are Korean drinking games devoted entirely to pouring it correctly.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass, leaving room at the top.
Add the soju — either poured in or dropped in the shot glass whole.
Cover the top with your palm and tap the glass once on the table to mix it.
Drink promptly, while it is still fizzing.

name: Yogurt Soju
description: Soju, Yakult and lemon-lime soda. Tastes like a children's drink, disappears like one, and is not one.
funFact: Yakult has been sold in Korea since 1971 and is delivered door to door by the 'Yakult ajumma'; the cocktail is the reason Korean convenience stores stock it next to the soju.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the soju and the Yakult.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and serve immediately — it separates if it sits.

name: Agua de Valencia
description: Cava, orange juice, gin and vodka in a jug. Tastes like a Mimosa, behaves like something else entirely.
funFact: Invented at Café Madrid in Valencia in 1959, when a group of Basque regulars kept ordering 'Agua de Bilbao' — the house sparkling wine — and the barman offered them a Valencian alternative made with local oranges.

steps: Stir the sugar into the orange juice in a large jug until dissolved.
Add the gin and vodka and stir again.
Top with cold cava and stir once, gently.
Serve immediately in wine glasses over a little ice.
Make it in front of people — half the drink is the theatre of the jug.

name: Leche de Pantera
description: 'Panther's milk': gin or rum, condensed milk and cinnamon, shaken cold. Spanish Legion issue, now a Madrid dive-bar staple.
funFact: The recipe is traditionally attributed to the Spanish Legion, whose founder Millán-Astray is said to have served it to recruits — the modern Madrid version usually swaps the original brandy for gin.

steps: Add the gin, condensed milk, milk and cinnamon to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds until thick and cold.
Strain into a chilled tumbler.
Dust with more cinnamon and serve very cold.

name: Queimada
description: Orujo set alight in a clay bowl with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel while somebody reads a spell over it. Galicia does not do this ironically.
funFact: The conxuro — the incantation read while it burns — invokes the meigas, Galician witches, and asks them to leave. The ritual is old-looking but was largely written in the 1950s.

steps: Pour the orujo into a wide clay bowl and add most of the sugar, the coffee beans and the lemon peel.
Put a ladleful of orujo and the remaining sugar into a separate ladle and set it alight.
Lower the burning ladle into the bowl to ignite the whole surface.
Stir with the ladle, lifting burning liquid and pouring it back, for several minutes until the flame turns low and blue.
Cover to extinguish, then serve hot in small clay cups.

name: Rebujito
description: Manzanilla sherry lengthened with lemon-lime soda over crushed ice — the drink that keeps Seville upright through a week of Feria.
funFact: It is drunk by the jug at the Feria de Abril in Seville and the Feria del Caballo in Jerez, where the sherry comes from — and where sherry purists have made their peace with it.

steps: Fill a tall glass with crushed ice.
Pour in the cold manzanilla.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and add a mint sprig if you like.
Drink fast — it dies as the ice melts.

name: Sol y Sombra
description: 'Sun and shade': brandy and anís in equal parts, no ice. A Spanish breakfast that predates any conversation about moderation.
funFact: The name comes from the bullring, where seats are priced by whether they sit in sun or shade; the drink mixes the dark brandy and the clear anís the same way.

steps: Pour the brandy and the anís into a small tumbler.
Stir once to combine.
Serve at room temperature, without ice.
Traditionally taken standing at the bar, with coffee.

name: Vermut
description: Red vermouth on ice with a splash of soda, an olive and a slice of orange. Sunday noon in Barcelona has a drink and this is it.
funFact: 'Fer el vermut' — to do the vermouth — is a whole social occasion in Catalonia, held late on Sunday morning, and the best bars still draw their vermouth from the barrel.

steps: Fill a tumbler with ice.
Pour in the cold red vermouth.
Add a short splash of soda.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice and a skewered olive.
Serve with crisps and tinned seafood, if you are doing it properly.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a green olive

name: Arrack and Ginger Beer
description: Ceylon coconut arrack with ginger beer and lime — the island's standing highball, and better than it has any right to be.
funFact: Ceylon arrack is distilled from fermented coconut flower sap, tapped by climbers who move between palm crowns on ropes — a job with its own hereditary caste of specialists.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the arrack and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Glögg
description: Nordic mulled wine with raisins and blanched almonds waiting at the bottom of the cup — you drink it, then eat it with a spoon.
glassware: Small mug or glass with a handle
funFact: Cardamom is the marker that separates Nordic glögg from German Glühwein, and the spoon is not optional — the raisins and almonds are considered part of the serving.

steps: Warm the wine with the sugar, spices and orange peel to about 70°C and hold for 30 minutes; do not boil.
Strain out the whole spices.
Put a spoonful of raisins and almonds into the bottom of each mug.
Add the aquavit to the pot off the heat, then ladle over the raisins and almonds.
Serve hot with a small spoon.
recipe.garnish: Raisins and slivered almonds in the cup

name: Grogg
description: Swedish shorthand for spirit plus mixer, poured strong: whisky or vodka with soda or cola, and no further ceremony.
funFact: The Swedish 'grogg' descends from British naval grog — watered rum named after Admiral Vernon's grogram coat — but travelled north and lost the rum along the way.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the spirit.
Top with cold soda water or cola.
Stir once and serve, with a lemon wedge if using soda.

name: Kafi Fertig
description: Coffee with schnapps, served in a stemmed glass so you can see the colour. Swiss farmhouse fuel with a colour code all its own.
funFact: In parts of central Switzerland the strength is judged by colour: it should be dark enough that a coin dropped in the glass disappears, and no darker.

steps: Put the sugar in a small stemmed glass.
Pour in the hot coffee and stir until dissolved.
Add the schnapps and stir once more.
Serve hot, in the glass, never in a cup.

name: Boba Cocktail
description: Milk tea, rum and tapioca pearls in a shaker. Taipei's bars took the island's most famous export and put a wide straw in it.
glassware: Tall glass with a wide straw
funFact: Bubble tea was invented in Taichung in the 1980s; Taipei's cocktail bars started spiking it in the 2010s, and the brown-sugar version is now a fixture across East Asian bar menus.

steps: Cook the tapioca pearls and toss them in a little brown sugar syrup while still warm.
Spoon the pearls into the bottom of a tall glass.
Shake the rum, cooled tea, milk and remaining syrup hard with ice.
Strain over the pearls and add fresh ice.
Serve with a wide boba straw.
recipe.garnish: Brown sugar syrup streaked down the glass

name: Konyagi and Tonic
description: Tanzania's own clear spirit with tonic and lime — light, faintly sweet, and poured on every Dar es Salaam terrace at sunset.
funFact: Konyagi occupies an odd legal space — it is bottled at 35% and labelled as a spirit rather than a gin, though it drinks like a light, sweetened one.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the Konyagi and lime juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Thai Bucket
description: Thai rum, Red Bull and cola in a child's sand bucket with several straws. Structurally a punch, spiritually a warning.
funFact: Thai Red Bull — Krating Daeng — is uncarbonated, sweeter and more heavily caffeinated than the export version, which is a meaningful part of why the buckets have the reputation they do.

steps: Fill a small plastic bucket with ice.
Pour in the half-bottle of Sangsom.
Add the bottle of Thai Red Bull.
Top with cola and stir with a straw.
Share it — the bucket is designed for four straws, not one.

name: Sorrel
description: Christmas red: hibiscus calyces steeped with clove, ginger and orange peel, sweetened and cut with rum. Tart, spiced and unmistakably festive.
funFact: The sorrel plant is a hibiscus relative that fruits right at Christmas across the Caribbean, which is precisely why the drink became a December tradition from Trinidad to Jamaica.

steps: Put the sorrel, ginger, cloves and orange peel in a large heatproof jug.
Pour over the boiling water, cover, and leave to steep for at least 12 hours.
Strain out the solids and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Add the rum to taste and refrigerate.
Serve very cold over ice.

name: Boukha and Orange
description: Tunisian fig brandy over ice with fresh orange juice — dry, faintly floral, and the standard way to serve boukha long.
funFact: Boukha has been distilled from Mediterranean figs in Tunisia since the nineteenth century; unlike most fruit brandies it carries no added sugar, which is why it drinks surprisingly dry.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the boukha.
Top with fresh orange juice.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice.

name: Aslan Sütü
description: 'Lion's milk': rakı and cold water in equal parts, which turns it milky white. Sipped slowly over a long table of meze, never rushed.
funFact: The order matters: rakı first, then water, then ice — adding ice before water shocks the anise oils and leaves the drink cloudy in the wrong way. Turks call the milky effect the louche, and drinking it fast is considered poor form.

steps: Pour the rakı into a tall narrow glass, filling it about a third.
Add cold water in roughly equal measure and watch it turn opaque white.
Only now drop in one or two ice cubes.
Sip slowly alongside white cheese, melon and meze — rakı is a meal-length drink.
recipe.garnish: None — the meze is the garnish

name: Waragi and Tonic
description: Uganda's juniper-flavoured banana spirit, lengthened with tonic and lime. Sharper and drier than the gin it is usually compared to.
funFact: The name comes from 'war gin', from the colonial era; commercial Uganda Waragi is distilled from bananas or cassava and then flavoured with juniper, which makes it gin-adjacent rather than gin.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the waragi and lime juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Horilka z Pertsem
description: Ukrainian vodka steeped with chilli and honey. Sweet at the front, hot at the back, drunk cold with something salted.
funFact: It is traditionally taken with salo — cured pork fat — on dark bread, a pairing that sounds unlikely and works because the fat blunts the burn.

steps: Put the chillies and peppercorns into a bottle of horilka.
Add the honey and shake until it dissolves.
Leave to infuse for three to seven days, tasting as you go — chillies work fast.
Strain out the solids once it is hot enough for you.
Serve ice cold in shot glasses.

name: Angel Face
description: Equal parts gin, apricot brandy and calvados. Three spirits, no citrus, and a name that undersells it considerably.
funFact: It appears in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book with no story attached — one of many equal-parts drinks from that era that survive on balance alone.

steps: Add all three spirits to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an apple slice or a lemon twist.

name: Atholl Brose
description: Oatmeal steeped in water, strained, then stirred with honey, cream and whisky. A Highland recipe old enough to have won a battle.
funFact: Legend holds that the Earl of Atholl put down a Highland rebellion in 1475 by filling his enemy's well with the mixture and capturing him while he was drinking it.

steps: Soak the oatmeal in the water for at least six hours, then strain through muslin, pressing to extract the creamy liquid.
Discard the oats and stir the honey into the oat liquid until dissolved.
Whisk in the whisky.
Fold in the lightly whipped cream just before serving.
Serve chilled in small glasses; it keeps a couple of days in the fridge.

name: Black Velvet
description: Stout and champagne, poured half and half so the black sits under the gold. Invented for a funeral and never quite shook the mood.
funFact: Created at Brooks's Club in London in 1861 after Prince Albert's death, when the steward decided even the champagne should be in mourning.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the stout and the champagne well.
Pour the stout into a tall glass and let the head settle.
Pour the champagne slowly over the back of a spoon to layer it on top.
Serve immediately, while the two are still separate.

name: Buck's Fizz
description: Two parts champagne to one part orange juice — the older, stronger, more London answer to the Mimosa, and the two have been arguing ever since.
funFact: Created at the Buck's Club in Mayfair in 1921 by barman Malachy McGarry, three years before the Mimosa appeared at the Ritz Paris — the difference is the ratio, and Londoners will tell you so.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the champagne and the orange juice thoroughly.
Pour the orange juice into a flute first.
Top slowly with champagne, tilting the glass to preserve the bubbles.
Do not stir — the pour mixes it.

name: John Collins
description: The Tom Collins made with whiskey instead of gin — lemon, sugar, soda, tall and cold. The original of the family, depending who you ask.
funFact: John Collins was the head waiter at Limmer's Hotel in London in the early 1800s; the gin version took his colleague's name, and the two have been confused with each other ever since.

steps: Shake the whiskey, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Paradise
description: Gin, apricot brandy and orange juice. Simple, apricot-forward and one of the few Savoy-era drinks that needs no adjustment at all.
funFact: Apricot brandy in these recipes means an apricot liqueur, not a distilled eau-de-vie — a distinction that ruins the drink for anyone who buys the wrong bottle.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

name: Pink Gin
description: Navy strength gin stained pink with Angostura and nothing else. Two ingredients, no ice, no apology.
funFact: Angostura was issued to Royal Navy officers as a stomach remedy; mixing it into the gin ration was the medicinal excuse that turned into an institution, and Plymouth Gin still trades on the association.

steps: Dash the Angostura into a chilled coupe and roll it around to coat the inside.
Discard any excess bitters, or leave them in for a stronger version.
Stir the gin over ice for 20 seconds, or serve it neat and cold from the freezer.
Strain into the coated coupe and serve without garnish.

name: Russian Spring Punch
description: Dick Bradsell's long, fizzing sour: vodka, crème de cassis, lemon and champagne over crushed ice. Modern London's house punch.
funFact: Bradsell — who also gave the world the Espresso Martini and the Bramble — created it in the 1980s at the Soho Brasserie, and it remains the drink London bartenders make when they want to show off without saying so.

steps: Shake the vodka, cassis, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a tall glass packed with crushed ice.
Top with champagne and stir gently once.
Add more crushed ice to cap the glass and garnish with berries and a lemon slice.
recipe.garnish: Fresh berries and a lemon slice

name: Snakebite
description: Lager and cider, half and half, with a shot of blackcurrant if you want it purple. The most-refused drink in British pubs.
funFact: Many British pubs refuse to serve it, citing an urban myth about the mix being unusually intoxicating — the real reason is that it is cheap, strong and popular with students.

steps: Pour the cider into a pint glass first.
Add the lager slowly at an angle to keep the foam down.
Add a dash of blackcurrant cordial if making a Snakebite and Black.
Do not stir.

name: Snowball
description: Advocaat and lemonade with a squeeze of lime — a yellow, foamy relic of the British Christmas drinks trolley that refuses to die.
funFact: Advocaat is Dutch, but the Snowball is entirely British — a 1960s Christmas fixture that has been ironically revived so many times it is now simply back.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the advocaat and lime cordial.
Top with lemonade and stir briskly until the drink foams pale yellow.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry and, if you are committing to it, a slice of orange.

name: Treacle
description: An Old Fashioned with a float of apple juice on top. Bradsell again, and one of the few modern riffs the classicists never argued with.
funFact: Bradsell built it at the Player in Soho as a rum Old Fashioned, then floated cloudy apple juice over the top — the apple reads as freshness on the nose and disappears entirely by the second sip.

steps: Stir the rum, sugar syrup and bitters over ice until chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Float the apple juice gently over the top so it sits as a distinct layer.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Whisky Mac
description: Scotch and green ginger wine, in equal measure, no ice. The drink Scotland reaches for when the weather turns properly hostile.
funFact: Named for Colonel Hector Macdonald, and traditionally made with Stone's Ginger Wine — a British fortified ginger wine that has been made since 1740 and exists almost solely for this purpose.

steps: Pour the Scotch and the ginger wine into a small tumbler.
Stir briefly to combine.
Serve at room temperature — ice is considered a mistake.
Drink beside something warm.

name: White Lady
description: Gin, triple sec and lemon, shaken with egg white to a dense pale foam. The Sidecar's gin cousin, and quietly one of the best.
funFact: Harry MacElhone first made it with crème de menthe in 1919, then rebuilt it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929 — the second version is the one that survived.

steps: Dry-shake all the ingredients without ice for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before garnishing with a lemon twist.

name: Wibble
description: Gin, sloe gin, grapefruit and lemon — pink, brambly and named for what it does to your legs, not your speech.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it at The Player and said the name came from the fact that 'it makes you wibble, not wobble' — sloe gin was deeply unfashionable at the time and the drink helped rescue it.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Alaska
description: Gin and yellow Chartreuse, stirred cold. Two ingredients, and the Chartreuse does exactly as much work as you would expect.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book insists that 'so far as can be ascertained this delectable potion is NOT the staple diet of the Esquimaux' — which is roughly all anyone knows about the name.

steps: Combine the gin, Chartreuse and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Between the Sheets
description: A Sidecar with rum added — cognac, rum, triple sec and lemon. Prohibition-era, and it does not pretend to be gentle.
funFact: The name is usually credited to Harry MacElhone at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, though the drink appears in American sources around the same time — it is a Sidecar with the volume turned up.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and discard.

name: Bijou
description: 'Jewel': gin, green Chartreuse and sweet vermouth — diamond, emerald and ruby, in equal parts, as the name intends.
funFact: Harry Johnson's 1900 recipe explains the name directly: the gin is the diamond, the Chartreuse the emerald and the vermouth the ruby — three jewels in one glass.

steps: Combine everything in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry and a lemon twist.

name: Blue Blazer
description: Burning whisky poured between two mugs in a long arc of fire. Jerry Thomas's showpiece, and still the most dangerous thing on any menu.
funFact: Thomas performed it at the El Dorado in gold-rush San Francisco with silver mugs he had made specially; he advised practising with cold water first, which remains excellent advice.

ingredients.item: Two heatproof metal mugs with handles

steps: Warm both metal mugs. Put the whisky in one and the boiling water in the other.
Clear the area of anything flammable, then set the whisky alight.
Pour the burning whisky into the second mug, then back again, in a long steady stream — four or five passes.
Cover to extinguish the flame, stir in the sugar, and pour into a heatproof glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist. Practise with cold water before you ever light it.

name: Boilermaker
description: A shot of whiskey and a beer. Drop the shot in, or drink them side by side — the argument is older than most bars.
glassware: Beer glass and a shot glass
funFact: The name comes from the industrial workers who drank them after shifts; purists insist the shot is drunk beside the beer, not dropped into it — dropping it makes a Depth Charge.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass and let the head settle.
Pour the whiskey into a separate shot glass.
Either drink the shot and chase it with the beer, or drop the shot glass in whole.
Do not overthink it.

name: Bronx
description: Gin, both vermouths and orange juice — a Perfect Martini with juice in it. Once the third most-ordered cocktail in America.
funFact: Created at the Waldorf-Astoria around 1906 and named after the Bronx Zoo; barman Johnnie Solon said he was inspired by the strange animals people claimed to see after drinking.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

name: Brooklyn
description: The Manhattan's overlooked sibling: rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and Amer Picon. Drier, more bitter, and far harder to find.
funFact: It languished for a century largely because Amer Picon was reformulated and became unavailable in the US — the modern revival relies on substitutes like Amaro CioCiaro or Bigallet China-China.

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.

name: Cable Car
description: A spiced-rum Sidecar with a cinnamon-sugar rim, invented at the top of a San Francisco hotel and served by the thousand.
funFact: Tony Abou-Ganim built it in 1996 for the Starlight Room on the 21st floor of the Sir Francis Drake Hotel, and it became one of the few 1990s hotel-bar drinks to survive the cocktail revival with its reputation intact.

steps: Rim a coupe with lemon and cinnamon sugar, then chill it.
Shake the rum, curaçao, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Double-strain into the rimmed coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist on a cinnamon-sugar rim

name: Casino
description: Old Tom gin, maraschino, orange bitters and lemon. Sharp, floral and considerably drier than the ingredient list suggests.
funFact: Maraschino is distilled from whole Marasca cherries — stones, stems and all — which is why it tastes nutty and dry rather than like the syrup in a jar of cocktail cherries.

ingredients.item: Old Tom or London dry gin

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry and a lemon twist.

name: Eggnog
description: Eggs, cream, sugar and spirit, whisked thick and dusted with nutmeg. Every American December, and better if you make it months early.
funFact: Aged eggnog is a real practice — the alcohol sterilises the mixture, and batches left in the fridge for a year develop a smooth, almost cheese-like complexity. Food scientists have tested this and it holds up.

steps: Whisk the egg yolks with the sugar until pale and thick.
Slowly whisk in the milk and cream.
Whisk in the bourbon and rum — add the spirit gradually or the eggs will seize.
Refrigerate for at least a day; a month is better, a year is better still.
Serve cold in small cups with plenty of grated nutmeg.

name: French Connection
description: Cognac and amaretto, equal parts, over ice. Two ingredients, no dilution to speak of, and a name borrowed from a car chase.
funFact: Named after the 1971 film; it belongs to a family of two-ingredient duos — Godfather with Scotch, Godmother with vodka, French Connection with cognac — that were the whole of 1970s bartending in some hotels.

steps: Put a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Pour over the cognac and the amaretto.
Stir gently for 10 seconds.
Serve with no garnish — or a lemon twist if the amaretto is very sweet.

name: Godfather
description: Scotch and amaretto over a big cube. The smoke and the marzipan should fight, and instead they get on.
funFact: Legend attaches it to Marlon Brando and the 1972 film, which is almost certainly marketing — but Disaronno has never had any reason to correct the record.

steps: Put a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Add the Scotch and the amaretto.
Stir gently for 10 seconds to chill without over-diluting.
Serve with an orange twist if you want to lift it.

name: Golden Dream
description: Galliano, triple sec, orange juice and cream, shaken to a pale gold froth. Unapologetically of its decade.
funFact: Galliano's tall bottle was designed to stand out on a back bar and is named after an Italian hero of the Abyssinian war; the 1970s put it in almost everything, including this.

steps: Add all four ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds — the cream needs the work.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish, or dust with nutmeg.

name: Greenpoint
description: Rye, yellow Chartreuse and sweet vermouth — the Brooklyn neighbourhood series' best entry, and the one that stuck.
funFact: Milk & Honey's bartenders named a series of drinks after Brooklyn neighbourhoods — Red Hook, Greenpoint, Bensonhurst, Carroll Gardens — all built as Manhattan variations, all riffing on the near-lost Brooklyn cocktail.

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.

name: Horse's Neck
description: Bourbon and ginger ale with a lemon peel spiralled around the inside of the glass. The peel is the whole point of the name.
funFact: It began in the 1890s as an alcohol-free drink — just ginger ale and the lemon spiral. The bourbon was added later, and the version with it was for a while distinguished as a 'Horse's Neck with a kick'.

steps: Peel a lemon in one continuous spiral and hang it inside a highball glass with one end over the rim.
Fill the glass carefully with ice, holding the spiral in place against the side.
Add the bourbon and the bitters.
Top with cold ginger ale and stir once.

name: Hot Buttered Rum
description: Dark rum, spiced butter batter and boiling water. Colonial American, and the butter is not a novelty — it is the whole texture.
funFact: Colonial New England imported molasses from the Caribbean to distil its own rum, which is why a butter-and-spice rum drink became a northeastern winter tradition rather than a tropical one.

steps: Cream the softened butter with the brown sugar, spices and vanilla to make a batter.
Put a heaped spoonful of the batter in a warmed heatproof mug.
Add the rum and stir until the batter starts to melt.
Top with boiling water and stir until fully combined and glossy.
Grate nutmeg over the top.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a cinnamon stick

name: Illegal
description: Mezcal and rum with lime, falernum and agave — smoke and clove in a sour that hits harder than it reads.
funFact: It joined the IBA list in the 2020 revision, one of the first official cocktails built on mezcal — a category that barely existed outside Mexico twenty years earlier.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe, or serve over a large cube.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Jasmine
description: Gin, Campari, Cointreau and lemon — a bitter, grapefruit-pink sour that tastes far more complicated than its four ingredients.
funFact: Paul Harrington created it at a Berkeley bar in the 1990s and named it after a regular; there is no grapefruit in it, which is the drink's best trick.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Lava Flow
description: A frozen Piña Colada poured over blended strawberry so the red bleeds up through the white. Hawaii's most photographed drink.
funFact: The strawberry goes in the glass first and the colada is poured down the middle — the eruption effect only works if you pour into the centre, not down the side.

steps: Blend the strawberries with a splash of the pineapple juice until smooth, then pour into the bottom of a hurricane glass.
Rinse the blender and add the rums, coconut cream, remaining pineapple juice, banana and ice.
Blend until thick and smooth.
Pour slowly into the centre of the glass so the strawberry rises up the sides.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.

name: Little Italy
description: A Manhattan with Cynar in place of some of the vermouth. Artichoke bitterness against rye, which sounds wrong and lands beautifully.
funFact: Audrey Saunders created it at Pegu Club, and it did more than almost any other drink to make Cynar — a bitter liqueur made from artichokes — a standard American back-bar bottle.

steps: Combine the rye, vermouth and Cynar in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with brandied cherries.

name: Pisco Punch
description: Pisco, pineapple gum syrup and lemon — the drink that made gold-rush San Francisco famous, with a recipe its inventor took to the grave.
funFact: Duncan Nicol served it at the Bank Exchange saloon and refused to give up the recipe; when Prohibition closed the bar in 1920 the original formula was genuinely lost, and every modern version is a reconstruction.

steps: Shake the pisco, pineapple gum syrup, lemon juice and water with ice.
Strain into a chilled punch cup or coupe.
Garnish with a chunk of fresh pineapple.
Make a second one — the original was famous for tasting far weaker than it was.

name: Remember the Maine
description: Rye, sweet vermouth, cherry brandy and absinthe. Charles H. Baker recorded it in Havana during a revolution and told you to stir it clockwise.
funFact: Baker's original note instructs the reader to 'stir this one with a long spoon; and mind you, always in a clockwise direction' — the kind of instruction that tells you more about Baker than the drink.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Stir the rye, vermouth and Cherry Heering over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.

name: Revolver
description: Bourbon, coffee liqueur and orange bitters with a flamed orange peel. A Manhattan that drinks its coffee black.
funFact: Jon Santer created it at Bruno's in San Francisco in the early 2000s; the flamed orange peel is not decoration — the caramelised oils are what tie the coffee to the bourbon.

steps: Stir the bourbon, coffee liqueur and bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Hold a wide strip of orange peel over the glass, warm it briefly with a flame, then squeeze it through the flame to flare the oils.
Drop the peel into the drink.

name: Rob Roy
description: A Manhattan built on Scotch. The smoke changes everything, and the drink has been quietly better than its reputation for 130 years.
funFact: Created at the Waldorf Hotel in 1894 and named after an operetta about the Scottish outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor that had just opened a few blocks away.

steps: Combine the Scotch, vermouth and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry, or a lemon twist for a drier read.

name: Salty Dog
description: A Greyhound with a salted rim. The salt does not make it salty — it makes the grapefruit taste less bitter, which is the whole trick.
funFact: Salt suppresses the bitterness receptors on the tongue, which is why a salted rim makes grapefruit juice read as sweeter — the same principle behind salting a Margarita.

steps: Rim a highball glass with a grapefruit wedge and coarse salt.
Fill the glass with ice.
Pour in the spirit.
Top with fresh grapefruit juice and stir once.
Garnish with a grapefruit wedge.
recipe.garnish: Grapefruit wedge on a salted rim

name: Siesta
description: A Hemingway Daiquiri rebuilt on tequila, with Campari instead of maraschino. Grapefruit, lime and bitterness in balance.
funFact: Katie Stipe created it at Flatiron Lounge in 2006, and it became one of the first modern cocktails to convince American bartenders that Campari belonged with tequila.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.

name: Southside
description: Gin, lime, sugar and mint, shaken hard. A Mojito without the soda, or a Daiquiri with mint — either way it disappears fast.
funFact: Two stories compete: that it comes from Chicago's South Side during Prohibition, where rough gin needed mint to hide it, and that it comes from the 21 Club in New York. The New York version has better records.

steps: Put the mint leaves in the shaker and add the lime juice and syrup.
Press the mint gently with a muddler — bruise it, do not tear it.
Add the gin and ice, then shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a fresh mint leaf on top.

name: Stinger
description: Cognac and white crème de menthe, shaken hard. A nightcap so clean it was once considered acceptable at any hour.
funFact: It was the drink of the American upper class in the early twentieth century — Reginald Vanderbilt is credited with popularising it, and it appears in enough novels to count as a character trait.

steps: Add the cognac and crème de menthe to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds — the Stinger is traditionally shaken, not stirred.
Strain into a chilled coupe, or over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig if serving over ice.

name: Stone Fence
description: Rum or whiskey topped with hard cider. Ethan Allen's men reportedly drank it before taking Fort Ticonderoga, which explains a great deal.
funFact: It is one of the oldest recorded American mixed drinks, predating the word 'cocktail' — colonial New England had cider and rum in abundance and very little else to mix.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum or whiskey and the bitters.
Top with cold hard cider.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice.

name: Tom and Jerry
description: A hot eggnog batter spiked with rum and brandy, topped with boiling milk. American Christmas before eggnog took over the marketing.
funFact: Jerry Thomas claimed to have invented it, which is doubtful — but he popularised it so thoroughly that dedicated Tom and Jerry mug sets were sold across America for a century.

steps: Beat the egg whites to stiff peaks, then beat the yolks separately with the sugar and spices.
Fold the yolk mixture into the whites to make a thick batter — this keeps for days in the fridge.
Put two heaped tablespoons of batter in a warmed mug.
Add the rum and brandy and stir to loosen.
Top with hot milk, stir until foamy, and grate nutmeg over the top.

name: Tuxedo
description: A Martini with maraschino and absinthe. Dry, faintly nutty and named for the New York enclave that also named the dinner jacket.
funFact: The Tuxedo Club in Tuxedo Park gave its name to both the jacket and the drink; the cocktail is essentially a Martinez cousin that never became as famous as either.

ingredients.item: Old Tom or London dry gin

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry and a lemon twist.

name: Twelve Mile Limit
description: Rum, rye, brandy, lemon and grenadine — three spirits in one glass, named for the line where Prohibition stopped applying.
funFact: The twelve-mile limit was the boundary of US jurisdiction after 1924 — beyond it sat 'Rum Row', a floating line of ships selling legally to anyone who sailed out far enough.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Widow's Kiss
description: Calvados, Bénédictine and yellow Chartreuse with Angostura. Autumnal, herbal and considerably heavier than its delicate name suggests.
funFact: It first appears in George Kappeler's 1895 'Modern American Drinks', from the Holland House Hotel in New York — a rare nineteenth-century cocktail with no base spirit dilution at all.

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 to 30 seconds — this one needs the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry or an apple slice.

name: Medio y Medio
description: Half sparkling wine, half sweet white — Uruguay's national aperitif, poured at the Mercado del Puerto beside a plate of grilled meat.
funFact: The Roldós stall in Montevideo's Mercado del Puerto has been mixing it since 1886 and bottles its own; the ratio is exactly what the name says, and nobody there will negotiate.

steps: Chill both wines thoroughly.
Pour the sweet white wine into a wine glass first.
Top with the sparkling wine, poured slowly down the side to preserve the bubbles.
Serve immediately, without ice.

name: Guarapita
description: Rum or aguardiente loaded with passionfruit and sugar, mixed in a jug and served from a plastic bottle at the beach. Deceptively fruity.
funFact: Guarapita is Venezuelan beach and street-party currency, usually sold in recycled water bottles — the fruit hides the proof so effectively that it is known as 'the liar'.

steps: Stir the sugar into the passionfruit and orange juice until fully dissolved.
Add the rum and mix well.
Chill for at least two hours.
Serve very cold over ice, and warn people.

name: Ponche Crema
description: Venezuela's Christmas cream: eggs, milk, sugar and rum cooked into a custard-thick liqueur that coats the glass and the season.
funFact: Eliodoro González P. commercialised it in 1900 and the brand still dominates December in Venezuela, but home-made versions with a heavier rum hand remain the point of pride.

steps: Whisk the egg yolks with the condensed milk over a very low heat until slightly thickened; do not let it scramble.
Remove from the heat and whisk in the evaporated milk and vanilla.
Cool completely to room temperature.
Stir in the rum, then bottle and refrigerate overnight.
Serve chilled with nutmeg grated over the top.

name: Rượu Rắn
description: Rice wine with a snake in the bottle. Sold as a tonic, drunk as a dare, and genuinely traditional across northern Vietnam.
funFact: The ethanol denatures the venom, which is why the practice is not as dangerous as it looks — though the bottles are still confiscated at most international borders.

steps: Clean and prepare the snake thoroughly — this step is traditionally done by a specialist.
Place it in a large sealed glass jar with the herbs and ginseng.
Cover completely with rice wine and seal airtight.
Leave to infuse for several months to a year.
Serve in very small cups, at room temperature.

name: Sahti
description: Finland's living-fossil farmhouse ale: rye and juniper, strained through a hollowed spruce trough, never boiled and never hopped much. Banana, juniper and bread.
funFact: Sahti is unboiled and unfiltered, so it stays cloudy and perishable — it is one of the very few beer styles the EU has granted protected traditional status, and it barely travels.

serve.how: Pour gently into a mug and expect almost no head — sahti is nearly still, and a big foam would mean something went wrong. Serve it cool rather than cold so the banana esters and juniper resin come forward together; ice-cold sahti tastes like flat bread. Drink it fresh, within days if you can, because there is no boil and no real hop cover to protect it.

composition.summary: An unboiled rye-and-barley farmhouse ale flavoured and filtered by juniper.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a large proportion of rye, sometimes oats.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Almost none — juniper branches do the preserving and seasoning instead.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Traditionally baker's yeast, fermented warm, which is where the banana comes from.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Fresh juniper twigs and berries, used both as flavour and as the filter bed.

composition.process: The mash is lautered through juniper branches laid in a hollowed log trough, then fermented warm with baker's yeast and drunk young without boiling.

name: Gotlandsdricka
description: Sahti's Swedish cousin from the island of Gotland: smoked malt, juniper and a farmhouse yeast character, brewed at home for centuries and almost nowhere else.
funFact: Gotland farmers brewed it for holidays and haymaking under a customary right that survived Sweden's alcohol monopoly; the recipes stayed inside families rather than breweries.

serve.how: Serve it cool and still, in a mug rather than a glass, and expect a hazy amber pour with very little foam. Let it sit a minute so the smoke settles behind the juniper instead of dominating it. Like sahti it is meant to be drunk young and local, so treat a bottle as perishable rather than something to age.

composition.summary: A smoked, juniper-infused farmhouse ale from Gotland, fermented warm with a farmhouse yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Home-smoked barley malt, often with rye and a little honey.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Sparing — juniper carries most of the seasoning.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Farmhouse or baker's yeast worked warm, giving spice and stone fruit.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Juniper branches for both flavour and lautering.

composition.process: Malt is dried over an open wood fire, mashed and strained through juniper, then fermented warm and served within weeks.

name: Maltøl
description: Norwegian farmhouse ale fermented with kveik — a hardy house yeast pitched blisteringly hot that finishes clean in two days and tastes of orange and stone fruit.
funFact: Kveik yeast was kept alive on dried wooden rings passed down through Norwegian farm families for generations; when brewers rediscovered it in the 2010s it changed brewing worldwide, because it ferments cleanly at 35–40°C.

serve.how: Pour into a wide vessel and give it a moment — the aroma is the point, and kveik throws citrus and stone fruit that a narrow glass hides. Serve cool rather than cold, since the warmth of the ferment leaves a rounded malt body that goes flat and thin under refrigeration. Traditionally it is passed around a shared bowl rather than poured into individual glasses.

composition.summary: A strong, juniper-tinged farmhouse ale fermented very warm with heritage kveik yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale barley malt, often with a caramelised or long-boiled wort for colour.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Minimal, with juniper infusion standing in for much of the character.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Kveik — a heritage farmhouse culture pitched at 35–40°C that finishes in days.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Juniper infusion water used for mashing and sparging.

composition.process: Mashed with juniper infusion, sometimes with a long caramelising boil, then fermented hot with kveik and drunk fresh.

name: Koduõlu
description: Estonian island home-brew: unboiled, juniper-strained and fermented warm, closer to liquid rye bread than to anything on a modern taplist.
funFact: On Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, koduõlu was brewed for weddings and midsummer by designated village brewers, and the tradition survived the Soviet period largely because it was never commercial.

serve.how: Serve cool and flat in a mug — carbonation is minimal and a head is not expected. Give it a few minutes out of the cold so the bready malt and juniper open up; too cold and all you get is sourness. It is brewed to be drunk within days of being made, so freshness matters more than any serving detail.

composition.summary: An unboiled Estonian farmhouse ale strained through juniper and fermented warm.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with rye, often home-malted.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Very low, sometimes none at all.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Farmhouse or baker's yeast, warm-fermented for banana and spice.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Juniper branches in the lauter and juniper water in the mash.

composition.process: Mashed, strained through juniper without boiling, fermented warm for a couple of days and served young.

name: Kaimiškas
description: Lithuania's village farmhouse beer: unfiltered, raw, and fermented with a house yeast that leaves it honeyed and faintly tart. The northern Biržai region is its heartland.
funFact: Lithuanian farmhouse brewing survived unbroken through the twentieth century, which makes it one of the few living raw-ale traditions in Europe; Biržai alone has a cluster of legally operating village breweries.

serve.how: Pour into a plain glass and expect haze and a soft, low carbonation. Serve cool but not cold so the honeyed malt and the faint lactic edge stay in balance. These beers are raw — never boiled — so drink them fresh and do not expect the shelf stability of a modern lager.

composition.summary: A raw, unboiled Lithuanian village ale fermented with a local farmhouse yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale barley malt, often with a portion of unmalted grain.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low, boiled separately as a tea and added rather than boiled in the wort.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Regional farmhouse strains that finish honeyed and lightly tart.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Nothing beyond the grain — this is a deliberately plain beer.

composition.process: The wort is not boiled; hops are added as a separate infusion, and fermentation runs warm with a house culture before the beer is served young.

name: Keptinis
description: Lithuanian baked beer: the mash is shaped into loaves, baked in a bread oven until dark, then brewed. Tastes of crust, caramel and smoke without any smoked malt.
funFact: The baking step replaces a kiln — the mash literally goes into the oven as loaves before being returned to water, which is why keptinis tastes roasted despite using pale malt.

serve.how: Serve cool in a mug so the bread-crust aroma comes off the surface. Expect a dark, hazy beer with modest carbonation and a long toasty finish. It rewards slow drinking at cellar temperature; cold suppresses exactly the baked-crust character that makes it worth brewing this way.

composition.summary: A farmhouse ale whose mash is baked into loaves before brewing, giving deep crust flavour.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale barley malt, transformed by baking rather than by kilning.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low, added as an infusion in the farmhouse manner.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lithuanian farmhouse yeast, warm-fermented.

components.label: Other
components.detail: The oven itself — the baking step is the defining ingredient.

composition.process: The mash is formed into loaves and baked until dark, then broken back into hot water, lautered, and fermented warm without a conventional boil.

name: Czech Amber Lager
description: Polotmavé — the 'half-dark' lager sitting between Czech pale and Czech dark. Caramel and Saaz hops, decoction-rich, and almost unknown outside Bohemia.
funFact: Czech beer law grades lagers by original gravity rather than colour or strength, and polotmavé is a recognised category in its own right — a distinction most brewing countries never made.

serve.how: Pour hard down the middle to raise a thick, creamy head — Czech service treats foam as part of the drink, not a byproduct. Serve a touch warmer than a mass-market lager so the caramel malt and the peppery Saaz character both register. If you can get it on a side-pull tap, order it with a dense wet foam cap and drink through it.

composition.summary: A decoction-mashed amber lager balancing caramel malt against Czech Saaz hops.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Bohemian floor-malted barley with caramel and Munich malts.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Saaz, in generous late additions for spice rather than bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Czech lager yeast, fermented cold and lagered for weeks.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Extremely soft Bohemian water, which is why the bitterness lands round.

composition.process: Double or triple decoction mashing builds the malt depth, followed by cold fermentation and a long cold lagering.

name: Kvass
description: Fermented rye bread, barely alcoholic, sold from street tankers all summer. Sour, sweet and bready — a soft drink by law and a beer by method.
funFact: Kvass is classified as a soft drink across most of Eastern Europe because it usually finishes under 1.2% ABV, which is how it stayed legal and ubiquitous through every temperance campaign.

serve.how: Serve very cold in a tall glass, straight from the fridge or the tanker. Expect a hazy brown pour with a fine, short-lived foam and a distinctly sour-sweet bread aroma. Drink it fast on a hot day — it is a thirst-quencher rather than a sipper, and it flattens quickly once poured.

composition.summary: A low-alcohol lactic ferment of rye bread and water, sweetened and drunk young.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Rye bread or rye malt, often toasted dark before steeping.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: None.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: A mixed yeast and lactic culture that leaves it sour and barely alcoholic.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Sugar or raisins to feed the ferment and round the finish.

composition.process: Toasted rye bread is steeped, sweetened and fermented briefly with a mixed culture, then chilled and drunk within days.

name: Belgian Amber Ale
description: Antwerp's house beer: copper-coloured, lightly fruity and built for the second and third glass. Ordered by the glass shape rather than the name.
funFact: In Antwerp you order it by asking for a 'bolleke' — the round stemmed glass — rather than by the brewery's name, which is one of the few places a glass has become the name of the drink.

serve.how: Serve in a round stemmed glass, filled to leave a proper two fingers of foam, and drink it cool rather than cold. The malt is the point: toasted and biscuity with just enough hop to keep it moving. It is a session beer by Belgian standards, so pour it with the expectation of ordering another rather than contemplating one.

composition.summary: A copper Belgian ale balancing toasted malt against a restrained ale-yeast fruitiness.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale and Vienna malts with a touch of caramel for copper colour.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Continental hops at modest, balancing levels.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: A Belgian ale strain kept deliberately restrained — fruit, not spice.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Nothing — this is a plain beer by Belgian standards.

composition.process: Warm-fermented with a house Belgian strain and conditioned cool so the malt stays forward.

name: Bokbier
description: The Dutch autumn bock: dark, malty and released each October, when the whole country's breweries put one out at once.
funFact: Dutch bokbier is a seasonal event rather than a year-round style — the Bokbierfestival in Amsterdam exists to taste the year's releases side by side, and most disappear by December.

serve.how: Serve cool rather than cold, in a tulip that holds the malt aroma. Pour to a modest head and give it a few minutes; the raisin and toast notes need a little warmth to separate from the alcohol. It is an autumn beer by design and pairs with the heavier food of that season rather than anything light.

composition.summary: A dark, malt-forward seasonal lager brewed to a bock strength.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Munich and caramel malts over a pale base for depth and colour.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low, present only to keep the malt from cloying.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast, cold-fermented and lagered.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Seasonal release — traditionally brewed for autumn only.

composition.process: Cold-fermented on a heavy Munich-and-caramel grist, then lagered for weeks before an autumn release.

name: Bière Bretonne
description: Brittany's revived brewing tradition: often buckwheat-inflected, sometimes seaweed-salted, and always defined against the cider the region is better known for.
funFact: Breton brewing was effectively extinct by the 1970s and was rebuilt from scratch in the 1980s as part of the wider Breton cultural revival — the beers carry Breton-language names as a deliberate political statement.

serve.how: Serve cool in a wide glass so the buckwheat and toasted character can open. Expect an amber to dark pour with a soft, bready body rather than a crisp one. It suits the region's food directly — buckwheat galettes and shellfish — and drinks better alongside a meal than on its own.

composition.summary: A revived regional French ale often built on buckwheat alongside barley malt.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a proportion of buckwheat, the regional grain.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Continental, moderate and herbal rather than citric.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast fermented warm for a soft, bready profile.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Occasionally seaweed or salt, reflecting the coastal setting.

composition.process: Warm ale fermentation on a mixed barley-and-buckwheat grist, conditioned briefly and sold regionally.

name: Bia Hơi
description: Vietnam's fresh draught: brewed daily, delivered in kegs by moped, drunk on a plastic stool by the afternoon. Unpasteurised, barely carbonated, cheap as water.
funFact: Bia hơi has no shelf life at all — it is brewed, delivered and drunk within about 24 hours, which is why it exists only in Vietnam and why every street corner has its own supplier.

serve.how: Serve it very cold, and do not be alarmed when ice goes in the glass — that is the local custom and the beer is brewed light enough to take it. Pour into a plain glass with no expectation of head. Drink it the day it was made; there is no pasteurisation, no filtration and no attempt at stability, which is exactly the trade-off that makes it taste fresh.

composition.summary: An unpasteurised, low-strength draught lager brewed for immediate consumption.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt cut generously with rice for lightness.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Minimal — just enough to keep it from tasting flabby.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: A fast lager strain, fermented and shipped within days.

components.label: Other
components.detail: No pasteurisation and no filtration, which is the defining choice.

composition.process: Fermented quickly, kegged unpasteurised and delivered the same day to be drunk before it can stale.

name: Happoshu
description: Japan's tax-engineered beer: deliberately brewed below the malt threshold that triggers the higher beer duty. A category invented by accountants and perfected by brewers.
funFact: Japanese liquor tax scales with malt content, so brewers reformulated below 67% malt to sell cheaper — the government kept lowering the bracket, and brewers kept reformulating, producing a genuine arms race in beer law.

serve.how: Serve very cold in a tall, narrow glass to hold what head there is. Pour with a bit of height to build foam, because the reduced malt gives a thinner body that benefits from the texture. It is engineered for refreshment rather than complexity, so drink it cold and fast alongside food rather than contemplating it.

composition.summary: A low-malt beer-like beverage formulated to sit under Japan's malt-based tax threshold.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Under the legal malt threshold, supplemented with barley, corn or pea protein.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Light, clean and restrained.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Standard Japanese lager yeast, fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Adjuncts chosen as much for tax law as for flavour.

composition.process: Brewed as a lager but with the malt bill kept deliberately below the taxable percentage, then fermented cold and filtered bright.

name: Filipino Pale Pilsen
description: A deep-golden, all-malt pilsen with more bitterness than most tropical lagers dare — the Philippines' national beer since 1890 and still poured in stubby brown bottles.
funFact: San Miguel began brewing it in 1890 under a royal grant from Spain, making it the first brewery in Southeast Asia — the Philippine company later ended up owning the Spanish brand that named it.

serve.how: Serve cold from the bottle into a small glass, refilling often so it never warms — the Filipino habit of sharing one bottle around a table of small glasses exists for exactly that reason. Expect a firmer, drier bitterness than a typical tropical lager. It stands up to fried and vinegary food better than lighter lagers do.

composition.summary: An all-malt pale lager with assertive hopping, brewed in the Philippines since 1890.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: All barley malt, with no rice or corn adjunct.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Noble-style hopping at a level that reads genuinely bitter.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast fermented cool and conditioned.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Nothing — the absence of adjunct is the point of the style.

composition.process: A conventional cold lager fermentation, distinguished by an all-malt grist and a bitterness level unusual for the tropics.

name: Lion Stout
description: A full-strength tropical stout brewed at altitude in Sri Lanka and once dispensed from wooden casks in Kandy. Coffee, liquorice and dark fruit at eight percent.
funFact: Sri Lanka's stout tradition is a colonial inheritance that outlived its origin — Lion Stout was long served hand-pumped from wooden casks in hill-country pubs, a serving method Britain itself had largely abandoned.

serve.how: Serve cool rather than cold — at fridge temperature the coffee and dark fruit shut down completely. Pour into a snifter or a half-pint and give it ten minutes to open. At eight percent it is a sipping beer despite the tropical climate it was brewed for, and it takes sweet and spiced food better than it takes anything delicate.

composition.summary: A strong tropical stout built on roasted barley and dark crystal malt.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with roasted barley, chocolate and crystal malts.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Enough to balance a heavy dark grist, no more.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast fermented warm in a tropical climate.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Historically wooden cask conditioning, now largely bottled.

composition.process: Warm ale fermentation on a heavily roasted grist, conditioned to soften the roast into coffee and dried fruit.

name: Indian Strong Beer
description: India's dominant beer category: a high-strength lager built for maximum effect per rupee, sold in 650ml bottles and drunk very cold.
funFact: Strong beer accounts for the large majority of Indian beer sales — state excise structures and pricing make a 7–8% bottle better value than a 5% one, which is why the mild lagers barely sell.

serve.how: Serve extremely cold in a tall glass — this is a style that is helped rather than harmed by low temperature, since chilling mutes the alcohol and the sweetness. Pour into a chilled glass and refill from the large bottle as you go. Drink it with heavily spiced food, where its residual sweetness works as a counterweight to chilli heat.

composition.summary: A high-gravity pale lager brewed for strength, with adjuncts keeping the body drinkable.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a large adjunct fraction of rice or maize.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low — bitterness is not the selling point.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast pushed to a high final alcohol.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Adjuncts that raise strength without adding heaviness.

composition.process: A high-gravity cold fermentation with substantial adjunct, filtered bright and bottled at strength.

name: Chang
description: Himalayan grain beer of millet, barley or rice, fermented in a tub and drunk warm at altitude. Sour, cloudy and served with a wooden ladle.
funFact: At Himalayan altitude chang is drunk warm rather than cold, and often topped repeatedly with hot water from the same grain — the same practice as Nepali tongba, of which chang is the wider family.

serve.how: Serve warm rather than chilled — this is a cold-climate beer and refrigeration makes no sense at four thousand metres. Ladle it cloudy from the vessel, sediment and all. Expect a sour, bready ferment rather than anything crisp, and treat it as food as much as drink; it is calorie-dense by design.

composition.summary: A warm-served Himalayan grain beer fermented with a wild starter cake.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Millet, barley or rice, cooked rather than malted in the European sense.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: None.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: A dried starter cake carrying both yeast and mould cultures.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Hot water added repeatedly to the same grain bed.

composition.process: Cooked grain is inoculated with a starter cake, fermented for several days in a covered tub, then served warm and cloudy.

name: Chinese Rice Lager
description: The best-selling beer style on earth by volume, and almost nobody outside China thinks about it: pale, light-bodied, rice-heavy and brewed for drinking with food.
funFact: Snow, brewed in China, sells more volume than any other beer brand in the world — largely unknown outside the country because virtually all of it is drunk domestically.

serve.how: Serve cold in a small glass and refill often — Chinese table service pours small measures for repeated toasts rather than a single large glass. Expect very light body, low bitterness and a clean finish. It is engineered to sit under strongly flavoured food rather than compete with it, which is exactly what it does well.

composition.summary: A very light pale lager built on a large proportion of rice adjunct.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a substantial rice fraction for lightness.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Very low — bitterness is minimised deliberately.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean lager yeast, cold-fermented and filtered bright.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Rice, which thins the body and lightens the colour.

composition.process: Cold fermentation on a rice-heavy grist, filtered bright and pasteurised for a light, neutral beer.

name: Umqombothi
description: Sorghum and maize beer, thick and porridge-like, brewed at home for ceremonies. Drunk from a shared clay pot passed clockwise.
funFact: Umqombothi is central to Xhosa and Zulu ceremony — brewing it is how ancestors are honoured at weddings and funerals, so the beer is a ritual object as much as a drink.

serve.how: Serve at room temperature from a communal clay pot, never chilled and never individually glassed. Stir before serving, since the solids settle fast and the texture is part of it — this is a beer you can almost eat. Protocol matters: the pot is passed in one direction and the brewer or elder drinks first.

composition.summary: A thick, sour sorghum-and-maize beer fermented with wild lactic cultures.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Sorghum malt with unmalted maize meal.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: None.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Wild yeast alongside lactic bacteria, giving a yoghurt-like sourness.

components.label: Other
components.detail: The beer is served unfiltered, with the grain solids still suspended.

composition.process: Maize meal and sorghum malt are cooked, soured overnight, boiled and then fermented for a day or two before being drunk immediately, still actively fermenting.

name: Tella
description: Ethiopia's home-brewed beer, made with gesho instead of hops and often flavoured by the smoked gourd it ferments in. Smoky, sour and served in a flask.
funFact: Gesho — the same buckthorn that bitters tej honey wine — stands in for hops, and the fermenting vessel is often smoked with olive wood, which is where the beer's signature smokiness comes from.

serve.how: Serve cool or at ambient temperature in a flask or plain glass, cloudy and unfiltered. Expect smoke on the nose before anything else, then a dry, grainy sourness. It is a house beer rather than a bar beer, so treat variation between batches as the point rather than a fault.

composition.summary: A smoky, gesho-bittered grain beer fermented in a smoke-cured vessel.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley, often with teff, sorghum or maize.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: None — gesho, a native buckthorn, provides the bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Wild fermentation from the vessel and the environment.

components.label: Other
