description: Ginger beer and ginger ale over lime and Angostura, with an optional shot of gin. The Hong Kong club drink, and the city's answer to the Rock Shandy.
funFact: It is the standard order at Hong Kong's colonial-era clubs and rugby sevens, served alcohol-free by default with the gin added only if you ask for it 'with a kick'.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the lime juice and the Angostura, then the gin if you are using it.
Pour in equal measures of ginger beer and ginger ale.
Stir once to bring the bitters through.
Garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Baijiu Sour
description: Baijiu shaken with citrus, honey and egg white — Shanghai's project to make the world's best-selling spirit approachable to outsiders.
funFact: Baijiu outsells whisky, vodka and rum combined by volume, yet almost none of it leaves China — Shanghai's bar scene spent the 2010s working out how to mix it for people who did not grow up with it.

steps: Dry-shake the baijiu, lemon juice, honey syrup and egg white for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dash the bitters across the foam and draw a pattern through them.
Serve immediately.

name: Cynar Spritz
description: The spritz for people who find Aperol too sweet: artichoke amaro, prosecco and soda, darker and considerably more bitter.
funFact: Cynar is made from thirteen botanicals including artichoke leaves, and in the Veneto it is drunk as a spritz far more often than it is drunk neat.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the Cynar, then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Stir once, gently, to combine without killing the bubbles.
Garnish with an orange slice and an olive if you are in the Veneto.

name: Select Spritz
description: Venice's own spritz, made with Select rather than Aperol — deeper red, more bitter, and the local order since 1920.
funFact: Select was created in Venice in 1920 and remains the city's default spritz base; ordering an Aperol spritz in a Venetian bacaro marks you out immediately as being from elsewhere.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the Select and then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir once gently.
Garnish with a green olive — not an orange slice, which is the Padova style.

name: Puccini
description: Prosecco over fresh mandarin juice — the winter member of Harry's Bar's painter-and-composer family.
funFact: Harry's Bar named its sparkling drinks after Venetian artists and composers, and made each with whatever fruit was in season — the Puccini belongs to mandarin season in midwinter.

steps: Squeeze fresh mandarins and strain the juice; chill it thoroughly.
Pour the cold juice into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco, stirring gently with a bar spoon as you pour.
Serve immediately, with no garnish.

name: Tintoretto
description: Pomegranate and prosecco — the deepest red of the Harry's Bar family, named for the painter who filled the Scuola di San Rocco.
funFact: Tintoretto spent over twenty years decorating the Scuola Grande di San Rocco, often working for nothing to keep rivals out — a level of commitment the drink does not attempt to match.

steps: Juice fresh pomegranate and strain out the solids.
Chill the juice thoroughly before use.
Pour the juice into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco and stir once with a bar spoon.
Garnish with a few pomegranate seeds.

name: Carajillo 43
description: Licor 43 shaken over espresso until it foams — Mexico's after-dinner drink, and ordered in vast quantities across the country.
funFact: Spain's carajillo is coffee with brandy or rum; Mexico rebuilt it around Licor 43 and shakes it cold, which is now so dominant that the Spanish original is barely known there.

ingredients.amount: cubed, plus one large cube to serve

steps: Pull a fresh espresso and let it cool for a few seconds.
Add the Licor 43 and espresso to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds until a thick crema forms.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Serve immediately, while the foam holds.

name: Mastiha Spritz
description: Chios mastiha with soda and citrus — resinous, pine-fresh and made from the tears of a tree that grows nowhere else on earth.
funFact: Mastic resin is harvested only in southern Chios — attempts to grow the trees productively elsewhere have consistently failed — and the villages that farm it are collectively called the Mastichochoria.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the mastiha and the lemon juice.
Pour in the prosecco, then top with soda water.
Stir once gently.
Garnish with a lemon twist and a sprig of thyme.

name: Herrengedeck
description: A beer with a glass of sparkling wine beside it — 'the gentlemen's set menu', and a genuine Berlin tradition rather than a joke.
glassware: Beer glass and a sekt flute
funFact: In the West it means beer and sekt; in the former East it usually meant beer and a shot of clear spirit, and Berliners will still tell you which version their side of the city drank.

steps: Pour the pilsner into a beer glass and let the head settle.
Pour the chilled sekt into a separate small flute.
Serve the two side by side, not mixed.
Alternate between them — the sekt resets the palate between mouthfuls of beer.

name: Cubanito
description: Havana's Bloody Mary: rum instead of vodka, with lime, Worcestershire and a heavy hand of hot sauce.
funFact: Cuba's answer to the Bloody Mary predates most of the vodka versions, for the simple reason that Havana had excellent rum and almost no vodka.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the rum, lime juice, Worcestershire and hot sauce.
Top with tomato juice and season with salt and pepper.
Roll the drink between two tins rather than shaking, to mix without frothing.
Garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Grzaniec
description: Mulled beer or wine with honey, cloves and ginger — Polish winter, served in mountain shelters and Christmas markets alike.
funFact: The beer version — grzane piwo — is the older of the two, and mulling beer was standard across northern Europe long before mulled wine became the Christmas default.

steps: Warm the beer or wine gently with the spices and orange peel — never boil it.
Hold at about 70°C for ten minutes so the spices infuse.
Stir in the honey until fully dissolved.
Strain into a heatproof mug.
Serve hot with a cinnamon stick.

name: Almdudler Spritzer
description: White wine with Almdudler, the Alpine herb soda that Austria treats as a national institution.
funFact: Almdudler has been made since 1957 from 32 Alpine herbs and is so entrenched that Austrians describe it as the country's second national drink after beer.

steps: Chill both the wine and the Almdudler well.
Pour the wine into a tall glass.
Top with the Almdudler.
Stir once, gently, and serve without ice in the Austrian manner.

name: Dutch Mule
description: Jenever with ginger beer and lime — the mule format handed to the malty grandfather of gin, which changes it entirely.
funFact: Jenever is distilled from malt wine and tastes closer to a light whisky than to London dry gin, which is why it holds up against ginger where gin can disappear.

steps: Fill a copper mug or highball with ice.
Add the jenever and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Irish Mule
description: Irish whiskey with ginger beer and lime. The mule's gentlest branch, and the one that goes down fastest.
funFact: Irish whiskey's triple distillation leaves it lighter and smoother than Scotch or bourbon, which is exactly why it disappears into ginger beer so easily.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the Irish whiskey and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge and a mint sprig.

name: Sima
description: Finnish spring mead: lemon, sugar and yeast fermented for a couple of days and bottled with raisins that float when it is ready.
funFact: The raisins are a timer: a few are dropped into each bottle, and when they rise to the surface the fermentation has produced enough carbonation to drink.

steps: Boil the water with both sugars and the lemon slices, then cool to lukewarm.
Stir in the yeast and leave covered at room temperature overnight.
Bottle, adding a teaspoon of sugar and a few raisins to each bottle.
Leave at room temperature until the raisins float, usually two to three days.
Refrigerate and drink within a week, at Vappu if you are doing it properly.
recipe.garnish: The floating raisins and a lemon slice

name: Medovukha
description: Honey fermented with water and spices — an East Slavic drink older than distillation, lighter and quicker than true mead.
funFact: Traditional medovukha was fermented for decades; the boiled quick version was developed in the fifteenth century because nobody wanted to wait twenty years for a drink.

steps: Boil the water and honey together, skimming the foam that rises.
Add the spices and hops, simmer briefly, then cool to lukewarm.
Pitch the yeast and ferment in a covered vessel for about a week.
Strain and bottle, then refrigerate for several days to carbonate lightly.
Serve cool in ceramic mugs.

name: Uvita
description: Sweet red wine with grape must and spices, warmed and drunk at winter festivals along the Uruguayan coast.
funFact: Uruguay drinks more wine per head than any other country in the Americas, most of it Tannat, and its winter street festivals run on warmed sweet wine rather than beer.

steps: Combine the wine, must, sugar and spices in a pan.
Warm gently to about 65°C without boiling.
Hold for fifteen minutes so the spices infuse.
Strain into small glasses.
Serve warm, with the orange peel.

name: Íslenskur Kaffi
description: Strong coffee with brennivín and cream — the Icelandic answer to Irish coffee, with caraway in place of the sweetness.
funFact: Iceland drinks more coffee per head than almost anywhere on earth, and brennivín's caraway edge makes for a markedly drier coffee drink than the Irish version.

steps: Warm a glass mug and add the sugar.
Pour in the hot coffee and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the brennivín and stir once.
Float lightly whipped cream over the back of a spoon.
Drink through the cream without stirring.

name: Cà Phê Trứng Rum
description: Hanoi egg coffee with rum stirred through — egg yolk whipped with condensed milk into a meringue that sits on the coffee like a custard.
glassware: Small glass in a bowl of hot water
funFact: Egg coffee was invented in 1946 when a milk shortage in Hanoi led a Metropole bartender to whip egg yolk as a substitute; the café his family still runs serves it in glasses set in hot water.

steps: Brew strong Vietnamese coffee with a phin filter and keep it hot.
Whisk the egg yolk with the condensed milk until pale, thick and roughly tripled in volume.
Stir the rum into the hot coffee in a small glass.
Spoon the egg foam over the top so it floats as a distinct layer.
Stand the glass in a bowl of hot water and serve with a small spoon.

name: Nam Manao Soda
description: Thai rum with fresh lime soda and a pinch of salt — the format street vendors have sold for decades, given a measure of Sangsom.
funFact: The salt is not optional in Thai citrus drinks — it suppresses bitterness and lifts sweetness, which is why nam manao tastes rounder than a plain lime soda.

steps: Stir the lime juice, sugar syrup and salt together until the salt dissolves.
Fill a tall glass with ice and add the rum.
Pour in the lime mixture.
Top with cold soda water and stir once.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Palm Wine Punch
description: Fresh palm wine lengthened with citrus, ginger and a little gin — the village drink dressed for a Lagos party.
funFact: Palm wine ferments so fast that it changes character between morning and evening, which is why punches built on it are mixed to order rather than made ahead.

steps: Stir the ginger juice, lime juice and honey syrup together in a jug.
Add the gin and stir again.
Pour in the fresh palm wine last and stir gently once.
Serve over ice, immediately — it keeps fermenting in the glass.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Tej Spritz
description: Ethiopian honey wine lengthened with soda and citrus — the berele flask reimagined for a rooftop bar.
funFact: Gesho, the buckthorn that bitters tej, plays the same role hops play in beer — which is why tej takes to a spritz format better than most honey wines would.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the tej, lemon juice and honey syrup.
Top with soda water.
Stir once gently to combine.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.

name: Ceylon Arrack Sour
description: Coconut arrack shaken with lime, jaggery and egg white — the island's spirit given the sour treatment.
funFact: Jaggery — unrefined palm sugar — is the traditional sweetener here rather than cane sugar, and it gives the drink a smoky, caramel depth that simple syrup cannot.

steps: Dry-shake the arrack, lime juice, jaggery syrup and egg white for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dash the bitters over the foam.
Serve immediately.

name: Chacha Sour
description: Georgian grape marc spirit with lemon, honey and tarragon — the Caucasus answer to a pisco sour.
funFact: Tarragon is a defining Georgian flavour, most famously in the bright green tarkhuna soda, and it turns up in the country's modern bar scene as readily as mint does elsewhere.

steps: Press two tarragon sprigs gently in the shaker with the honey syrup.
Add the chacha, lemon juice and ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a fresh tarragon sprig.

name: Moroccan Mint Cooler
description: Strong green tea with spearmint, sugar and a measure of fig brandy, served long over ice for the heat of the afternoon.
funFact: Moroccan mint tea is poured from a height to aerate it and build a foam head, a technique the cold version keeps purely because the tea tastes flat without it.

steps: Brew strong green tea with a generous handful of spearmint and cool it completely.
Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the fig brandy, sugar syrup and lemon juice.
Top with the cold mint tea, pouring from a height to aerate it.
Garnish with a large mint sprig.

name: Masala Chai Toddy
description: Spiced milk tea with dark rum stirred in — the roadside chai format given a winter measure.
funFact: Indian chai is boiled rather than steeped — tea, milk, sugar and spice all go into the pan together, which is why it tastes nothing like tea with milk added afterwards.

steps: Boil the water with the ginger, cardamom and sugar for two minutes.
Add the tea leaves and boil for another minute.
Pour in the milk and bring back to a boil, then simmer briefly.
Strain into a glass and stir in the rum off the heat.
Serve very hot.

name: Caju Amigo
description: Cachaça and cashew fruit juice — a two-ingredient northeastern staple made from the fruit the cashew nut hangs beneath.
funFact: The cashew nut grows on the outside of the cashew apple, a soft astringent fruit that is too perishable to export — which is why almost nobody outside Brazil has tasted its juice.

steps: Combine the cachaça and cashew juice in a small glass.
Stir briefly to combine.
Serve at room temperature, or over a single ice cube if the day is hot.
Drink in one or two mouthfuls, as a between-meal pick-me-up.

name: Vermut Torrontés
description: Argentine vermouth over ice with soda and an orange slice — the aperitivo hour that Italian immigrants brought and Argentina kept.
funFact: Argentina's vermouth tradition arrived with mass Italian immigration and nearly disappeared in the twentieth century; a wave of small Mendoza producers rebuilt it from the 2010s onward.

steps: Fill a tumbler with ice.
Pour in the cold vermouth.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice and skewered olives.
Serve with something salty alongside.

name: Birra Korça
description: American Lager from Albania.
funFact: One of 949 beers in this atlas brewed to the American Lager style, across 146 countries.

serve.how: Serve it ice cold with a fast center pour into a frosted or well-chilled pint glass, building a short-lived white head and plenty of carbonic sparkle. Drink it promptly — its crisp, light-grain character is best in the first cold minutes and dullest once warm. Don't overthink it: this is the beer of stadiums and coolers, engineered for effortless refreshment.

composition.summary: Base malt cut heavily with corn or rice, barely hopped, fermented cold and filtered.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Six-row barley malt as the enzyme engine, kept very pale.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: A whisper of Cluster, Willamette, or hop extract.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean industrial lager yeast fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Corn grits or rice make up a large share of the grist.

composition.process: Cereal mashing of the adjuncts, then cold fermentation and filtration to bright clarity.

funFact: One of 24 beers in this atlas brewed to the Kölsch style, across 8 countries.

serve.how: Pour cold into a narrow stange — the slim glass preserves carbonation and keeps each serving small and fresh, just as Cologne intends. Take delicate sips and look for the whisper of white grape over cracker-crisp malt. Refill often rather than pouring a huge glass; kölsch fades fast as it warms, so small and frequent is the ritual.

name: Antares Barley Wine
description: American Barleywine brewed by Antares in Mar del Plata, Argentina.
funFact: One of 14 beers in this atlas brewed to the American Barleywine style, across 8 countries.

serve.how: Pour gently into a snifter, leaving any sediment in the bottle, and give it time — this beer changes more in the glass than almost any other. Warm it in your palm and swirl to pull up the pine and candied-orange hop aromas over the caramel base. If you have two bottles, cellar one for a year or three and taste how the sharp bitterness relaxes into marmalade; either way, sip it like an after-dinner drink, never in a hurry.

Drink it in proper pub measures, steady and social, noticing how soft the roast is compared to a stout. The gentle carbonation and modest strength make it a beer for the whole evening.

serve.how: Pour slowly into a thistle glass — or a snifter — filling only two-thirds so you can swirl and nose the caramel, plum, and whisper of smoke. Serve it warmer than any other beer in your fridge; straight from cold it hides everything, but near 60°F it turns plush and dessert-like. Small pours, slow sips: it drinks like a nightcap, and the alcohol warmth on the finish is part of the experience.

serve.how: Pour hard down the center of a tall, narrow pilsner glass to raise a dense two-finger cap of white foam, then let it settle before topping up. The head is part of the drink — sip through it and notice the cracker-dry malt giving way to a sharp herbal hop bite. Serve it fresh and cold; this style is all about the clean, bitter snap of the finish, so don't let it warm past cool.

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

serve.how: Pour the whole bottle in one gentle, steady motion into a stoneware mug, haze and all — swirl the last inch to rouse the yeast and add it in. Don't over-chill it; at cellar-cool temperature the fresh-dough and hop-sap character opens up the way it would in a Franconian beer garden. The carbonation is naturally soft, so expect a pillowy texture rather than fizz, and drink it while it's fresh.

name: Trumer Pils

serve.how: Pour hard down the center of a tall, narrow pilsner glass to raise a dense two-finger cap of white foam, then let it settle before topping up. serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

name: Cantillon Gueuze
description: Lambic brewed by Cantillon in Belgium.
funFact: One of 16 beers in this atlas brewed to the Lambic style, across 1 country.

serve.how: Store the bottle upright for a day so the sediment settles, then pour gently into a tumbler in one steady motion, leaving the last half-inch of yeasty dregs behind. Traditional unblended lambic is nearly still, so don't chase a head — just let it breathe for a few minutes as it warms. Sip slowly and hunt for the layers: tart green apple up front, hay and oak in the middle, and that unmistakable barnyard funk on the long dry finish.

name: Rodenbach Grand Cru
description: Flanders Red Ale brewed by Rodenbach in Belgium.

serve.how: Pour into a tulip at cellar temperature and treat it like a red wine: swirl, nose the cherry and balsamic, and give it ten minutes to open. name: Chimay Rouge

funFact: One of 44 beers in this atlas brewed to the Belgian Tripel style, across 9 countries.

serve.how: Pour steadily into a chalice to build a thick white head, leaving the yeast in the bottle for a brilliant golden glass. Sip with intention — the honeyed malt and champagne sparkle disguise 9% alcohol completely, which is exactly why one glass should last you a while.

Serve cold and notice the soft wheat tang, the perfumed spice, and how impossibly refreshing something this flavorful manages to be.

name: 3 Fonteinen Oude Geuze
description: Lambic brewed by 3 Fonteinen in Belgium.
funFact: One of 16 beers in this atlas brewed to the Lambic style, across 1 country.

serve.how: Store the bottle upright for a day so the sediment settles, then pour gently into a tumbler in one steady motion, leaving the last half-inch of yeasty dregs behind. Traditional unblended lambic is nearly still, so don't chase a head — just let it breathe for a few minutes as it warms. Sip slowly and hunt for the layers: tart green apple up front, hay and oak in the middle, and that unmistakable barnyard funk on the long dry finish.

name: Duvel
description: Belgian Golden Strong Ale from Belgium. Strong golden ale.
funFact: One of 6 beers in this atlas brewed to the Belgian Golden Strong Ale style, across 3 countries.

serve.how: Pour down the side of a tulip glass, straightening up at the end to raise a tall, rocky white head — the glass's flared lip is designed to hold that foam and funnel the pear-and-pepper aroma. Respect the strength: it drinks like a 5% blonde but lands like 8.5%, so pour small and sip slow.

name: Gouden Carolus Classic
description: Belgian Quadrupel brewed by Gouden Carolus in Belgium. Dark strong.
funFact: One of 19 beers in this atlas brewed to the Belgian Quadrupel style, across 6 countries.

serve.how: Open carefully — these are highly carbonated — and pour gently into a chalice, holding back the yeast sediment, then give it time; a quad served straight from the fridge is a quad wasted. Cup the bowl in your palm and let it warm while you nose the fig, plum, and port notes deepening. Drink it in small, slow sips like an after-dinner wine, and notice new layers of dark caramel and spice appearing every few minutes.

description: Oud Bruin brewed by Liefmans in Belgium.
funFact: One of 3 beers in this atlas brewed to the Oud Bruin style, across 1 country.

serve.how: Pour with moderate vigor down the center of a tulip to raise a tan collar of foam, then let it rest — this style opens up dramatically as the chill fades. Notice how the malty sweetness and gentle tartness trade places on your palate; the best examples balance them like sweet-and-sour sauce.

description: Belgian Dubbel from Belgium. Abbey.
funFact: One of 29 beers in this atlas brewed to the Belgian Dubbel style, across 7 countries.

serve.how: Pour slowly into a chalice at a slight tilt, finishing upright to crown it with a tan head, and leave the yeast dregs in the bottle for a clearer, cleaner glass. Serve at cellar temperature — the raisin, fig, and clove character only fully wakes up above 50°F. Sip contemplatively and track how the caramelized-sugar sweetness dries out into a surprisingly clean finish; that lightness is the monks' secret.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a pint glass with a quick, easy pour — this is the approachable weekday sour, and chill keeps its clean tartness crisp and refreshing. Don't hunt for funk; unlike wild ales it's deliberately clean, so what you should notice is bright citrusy acidity over a light body. If it's a fruited version, swirl gently to wake the aroma and drink it fresh.

name: Unibroue La Fin du Monde
description: Belgian Tripel brewed by Unibroue in Canada. Tripel, Québec.
funFact: One of 44 beers in this atlas brewed to the Belgian Tripel style, across 9 countries.

serve.how: Pour steadily into a chalice to build a thick white head, leaving the yeast in the bottle for a brilliant golden glass. Serve cool rather than cold so the pear, clove, and white-pepper notes lift out of the lively carbonation. Sip with intention — the honeyed malt and champagne sparkle disguise 9% alcohol completely, which is exactly why one glass should last you a while.

name: Unibroue Maudite
description: Belgian Quadrupel brewed by Unibroue in Canada. Dark strong.
funFact: One of 19 beers in this atlas brewed to the Belgian Quadrupel style, across 6 countries.

serve.how: Open carefully — these are highly carbonated — and pour gently into a chalice, holding back the yeast sediment, then give it time; a quad served straight from the fridge is a quad wasted. Cup the bowl in your palm and let it warm while you nose the fig, plum, and port notes deepening. Drink it in small, slow sips like an after-dinner wine, and notice new layers of dark caramel and spice appearing every few minutes.

serve.how: Pour two-thirds into the heavy hexagonal tumbler, swirl the remaining beer to rouse the yeast, and top the glass so it pours hazy pale with a pillowy white head. An orange slice is optional and debated — the coriander and orange peel are already brewed in, so try it naked first. Serve cold and notice the soft wheat tang, the perfumed spice, and how impossibly refreshing something this flavorful manages to be.

Look for gentle honey and fresh bread on the nose and a soft, clean swallow with barely-there bitterness. It is the ideal porch and lawnmower beer: unfussy, refreshing, and welcoming to whoever you hand one to.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a snifter — this is a beer to treat like a fine spirit, not a pint. Cup the bowl in your palm to warm it, swirling occasionally to release waves of espresso, molasses, and dark chocolate as it opens up over half an hour. Share the bottle if it's a big one; the last warm sips are often the best, when the dried-fruit sweetness and warming alcohol fully unfold.

name: Dieu du Ciel Aphrodisiaque
description: Irish Dry Stout brewed by Dieu du Ciel in Canada.
funFact: One of 86 beers in this atlas brewed to the Irish Dry Stout style, across 35 countries.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. The proper two-part draught pour is worth imitating: patience is the ritual. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

serve.how: Pour down the middle of a pint glass to raise a fluffy white head — the wheat protein gives it great foam, so use it. Skip the fruit garnish; a clean example doesn't need one. Drink it cold and easy, noticing the soft grainy middle and the light citrusy hop finish where a German wheat would put banana and clove — the whole point is crisp, no-drama refreshment.

Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

name: Moonshine Sombra

funFact: One of 86 beers in this atlas brewed to the Irish Dry Stout style, across 35 countries.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. serve.how: Open carefully — these are highly carbonated — and pour gently into a chalice, holding back the yeast sediment, then give it time; a quad served straight from the fridge is a quad wasted. Drink it in small, slow sips like an after-dinner wine, and notice new layers of dark caramel and spice appearing every few minutes.

name: Matuška Raptor
description: American IPA brewed by Matuška in Czechia.
funFact: One of 297 beers in this atlas brewed to the American IPA style, across 47 countries.

serve.how: Give the fridge-cold can 10 minutes on the counter, then pour hard enough to raise a solid head — that foam carries the grapefruit and pine aroma that defines the style. Drink it as fresh as possible; check the canning date and favor anything under two months old. Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

name: U Fleků Flekovský Ležák
description: Munich Dunkel from Czechia. Dark lager — brewed since 1499.
funFact: One of 43 beers in this atlas brewed to the Munich Dunkel style, across 28 countries.

serve.how: Pour steadily down the center of a mug to raise a thick, creamy head that traps the bready aroma. Resist serving it too cold — around 48°F the bread-crust and light cocoa character blooms while the beer stays soft and smooth. Take note of what's missing: despite the brown color there's almost no roast bite, just gentle, nutty malt from first sip to last.

name: Mikkeller Beer Geek Breakfast
description: Oatmeal Stout brewed by Mikkeller in Denmark.
funFact: One of 2 beers in this atlas brewed to the Oatmeal Stout style, across 2 countries.

serve.how: Pour with moderate vigor into a pint glass for a finger of dense, lasting foam. Let it lose its chill for a few minutes — the milk chocolate and nutty notes hide when it's too cold. The signature is texture, so pay attention to the mouthfeel: the oats give it a silky, pillowy slide that plain stouts can't match, making it dangerously easy drinking for something this roasty.

composition.summary: An English stout grist with flaked oats in the mash for a silken texture.

components.detail: Pale malt, chocolate malt, roasted barley, and five to fifteen percent flaked oats.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: English hops at modest bitterness — Fuggle or Goldings.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast leaving a touch of residual sweetness.

composition.process: Oats in the mash contribute beta-glucans and lipids that give the beer its slick body.

name: Mikkeller Spontan
description: Kettle Sour brewed by Mikkeller in Denmark.
funFact: One of 55 beers in this atlas brewed to the Kettle Sour style, across 16 countries.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a pint glass with a quick, easy pour — this is the approachable weekday sour, and chill keeps its clean tartness crisp and refreshing. Don't hunt for funk; unlike wild ales it's deliberately clean, so what you should notice is bright citrusy acidity over a light body. If it's a fruited version, swirl gently to wake the aroma and drink it fresh.

composition.summary: Ordinary wort soured with Lactobacillus in the kettle, then boiled and fermented clean.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Usually pilsner malt with wheat or oats for body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Held back before souring, since hop acids inhibit Lactobacillus.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean ale yeast, pitched after the boil has killed the bacteria.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Fruit purée is a near-standard addition in modern taproom versions.

composition.process: Wort is held warm with Lactobacillus for a day or two, then boiled to lock in acidity.

name: Mikkeller 1000 IBU
description: Double IPA brewed by Mikkeller in Denmark.
funFact: One of 44 beers in this atlas brewed to the Double IPA style, across 12 countries.

serve.how: Pour into a tulip rather than a shaker pint — the smaller bowl concentrates the resin and candied-citrus aroma and politely suggests a slower pace. Let it warm slightly from fridge temperature so the apricot and malt sweetness open up around the bitterness. Respect the ABV: pour half the can, savor it, and remember this drinks far easier than eight-plus percent should.

composition.summary: An IPA scaled up: more pale malt, far more hops, and higher alcohol.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Mostly pale two-row, kept simple so the hops dominate.

components.label: Hops

name: Meister Max Strong
description: Malt Liquor brewed by Meister in Egypt. Strong lager.
funFact: One of 47 beers in this atlas brewed to the Malt Liquor style, across 28 countries.

serve.how: This one wants to be as cold as your fridge can make it — warmth only amplifies the sweet grain and alcohol heat. Drink it fast while the chill lasts, noticing the smooth corn sweetness up front and the warming finish that reminds you it punches above lager weight.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a snifter — this is a beer to treat like a fine spirit, not a pint. Share the bottle if it's a big one; the last warm sips are often the best, when the dried-fruit sweetness and warming alcohol fully unfold.

serve.how: Treat it exactly like a full-strength lager: pour down the middle of a tall pilsner glass to raise two fingers of white foam, which carries most of the aroma. serve.how: Pour into a standard pint with enough vigor to raise a solid head, which carries the citrusy hop aroma to your nose. Drink it on the cool side of cellar temperature — too cold mutes the caramel and toffee, too warm and the hops turn dull. Notice the seesaw each sip rides between sweet toasted malt and grapefruity American hop bite; the best ambers never let either side win.

funFact: One of 18 beers in this atlas brewed to the Doppelbock style, across 4 countries.

serve.how: Pour slowly into a pokal and give the beer ten minutes out of the fridge before you start — the toffee, dark fruit, and toasted bread flatten out when served cold. Swirl lightly between sips and let the velvet body coat your palate; this is the monks' 'liquid bread,' meant to be savored like a meal. Watch for the warming finish that builds gently as the glass empties.

name: Franziskaner
description: Hefeweizen from Germany. Weissbier.
funFact: One of 49 beers in this atlas brewed to the Hefeweizen style, across 24 countries.

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

name: Franziskaner Kristallklar
description: Kristallweizen brewed by Franziskaner in Germany.
funFact: One of 2 beers in this atlas brewed to the Kristallweizen style, across 1 country.

serve.how: Pour slowly down the side of a rinsed weizen vase — with no yeast to weigh it down, the champagne-bright carbonation will foam enthusiastically. There's no sediment swirl here; the whole point is the polished clarity, so hold it up to the light and admire the sparkle. Serve well chilled and note the crisp wheat snap and faint banana echo; skip the lemon slice unless you enjoy scandalizing purists.

name: Gilde
description: German Pilsner from Germany. Hannover pils.
funFact: One of 134 beers in this atlas brewed to the German Pilsner style, across 34 countries.

serve.how: Pour hard down the center of a tall, narrow pilsner glass to raise a dense two-finger cap of white foam, then let it settle before topping up. The head is part of the drink — sip through it and notice the cracker-dry malt giving way to a sharp herbal hop bite. Serve it fresh and cold; this style is all about the clean, bitter snap of the finish, so don't let it warm past cool.

Take delicate sips and look for the whisper of white grape over cracker-crisp malt. Refill often rather than pouring a huge glass; kölsch fades fast as it warms, so small and frequent is the ritual.

As you sip, notice how the roast flashes and then vanishes into a bone-dry finish instead of coating your tongue like a stout would.

Don't overthink it: this is the beer of stadiums and coolers, engineered for effortless refreshment.

Sip in tiny amounts and notice how dense and silky the body is; at up to 14% this is the lager world's answer to a dessert wine.

funFact: One of 134 beers in this atlas brewed to the German Pilsner style, across 34 countries.

serve.how: Pour hard down the center of a tall, narrow pilsner glass to raise a dense two-finger cap of white foam, then let it settle before topping up. The head is part of the drink — sip through it and notice the cracker-dry malt giving way to a sharp herbal hop bite. Serve it fresh and cold; this style is all about the clean, bitter snap of the finish, so don't let it warm past cool.

name: Schlenkerla Urbock

name: Schöfferhofer
description: Hefeweizen from Germany. Grapefruit weizen.
funFact: One of 49 beers in this atlas brewed to the Hefeweizen style, across 24 countries.

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

name: Spezial Rauchbier
description: Rauchbier brewed by Spezial in Germany. Bamberg smoked.
funFact: One of 8 beers in this atlas brewed to the Rauchbier style, across 6 countries.

serve.how: Pour into a stout seidel with a solid head and — crucially — let it warm out of the fridge for ten minutes; too cold and all you'll taste is smoke, too warm and it turns ashy. First sips can be startling, like drinking a campfire, so give your palate three or four swallows to recalibrate. Then notice the magic: the beechwood smoke and ham notes settle into a smooth, toasty Märzen backbone that keeps you coming back.

name: Berliner Kindl Weisse
description: Berliner Weisse from Germany.
funFact: One of 5 beers in this atlas brewed to the Berliner Weisse style, across 3 countries.

serve.how: Pour chilled into a wide goblet and take it straight, at least at first — it's spritzy, lemony, and lighter than almost any beer you'll own. If the tartness is too sharp, do as Berliners do and add a small pour of raspberry or woodruff syrup to the glass ('mit Schuss'). At barely 3% it's a hot-afternoon beer: keep it cold, drink it fast, notice how the wheat softens the acid.

name: Moza
description: Bock from Guatemala.
funFact: One of 24 beers in this atlas brewed to the Bock style, across 18 countries.

serve.how: Pour into a pokal with a steady hand to get a creamy head over the deep amber-brown body. Serve at cool cellar temperature; too cold and the rich toffee and dark-bread malt go mute. Sip rather than swig and notice the gentle warmth in the finish — this is a strong lager wearing a smooth disguise, best enjoyed over a slow evening.

name: Barbican
description: Non-Alcoholic Lager from Gulf States. Non-alcoholic malt — region-wide.
funFact: One of 25 beers in this atlas brewed to the Non-Alcoholic Lager style, across 18 countries.

serve.how: Treat it exactly like a full-strength lager: pour down the middle of a tall pilsner glass to raise two fingers of white foam, which carries most of the aroma. Serve properly cold — NA beers can taste worty as they warm, so smaller pours kept cool beat one big glass going flat. Notice the clean grainy malt and crisp finish, and enjoy the novelty of a genuinely refreshing beer you can have with lunch on a Tuesday.

name: Banks Beer (Guyana & Suriname)
description: American Lager brewed by Banks in Guyana & Suriname. Lager, Guyana.
funFact: One of 949 beers in this atlas brewed to the American Lager style, across 146 countries.

serve.how: Serve it ice cold with a fast center pour into a frosted or well-chilled pint glass, building a short-lived white head and plenty of carbonic sparkle. Drink it promptly — its crisp, light-grain character is best in the first cold minutes and dullest once warm. Don't overthink it: this is the beer of stadiums and coolers, engineered for effortless refreshment.

description: Irish Dry Stout brewed by Banks in Guyana & Suriname. Stout, Guyana.
funFact: One of 86 beers in this atlas brewed to the Irish Dry Stout style, across 35 countries.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. The proper two-part draught pour is worth imitating: patience is the ritual. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

serve.glass: Pint glass or straight from the can
serve.how: The colder the better — serve it near-freezing, straight from the bottom of the cooler, in a chilled glass or right from the can. The flavor is intentionally a whisper of corn and clean fizz, so freshness and frigid temperature are everything. This is hydration-adjacent tailgate fuel: crack it, drink it cold, and reach for the next one before this one warms.

description: Gose brewed by Young Master in Hong Kong.
funFact: One of 5 beers in this atlas brewed to the Gose style, across 4 countries.

serve.how: Pour chilled into a tall cylindrical gose glass — or any slender glass — with a soft head, and take your first sip without preconceptions. The salt shouldn't taste like seawater; it should just make the tart lemon and coriander pop, the way salt on the rim lifts a margarita. Notice how it makes your mouth water for the next sip: that saline snap is the whole trick of the style.

name: Young Master Another IPA
description: American IPA brewed by Young Master in Hong Kong.
funFact: One of 297 beers in this atlas brewed to the American IPA style, across 47 countries.

serve.how: Give the fridge-cold can 10 minutes on the counter, then pour hard enough to raise a solid head — that foam carries the grapefruit and pine aroma that defines the style. Drink it as fresh as possible; check the canning date and favor anything under two months old. Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

name: Einstök White Ale

serve.how: Pour two-thirds into the heavy hexagonal tumbler, swirl the remaining beer to rouse the yeast, and top the glass so it pours hazy pale with a pillowy white head. An orange slice is optional and debated — the coriander and orange peel are already brewed in, so try it naked first. Serve cold and notice the soft wheat tang, the perfumed spice, and how impossibly refreshing something this flavorful manages to be.

serve.how: Pour slowly into a thistle glass — or a snifter — filling only two-thirds so you can swirl and nose the caramel, plum, and whisper of smoke. Serve it warmer than any other beer in your fridge; straight from cold it hides everything, but near 60°F it turns plush and dessert-like. Small pours, slow sips: it drinks like a nightcap, and the alcohol warmth on the finish is part of the experience.

name: Borg Brugghús Garún
description: Imperial Stout brewed by Borg in Iceland.
funFact: One of 53 beers in this atlas brewed to the Imperial Stout style, across 16 countries.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a snifter — this is a beer to treat like a fine spirit, not a pint. Cup the bowl in your palm to warm it, swirling occasionally to release waves of espresso, molasses, and dark chocolate as it opens up over half an hour. Share the bottle if it's a big one; the last warm sips are often the best, when the dried-fruit sweetness and warming alcohol fully unfold.

Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

Then notice the magic: the beechwood smoke and ham notes settle into a smooth, toasty Märzen backbone that keeps you coming back.

funFact: One of 47 beers in this atlas brewed to the Malt Liquor style, across 28 countries.

serve.how: This one wants to be as cold as your fridge can make it — warmth only amplifies the sweet grain and alcohol heat. Drink it fast while the chill lasts, noticing the smooth corn sweetness up front and the warming finish that reminds you it punches above lager weight.

Let it warm a few minutes and sniff for white pepper and lemon before sipping; the bone-dry finish should leave your palate refreshed, not coated.

description: Dunkelweizen brewed by Kati Patang in India.

serve.how: Rinse the weizen vase with cold water, pour three-quarters of the bottle slowly down the tilted side, then swirl the last inch to rouse the yeast and crown the pour with it. Sip through the foam and notice the banana-bread and caramel layered over clove; it drinks like a hefeweizen that put on an autumn coat.

name: Behnoush
description: Non-Alcoholic Lager from Iran. Non-alcoholic malt.
funFact: One of 25 beers in this atlas brewed to the Non-Alcoholic Lager style, across 18 countries.

serve.how: Treat it exactly like a full-strength lager: pour down the middle of a tall pilsner glass to raise two fingers of white foam, which carries most of the aroma. Serve properly cold — NA beers can taste worty as they warm, so smaller pours kept cool beat one big glass going flat. Notice the clean grainy malt and crisp finish, and enjoy the novelty of a genuinely refreshing beer you can have with lunch on a Tuesday.

name: Guinness Draught
description: Irish Dry Stout brewed by Guinness in Ireland.
funFact: One of 86 beers in this atlas brewed to the Irish Dry Stout style, across 35 countries.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. The proper two-part draught pour is worth imitating: patience is the ritual. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

Sip slowly and track the arc from bittersweet chocolate through roast to that raisiny, almost port-like finish that made it a tropical legend.

No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

name: Fujizakura Kogen

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. funFact: One of 43 beers in this atlas brewed to the Munich Dunkel style, across 28 countries.

serve.how: Pour steadily down the center of a mug to raise a thick, creamy head that traps the bready aroma. Resist serving it too cold — around 48°F the bread-crust and light cocoa character blooms while the beer stays soft and smooth. Take note of what's missing: despite the brown color there's almost no roast bite, just gentle, nutty malt from first sip to last.

Then notice the magic: the beechwood smoke and ham notes settle into a smooth, toasty Märzen backbone that keeps you coming back.

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

name: Ocean Lab Brewing Co. Stout
description: Irish Dry Stout brewed by Ocean Lab Brewing Co. in Carolina, Puerto Rico.
funFact: Ocean Lab Brewing Co. has been brewing in Carolina since 2015.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. The proper two-part draught pour is worth imitating: patience is the ritual. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

name: BOB
description: Kettle Sour brewed by Ocean Lab Brewing Co. in Carolina, Puerto Rico. One of the fruit series.
funFact: Ocean Lab Brewing Co. has been brewing in Carolina since 2015.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a pint glass with a quick, easy pour — this is the approachable weekday sour, and chill keeps its clean tartness crisp and refreshing. Don't hunt for funk; unlike wild ales it's deliberately clean, so what you should notice is bright citrusy acidity over a light body. If it's a fruited version, swirl gently to wake the aroma and drink it fresh.

name: Condado West Coast Pilsner
description: German Pilsner brewed by Ocean Lab Brewing Co. in Carolina, Puerto Rico.
funFact: Ocean Lab Brewing Co. has been brewing in Carolina since 2015.

serve.how: Pour hard down the center of a tall, narrow pilsner glass to raise a dense two-finger cap of white foam, then let it settle before topping up. Serve it fresh and cold; this style is all about the clean, bitter snap of the finish, so don't let it warm past cool.

At barely 3% it's a hot-afternoon beer: keep it cold, drink it fast, notice how the wheat softens the acid.

Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

funFact: Ocean Lab Brewing Co. has been brewing in Carolina since 2015.

Don't overthink it: this is the beer of stadiums and coolers, engineered for effortless refreshment.

serve.how: Pour at a 45-degree angle and finish upright to build a creamy tan head that mirrors the beer's texture. serve.how: Treat it exactly like a full-strength lager: pour down the middle of a tall pilsner glass to raise two fingers of white foam, which carries most of the aroma. Notice the clean grainy malt and crisp finish, and enjoy the novelty of a genuinely refreshing beer you can have with lunch on a Tuesday.

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. name: Cape Brewing Krystal Weiss

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. description: Hefeweizen brewed by Ueli in Switzerland. Weissbier.
funFact: One of 49 beers in this atlas brewed to the Hefeweizen style, across 24 countries.

serve.how: The pour is the ritual: rinse the tall weizen vase, tilt it steeply, and pour slowly until an inch of beer remains in the bottle — then swirl that last inch to lift the yeast and pour it in to cloud the glass and cap the towering head. No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a pint glass with a quick, easy pour — this is the approachable weekday sour, and chill keeps its clean tartness crisp and refreshing. Don't hunt for funk; unlike wild ales it's deliberately clean, so what you should notice is bright citrusy acidity over a light body. If it's a fruited version, swirl gently to wake the aroma and drink it fresh.

name: Taihu Bravo
description: American IPA brewed by Taihu in Taiwan.
funFact: One of 297 beers in this atlas brewed to the American IPA style, across 47 countries.

serve.how: Give the fridge-cold can 10 minutes on the counter, then pour hard enough to raise a solid head — that foam carries the grapefruit and pine aroma that defines the style. Drink it as fresh as possible; check the canning date and favor anything under two months old. Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

serve.how: Pour chilled into a tall cylindrical gose glass — or any slender glass — with a soft head, and take your first sip without preconceptions. The salt shouldn't taste like seawater; it should just make the tart lemon and coriander pop, the way salt on the rim lifts a margarita. Notice how it makes your mouth water for the next sip: that saline snap is the whole trick of the style.

No lemon; purists consider it sacrilege, and the beer doesn't need it. Breathe in the banana and clove — remember, it's all yeast chemistry — and enjoy the creamy wheat body underneath.

funFact: One of 949 beers in this atlas brewed to the American Lager style, across 146 countries.

name: Nambawan Premium
description: American Lager brewed by Nambawan in Vanuatu.
funFact: One of 949 beers in this atlas brewed to the American Lager style, across 146 countries.

serve.how: Serve it ice cold with a fast center pour into a frosted or well-chilled pint glass, building a short-lived white head and plenty of carbonic sparkle. Drink it promptly — its crisp, light-grain character is best in the first cold minutes and dullest once warm. Don't overthink it: this is the beer of stadiums and coolers, engineered for effortless refreshment.

name: Polar Light
description: American Light Lager brewed by Polar in Venezuela.
funFact: One of 45 beers in this atlas brewed to the American Light Lager style, across 28 countries.

serve.glass: Pint glass or straight from the can
serve.how: The colder the better — serve it near-freezing, straight from the bottom of the cooler, in a chilled glass or right from the can. The flavor is intentionally a whisper of corn and clean fizz, so freshness and frigid temperature are everything. This is hydration-adjacent tailgate fuel: crack it, drink it cold, and reach for the next one before this one warms.

name: Polar Zero
description: Non-Alcoholic Lager brewed by Polar in Venezuela.
funFact: One of 25 beers in this atlas brewed to the Non-Alcoholic Lager style, across 18 countries.

serve.how: Treat it exactly like a full-strength lager: pour down the middle of a tall pilsner glass to raise two fingers of white foam, which carries most of the aroma. Serve properly cold — NA beers can taste worty as they warm, so smaller pours kept cool beat one big glass going flat. Notice the clean grainy malt and crisp finish, and enjoy the novelty of a genuinely refreshing beer you can have with lunch on a Tuesday.

name: Pasteur Street Jasmine IPA
description: American IPA brewed by Pasteur Street in Vietnam. IPA, Saigon.
funFact: One of 297 beers in this atlas brewed to the American IPA style, across 47 countries.

serve.how: Give the fridge-cold can 10 minutes on the counter, then pour hard enough to raise a solid head — that foam carries the grapefruit and pine aroma that defines the style. Drink it as fresh as possible; check the canning date and favor anything under two months old. Sip and track the arc from citrus burst to resinous bitter finish, with the caramel malt holding the middle together.

name: Pasteur Street Cyclo Imperial Chocolate Stout
description: Irish Dry Stout brewed by Pasteur Street in Vietnam.
funFact: One of 86 beers in this atlas brewed to the Irish Dry Stout style, across 35 countries.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. The proper two-part draught pour is worth imitating: patience is the ritual. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

composition.process: Roasted barley, not chocolate malt, supplies the coffee bite and the dry finish.

description: American Wheat Beer brewed by Pasteur Street in Vietnam.
funFact: One of 33 beers in this atlas brewed to the American Wheat Beer style, across 16 countries.

serve.how: Pour down the middle of a pint glass to raise a fluffy white head — the wheat protein gives it great foam, so use it. Skip the fruit garnish; a clean example doesn't need one. Drink it cold and easy, noticing the soft grainy middle and the light citrusy hop finish where a German wheat would put banana and clove — the whole point is crisp, no-drama refreshment.

name: Pasteur Street Spice Island Saison

funFact: One of 63 beers in this atlas brewed to the Saison style, across 16 countries.

serve.how: Pour with vigor down the center of a tulip to raise a tall, rocky white head — saison's high carbonation is part of the show. Leave the last half-inch of yeast in the bottle unless you like a hazier, earthier glass. Let it warm a few minutes and sniff for white pepper and lemon before sipping; the bone-dry finish should leave your palate refreshed, not coated.

name: Averna
description: Sicily's best-known amaro, made in Caltanissetta to a recipe a Benedictine abbey gave the Averna family in 1868. Softer and more caramelised than the northern amari, with orange peel and liquorice doing most of the work.
funFact: The monks of the Abbazia di Santo Spirito handed the recipe to Salvatore Averna as thanks for his patronage, and the abbey still appears on the label.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over a large cube with an orange twist. It is sweet enough to take ice without collapsing, and it is the friendliest entry point into Italian amari for anyone who finds Fernet punishing.

serve.how: Over a large cube with an orange wedge, which is how Bologna drinks it. It also does well long with tonic. Low enough in bitterness to work before dinner as easily as after.

name: Amaro Nonino Quintessentia
description: Friuli's amaro, built on aged grappa rather than neutral spirit, which puts it in a class of its own. Lighter, brighter and more expensive than its peers, and the reason a Paper Plane tastes the way it does.
funFact: The Nonino family began distilling single-varietal grappa in 1973, a move that dragged the whole grappa category upmarket almost single-handedly.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature so the grappa base shows. In cocktails it is the modifier in a Paper Plane, split evenly with bourbon, Aperol and lemon. Do not bury it under ice; the barrel character disappears.

composition.summary: Herbs and citrus infused into barrel-aged grappa.

composition.process: Using aged grappa rather than neutral alcohol is the whole point and the whole cost.

name: Meletti
description: A Marche amaro with saffron and violet in the blend, noticeably sweeter and more floral than its neighbours, in a bottle with a bulbous glass stopper that turns up in every Italian grandmother's cabinet.
funFact: Silvio Meletti built the recipe in the 1870s and the company also makes an anisette so well regarded that locals drink it in coffee as anisetta.

serve.how: Neat after dinner or over ice with an orange slice. It is sweet, so it works better as a dessert amaro than an aperitif, and it makes an excellent float on a coffee.

composition.process: Saffron is expensive enough that its presence sets the price of the bottle.

name: Sfumato Rabarbaro
description: Chinese rhubarb root smoked over open fire, then infused into an alpine amaro. Tastes of tar, campfire and bitter earth — the most divisive bottle in most bar backbars, and indispensable once you like it.
funFact: The rhubarb is grown in China, dried, then smoked in the Italian Alps — a supply chain that predates the amaro itself by centuries via the Silk Road.

serve.how: Cold and neat in a small pour, or a bar spoon in a Manhattan or Negroni where it adds smoke without peat. A little goes a very long way; treat it as a seasoning as much as a drink.

composition.process: Smoking the root over open flame is the single step that makes it unlike any other amaro.

name: Cardamaro
description: A Piedmontese amaro built on wine rather than spirit, flavoured with cardoon and blessed thistle and aged in oak. At 17% it is barely stronger than vermouth, and it drinks like an autumnal sherry with a bitter edge.
funFact: Cardoon is a thistle relative of the artichoke, which puts Cardamaro in the same botanical family as Cynar despite tasting nothing like it.

serve.how: Chilled and neat as an aperitif, or over ice with soda. Because the base is wine it works beautifully in place of sweet vermouth in low-alcohol cocktails, and it should be refrigerated once open.

composition.summary: Moscato wine infused with cardoon and thistle, then oak-aged.

composition.process: A wine base means it oxidises like wine — keep it cold and finish it within a month or two.

name: Amaro Lucano
description: Made in Basilicata since 1894 by a pastry chef who blended thirty herbs in the back of his shop. Balanced and mid-weight, and for decades the house amaro of the Italian royal family.
funFact: Pasquale Vena was a confectioner, not a distiller, which is often cited as the reason the sugar balance is so precise.

serve.how: Neat after dinner or over ice. It sits between Averna's sweetness and Ramazzotti's spice, which makes it the safest pour when you do not know your guest's taste in amari.

name: Amaro del Capo
description: Calabria's amaro, made with twenty-nine local herbs and drunk straight from the freezer. Sweeter and more citrus-driven than the northern styles, and enormously popular across southern Italy.
funFact: There is a chilli version, made with Calabrian peperoncino, which is exactly as aggressive as that sounds.

serve.how: The bottle lives in the freezer and the glass should too. It pours thick and cold, which mutes the sugar and lets the liquorice and mint through. Calabrians consider room-temperature service a mistake.

name: Zucca Rabarbaro
description: A Milanese rhubarb amaro from 1845, dark and gently smoky, and the original aperitivo of the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele. Drier than most amari and closer to a bitter than a digestive.
funFact: Zucca held a royal warrant from the House of Savoy and its bar in the Galleria was the fashionable place to be seen in nineteenth-century Milan.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and a lemon twist as an aperitif, which is how Milan drank it for a century. Neat it is dry and faintly smoky; it also improves a Negroni if you swap it for part of the Campari.

composition.summary: Chinese rhubarb root and cardamom infused in spirit and lightly sweetened.

composition.process: Rhubarb root gives the earthy, faintly smoky note that the whole rabarbaro category is built on.

name: China Martini
description: A cinchona-bark amaro from Turin, pronounced kee-na and named for the quinine tree rather than the country. Bitter, cocoa-toned, and the ancestor of most quinine liqueurs on the shelf.
funFact: Cinchona bark was the original source of quinine, which is why so many nineteenth-century bitters were marketed openly as anti-malarial tonics.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or the Piedmontese winter serve: warmed with a strip of lemon peel. It also works stirred into coffee, where the cocoa note in the bark meets the roast.

name: Cocchi Americano
description: A quinine-flavoured aromatised wine from Piedmont, bitter-sweet and citrus-driven. It is the closest thing available to Kina Lillet, which means it is what a Vesper is supposed to be made with.
funFact: Lillet reformulated in 1986 and dropped most of its quinine, which is why bartenders reaching for a period-correct Vesper use this instead.

serve.how: Cold with ice and a slice of orange as an aperitif. In cocktails it is the third of a Vesper, the Lillet stand-in in a Corpse Reviver No. 2, and the white half of a White Negroni. Refrigerate after opening.

composition.summary: Moscato d'Asti wine aromatised with cinchona and botanicals.

name: Bonal Gentiane-Quina
description: A Savoyard aperitif of gentian, cinchona and alpine herbs on a mistelle base, made since 1865 and advertised as the opener of the appetite. Deep, wine-dark and more bitter than it looks.
funFact: It was created by a monk at the Grande Chartreuse and marketed with the slogan ouvre l'appétit — which is why French bars still pour it before a meal rather than after.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice with a lemon twist. It substitutes well for sweet vermouth in a Manhattan or Boulevardier, bringing gentian bitterness where vermouth brings sweetness.

composition.process: Both signature botanicals are roots and barks rather than leaves, which is why the bitterness is so deep and slow.

name: Byrrh
description: A French quinquina from Roussillon, sold from 1866 as a health tonic through pharmacies because a medicinal label attracted less tax than an alcoholic one. Red wine, mistelle and cinchona, aged in enormous oak vats.
funFact: The Thuir cellars hold the largest oak vat in the world, at over a million litres, built in 1950 and still in use.

serve.how: Cold with ice and an orange slice, as a French café aperitif. It swaps neatly for sweet vermouth in a Manhattan and makes an excellent low-strength highball with soda.

composition.summary: Red wine and mistelle aromatised with cinchona and aged in oak.

composition.process: Selling it through pharmacies as a tonic was a deliberate tax strategy, and it worked for decades.

name: Dubonnet
description: Created in 1846 to persuade French Foreign Legionnaires in North Africa to take their quinine, by burying the bitterness in sweet fortified wine. It worked, and it outlived the empire that commissioned it.
funFact: Queen Elizabeth II reportedly drank it with gin and a slice of lemon before lunch, a combination the household referred to simply as the usual.

serve.how: Cold with ice and lemon, or the royal serve: two parts Dubonnet to one part gin over ice. It is sweet and low in strength, so it suits an afternoon better than an evening.

composition.process: Sweetening quinine into palatability was a genuine public-health problem in the 1840s, and this was the commercial answer.

name: Amer Picon
description: A bitter orange aperitif invented by a French soldier in Algeria in 1837, again as a quinine delivery system. Reformulated and weakened over the years, and the ghost that haunts a Picon Bière or a Brooklyn cocktail.
funFact: Gaétan Picon dropped it from 39% to 21% and later 18%, which is why old cocktail recipes calling for it never quite work with a modern bottle.

serve.how: The French serve is Picon Bière — a measure in the bottom of a glass of blonde beer, which sounds wrong and is excellent. In cocktails it belongs in a Brooklyn and a Liberal, though modern bottlings need a heavier hand than the original recipes assumed.

composition.process: It is not officially exported to many markets, which is why bar substitutes for it are a whole cottage industry.

name: Salers
description: A gentian aperitif from the Auvergne, made since 1885 from wild roots dug on volcanic uplands. Paler, drier and more austere than Suze, and the one gentian purists tend to reach for.
funFact: The roots are harvested by hand with a two-pronged fork called a fourche du diable, from plants that have grown for at least twenty years.

serve.how: Over ice with a splash of soda or tonic, which is the Auvergne café serve. It is drier than Suze and less sweet than Aveze, so it is the best of the three in a White Negroni.

name: Avèze
description: The third of the French gentian aperitifs, from the Cantal, sweeter and rounder than Salers and less citrus-forward than Suze. Made from roots dug in the volcanic pastures of the Massif Central.
funFact: All three major gentian aperitifs come from within a hundred kilometres of each other, because that is where the wild plant grows densely enough to harvest.

serve.how: Over ice with tonic or soda, or with cassis as an Auvergnat kir. Its extra sweetness makes it the gentler introduction to gentian for anyone who has bounced off Suze.

name: Peychaud's Bitters
description: Created by a Creole apothecary in 1830s New Orleans, lighter and more floral than Angostura, with anise and cherry where Angostura has clove. Without it a Sazerac is not a Sazerac.
funFact: Antoine Amédée Peychaud served his tonic in a double-ended egg cup called a coquetier, which is one of the more plausible origin stories for the word cocktail.

serve.glass: Used as a seasoning, not poured
serve.how: Three or four dashes in a Sazerac, alongside rye and absinthe. It is softer than Angostura and not a like-for-like substitute — using one where the recipe wants the other changes the drink noticeably.

name: Orange Bitters
description: Dried bitter orange peel, cardamom and caraway in a concentrated tincture. It vanished almost entirely after Prohibition and came back only in the 2000s, which is why a century of Martini recipes read strangely without it.
funFact: Pre-Prohibition Martini recipes almost universally called for orange bitters; the drink we now think of as classic is a version that lost an ingredient by accident.

serve.how: A dash or two in a Martini, a Manhattan or an Old Fashioned. It lifts and defines rather than adding obvious flavour — the effect is much more noticeable by its absence when you go back.

name: Malört
description: A wormwood liqueur brought to Chicago by a Swedish immigrant, and the city's initiation ritual. Relentlessly, uncompromisingly bitter, with a finish that people describe using words like grapefruit rind and burnt plastic.
funFact: Carl Jeppson sold it through Prohibition as a medicinal tonic, reportedly because agents who tasted it accepted immediately that nobody would drink it for pleasure.

serve.how: One shot, and the tradition is to watch the face of whoever is drinking it for the first time. Chicagoans chase it with cheap lager. Bartenders have found genuine uses for a small amount in cocktails, where the bitterness cuts sweetness sharply.

name: Fernet
description: Not one brand but the bitterest class of amaro: myrrh, saffron, gentian and menthol, minimally sweetened. A category invented in 1840s Milan as a stomach remedy and adopted wholesale by Argentina and San Francisco.
funFact: San Francisco drinks a wildly disproportionate share of the world's fernet, a habit usually traced to the city's Italian community and its bartending scene.

serve.how: Neat after a heavy meal, which is the intended use. Argentina drinks it long with cola in roughly a one-to-three ratio. Bartenders take it as a shot with ginger beer alongside, a pairing known as a handshake.

name: Kümmerling
description: A German herbal bitter sold almost exclusively in small single-serve bottles, like Underberg but sweeter and more anise-driven. A fixture of German festivals and petrol-station counters alike.
funFact: Hugo Kümmerling launched it in 1938 and the small-bottle format was chosen so it could be sold as a single measure rather than by the bottle.

serve.how: Cold, in one go, after eating. It is sweeter and less punishing than Underberg, which is why it has a following among people who find that one too austere.

name: Killepitsch
description: A Düsseldorf herbal liqueur of ninety-eight herbs, berries and fruits, made to a recipe devised in an air-raid shelter during the war. Deep red, sweet, and drunk in Altstadt bars by the thousand.
funFact: The name comes from Rhineland dialect roughly meaning to knock back and gasp, and the recipe was written down by two friends sheltering from bombing in 1944.

serve.how: Cold and neat, in one, alongside a glass of Altbier — the standard Düsseldorf order. Sweeter and fruitier than Jägermeister, and considerably stronger at 42%.

name: Blutwurz
description: A Bavarian Forest liqueur made from tormentil root, which stains the liquid blood red and gives it a dry, tannic bitterness. Sold in the region as a digestive and a folk remedy in equal measure.
funFact: Tormentil root was used against dysentery for centuries, which is where both the medicinal reputation and the astringency come from.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass after a heavy meal. At 50% it demands slow drinking. In the Bavarian Forest it is offered to guests almost automatically and refusing takes some doing.

description: An Abruzzese liqueur made by steeping gentian root in wine or spirit, produced at farmhouse scale across the Apennines. Rougher and more rustic than the French gentian aperitifs, and usually homemade.
funFact: Gentian harvesting is regulated across the Apennines, and in some Italian regions digging wild roots requires a permit.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal, in the small pours Abruzzese households offer. Wine-based versions are lower in strength and closer to a bitter vermouth; spirit-based ones are sharper.

name: Fernet Vallet
description: A Mexican fernet made to a recipe a French distiller brought to Veracruz in the 1880s. Sweeter and more cinnamon-driven than the Italian style, and long a fixture of cantinas in the south.
funFact: Henri Vallet emigrated from France, set up in Veracruz, and built a fernet that Mexico kept making long after the Italian originals had come to dominate elsewhere.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, or with cola in the Argentine manner. Its extra sweetness and cinnamon make it an easier fernet than Branca, and it works well in a Toronto or a Hanky Panky.

name: Amaro Sibilla
description: An intensely bitter amaro from the Sibillini mountains of the Marche, made with honey and mountain herbs to a nineteenth-century recipe. Dark, resinous and closer to a medicine than a digestive.
funFact: The Sibillini mountains are named for a mythical sibyl said to have lived in a cave there, and the amaro's label leans on the legend heavily.

serve.how: Neat in a small pour after a heavy meal. The honey rounds the front but the finish is long and genuinely bitter, so it rewards slow sipping rather than a shot.

name: Select Aperitivo
description: Venice's answer to Campari, made since 1920 with thirty botanicals and rhubarb root. It is what a spritz is made with in Venice, and Venetians will correct you firmly if you reach for Aperol instead.
funFact: The Venetian spritz predates Aperol's dominance entirely, and Select was created specifically for it in the year the drink took hold in the city.

serve.how: Three parts prosecco, two parts Select, a splash of soda, over ice, with a green olive rather than an orange slice — that olive is the Venetian marker. More bitter than an Aperol spritz and considerably better.

name: Cappelletti Aperitivo
description: A wine-based red aperitivo from Trentino, coloured with cochineal as Campari once was. Lower in alcohol and gentler than its Milanese rival, with more fruit and less quinine snap.
funFact: It is still coloured with carmine from cochineal insects, a practice Campari abandoned in 2006 and which makes this bottle unsuitable for vegans.

serve.how: Over ice with soda, or as the red third of a Negroni where its lower strength makes a gentler drink. Because the base is wine, refrigerate it once opened and finish it within a month.

name: Petrus Boonekamp
description: A Dutch-origin bitter now made in Italy, dry and root-driven with almost no sweetness. Boonekamp is a whole nineteenth-century category of stomach bitters, of which this is the surviving standard-bearer.
funFact: Petrus Boonekamp created the style in Leiden in 1777; it became generic enough that a dozen distillers sold their own boonekamp through the 1800s.

serve.how: Neat in a small measure after eating. It is drier than almost anything else in this category — there is essentially no sugar to hide behind, which makes it closer to Underberg than to Jägermeister.

name: Amaro Ciociaro
description: A Lazio amaro built heavily on bitter orange, softer and more approachable than most, and frequently used as a stand-in for Amer Picon in cocktails that can no longer get the original.
funFact: American bartenders adopted it as the closest available substitute for Amer Picon after the French original was reformulated and largely withdrawn from export.

serve.how: Neat or over ice after dinner. In cocktails it does duty in a Brooklyn or a Liberal, where the orange-and-gentian profile fills the gap Picon left.

name: Ferro China
description: A nineteenth-century Italian tonic of cinchona bark and iron salts, sold in pharmacies as a treatment for anaemia and now surviving as a bitter digestive. It genuinely tastes faintly of iron.
funFact: It was prescribed to children as a strengthening tonic well into the twentieth century, in doses that would raise eyebrows now.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or the traditional winter serve of warming it with a strip of lemon peel. Italians of a certain generation also stir it into coffee or milk.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

composition.process: The iron is not a flavouring accident; it was the active ingredient the whole product was sold on.

name: Amaro Nardini
description: Made by Italy's oldest distillery, in Bassano del Grappa since 1779, on a grappa base rather than neutral spirit. Mint-forward and unusually clean, with the grappa giving it a sharpness other amari lack.
funFact: Nardini has been distilling on the Ponte Vecchio in Bassano since 1779, which makes it the oldest continuously operating distillery in Italy.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or the Veneto habit of mixing it half and half with soda as a mezzo e mezzo. The mint is pronounced enough that it reads almost like a digestif and a palate cleanser at once.

composition.summary: Herbs and mint infused into a grappa base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grappa

components.label: Botanicals
