components.detail: Peppermint, gentian, bitter orange, herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused into distilled grappa

composition.process: A grappa base rather than neutral spirit gives a grip that a neutral base cannot.

name: Rabarbaro
description: The rhubarb-root class of Italian amaro, distinct enough to be its own category. Chinese rhubarb root gives a dry, earthy, faintly smoky bitterness that no other botanical produces.
funFact: The rhubarb in question is not the garden vegetable but Rheum palmatum, imported dried from China along trade routes that predate the amari themselves.

serve.how: Over ice with soda as an aperitif, or neat after a meal. The class sits drier than the citrus amari and is the natural bridge for someone moving from Campari toward Fernet.

composition.summary: Dried Chinese rhubarb root infused in spirit with supporting botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Rheum palmatum root, cardamom, bitter orange

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, sometimes with smoked root

composition.process: Smoking the root, as Sfumato does, is a variation within the class rather than the norm.

name: Crème de Cacao
description: Cacao bean and vanilla liqueur, made clear (white) or caramel-coloured (dark) from the same base. The crème refers to sugar content, not dairy — there is no cream in it at all.
funFact: EU rules require a crème liqueur to carry at least 250 grams of sugar per litre, which is where the name comes from — the texture, not the ingredient.

serve.how: Rarely drunk neat. White goes into a Grasshopper and an Alexander; dark into a Brandy Alexander or a Twentieth Century. Keep the white version when you need chocolate flavour without muddying the colour of a drink.

composition.summary: Cacao beans and vanilla infused into neutral spirit and heavily sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Roasted cacao beans, vanilla pod

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused or distilled, then sweetened; dark is caramel-coloured

composition.process: Distilling rather than infusing gives the white version, since the colour stays behind in the beans.

name: Crème de Banane
description: Banana liqueur, bright yellow and frankly artificial-tasting in its cheap forms, genuinely good in its better ones. A tiki staple and the making of a Banana Daiquiri.
funFact: Isoamyl acetate, the compound that reads as banana, is also produced naturally by fermenting yeast — which is why some Jamaican rums taste of banana with no banana involved.

serve.how: In a Banana Daiquiri with rum and lime, or a bar spoon in a tiki build where it bridges rum and citrus. Neat it is very sweet; the better bottlings made from real fruit are worth seeking out.

composition.summary: Banana infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Banana, natural or compounded, plus vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened

composition.process: Real-fruit versions are darker and less neon than the compounded ones, and taste noticeably less like confectionery.

name: Crème de Mûre
description: Blackberry liqueur, deep purple and tart under the sweetness. Without it there is no Bramble, which is the only cocktail invented in 1980s London that anyone still orders.
funFact: Dick Bradsell built the Bramble at Fred's Club in Soho, drizzling the mûre over crushed ice so it bleeds down through the drink.

serve.how: Drizzled over a gin sour on crushed ice to make a Bramble — pour it last and do not stir, the bleed is the point. It also lifts a Kir if you want something darker than cassis.

composition.summary: Blackberries macerated in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Blackberries, sometimes with raspberry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, pressed and sweetened

composition.process: Like cassis, it is a maceration rather than a distillate, so the fruit character stays raw and bright.

name: Crème de Noyaux
description: Made from apricot and cherry stones rather than nuts, which gives an almond flavour from a fruit source. Pink, old-fashioned, and the ingredient that makes a Pink Squirrel pink.
funFact: The almond note comes from benzaldehyde in the kernels — the same compound that makes marzipan taste of almond, present here without a single almond involved.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient rather than a sipper. It is the almond note in a Pink Squirrel and an Old Etonian, and it substitutes for orgeat in drinks where you want alcohol rather than syrup.

composition.summary: Apricot and cherry kernels macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Apricot and cherry stones, cracked

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened and coloured

composition.process: Kernels contain amygdalin, which is why the quantity used is carefully controlled.

name: Melon Liqueur
description: Bright green muskmelon liqueur, invented in Japan in 1978 and responsible for an entire decade of drinks. Sweet, unmistakable, and rehabilitated in recent years by bartenders who stopped being embarrassed by it.
funFact: Suntory launched it in 1978 and the colour comes entirely from added dye — the melon infusion itself is pale gold.

serve.how: With soda and lime over ice, which is far better than its reputation. In cocktails it makes a Midori Sour or a Japanese Slipper. Cut it with acid; the sugar needs something to push against.

composition.summary: Muskmelon infused into neutral spirit, sweetened and coloured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Yubari and muskmelon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened; colour added

composition.process: Two melon varieties are used, one for aroma and one for body.

name: Black Raspberry Liqueur
description: Black raspberries, blackberries, vanilla and honey infused into cognac, from the Loire. Sold in a round bottle bound like a medieval orb, and rather better than the packaging suggests.
funFact: The recipe is said to descend from a raspberry liqueur served to Louis XIV when he visited the Loire in the seventeenth century.

serve.how: Topped with champagne as a Kir Royale variant, or in a French Martini with vodka and pineapple. Neat over ice it is heavy going — it wants dilution and acid.

composition.summary: Berries infused into cognac with vanilla and honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Black raspberry, blackberry, Madagascar vanilla, honey

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused over weeks, then blended

composition.process: A cognac base rather than neutral spirit is what gives it weight behind the fruit.

name: Coconut Rum Liqueur
description: Caribbean rum flavoured with coconut and cut to around 21%. Dismissed for decades as a holiday drink, and quietly indispensable in any tiki bar that wants coconut without opening a fresh nut.
funFact: It was created in 1978 specifically to make Piña Coladas easier to serve at bar speed, which is exactly what it still does.

serve.how: With pineapple juice, or long with soda and lime. In a Piña Colada it replaces both the rum and the cream of coconut in a hurry. Keep it cold; warm it turns cloying fast.

composition.summary: Caribbean rum blended with coconut extract and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barbadian rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Coconut, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: The rum base is real and aged, which is why it mixes better than a neutral coconut liqueur would.

name: Anisette
description: The sweetest of the anise family, made from green anise seed and heavily sugared. Softer than pastis and lower in strength than ouzo, and a Mediterranean breakfast habit for older generations.
funFact: Marie Brizard began making it in Bordeaux in 1755 from a recipe she was reportedly given by a West Indian sailor she had nursed through illness.

serve.how: With cold water, which turns it milky, or over ice. In Italy and Spain it also goes into coffee. It is sweeter than pastis, so use less of it and more water than instinct suggests.

composition.summary: Green anise seed distilled into neutral spirit and heavily sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green anise seed, sometimes coriander and fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sugared

composition.process: The higher sugar is what separates it from pastis and ouzo more than the botanicals do.

name: Chinchón
description: Spain's protected anise spirit, from the town of Chinchón south of Madrid, made in dry, sweet and extra-strength versions. Distilled from anise grown locally rather than flavoured after the fact.
funFact: The seco especial is bottled at 74%, which makes it one of the strongest commercially available anise spirits anywhere.

serve.how: Dry over ice as an aperitif, sweet after a meal, and the 74% version with considerable respect and a great deal of water. Spaniards also add it to coffee as a carajillo.

composition.summary: Locally grown anise distilled in copper alembics.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Anise grown around Chinchón

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, distilled with the seed

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 35% to 74% depending on style

composition.process: Distilling with the seed rather than adding oil afterwards is what earns it protected status.

name: Herbsaint
description: New Orleans' anise spirit, created in 1934 as a legal substitute for absinthe when the real thing was still banned. It is what a Sazerac is rinsed with in its home city.
funFact: The name is a contraction of herbe sainte, the Creole French name for wormwood — a fairly transparent nod to what it was standing in for.

serve.glass: Used as a rinse; or a tumbler with water
serve.how: Rinse a chilled glass and discard the excess, then build a Sazerac in it. Neat it takes water like pastis and louches the same way. The Original formula is drier and closer to the pre-war recipe.

composition.summary: Anise and fennel distilled into neutral spirit, wormwood-free at first.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Star anise, fennel, herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the botanicals

composition.process: It was built to satisfy absinthe drinkers under a legal regime that banned the original, and it never lost that job.

name: Kümmel
description: Caraway, cumin and fennel in a clear, sweet liqueur with roots in sixteenth-century Holland and a devoted afterlife in Scottish golf clubhouses, where it is drunk against the shakes.
funFact: It is known in British golfing circles as the putting mixture, on the widely held theory that it steadies the hands.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass, or over ice. It also works in a Silver Bullet with gin and lemon. The caraway is assertive, so it divides a room much as aquavit does.

composition.summary: Caraway and cumin distilled into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Caraway seed, cumin, fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sweetened

composition.process: It shares its botanical backbone with aquavit; the difference is the sugar.

name: Cinnamon Schnapps
description: Neutral spirit heavily flavoured with cinnamon, sometimes carrying flakes of gold leaf. Bracing, sweet and hot, and the single most-ordered shot in a great many bars.
funFact: The gold-flake versions descend from Danziger Goldwasser, a sixteenth-century tradition of suspending edible gold in liqueur as a supposed medicine.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer, in one. Cold is essential — warm, the sugar dominates and the cinnamon turns medicinal. It also does real work in hot cider or a mulled drink.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with cinnamon and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Cassia cinnamon oil and extract

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended, not redistilled

composition.process: Cassia rather than true Ceylon cinnamon gives the sharper, hotter note the category is built on.

name: Parfait Amour
description: A violet-purple liqueur of citrus, rose petals, vanilla and almond, made since the eighteenth century and once sold as a love potion. More perfume than drink, and used accordingly.
funFact: It was marketed in the 1700s as an aphrodisiac, which is where the name — perfect love — comes from.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient rather than a sipper. A bar spoon adds colour and floral lift to a gin sour; more than that and the drink tastes of soap. Sits close to crème de violette but with citrus behind it.

composition.summary: Citrus peel, rose and violet infused into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or brandy

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Curaçao orange peel, rose petals, violet, vanilla, almond

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and sweetened; colour added

composition.process: It is essentially a curaçao with flowers, which is why the citrus is still detectable under the perfume.

name: Pistachio Liqueur
description: Sicilian pistachios, mostly from Bronte on the slopes of Etna, blended into a cream or clear liqueur. Intensely nutty, and a relatively modern addition to the Italian liqueur canon.
funFact: Bronte pistachios grow in volcanic soil on Etna, are harvested only every other year, and cost several times the price of ordinary pistachios.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after dinner, or poured over gelato. The cream versions separate if frozen, so chill rather than freeze.

composition.summary: Roasted pistachios infused into spirit, often with cream.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bronte pistachios, sugar, sometimes cream and vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then blended

composition.process: Roasting the nuts before maceration is what pushes it from green and raw to rounded.

name: Nocello
description: A walnut and hazelnut liqueur from Emilia-Romagna, lighter and less syrupy than nocino, which is made from green walnuts. This one uses ripe nuts, so it reads as toasted rather than bitter.
funFact: Its cousin nocino is made from green walnuts picked at midsummer, husks and all, which is why nocino is bitter and this is not.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, over ice, or poured onto vanilla gelato. It also works in coffee and stands in well for Frangelico when you want walnut rather than pure hazelnut.

composition.summary: Ripe walnuts and hazelnuts infused into neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ripe walnuts and hazelnuts

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: Ripe nuts rather than green ones is the entire distinction from nocino.

name: Blood Orange Liqueur
description: Made from Sicilian blood oranges grown on Etna's slopes, with the fruit's characteristic raspberry note intact. Deeper and less bitter than a curaçao, and a genuinely different thing from triple sec.
funFact: Blood oranges get their colour from anthocyanins that only develop when nights are cold, which is why Etna's altitude matters to the crop.

serve.how: Over ice with soda, or in place of triple sec in a Margarita or Sidecar where it brings berry as well as citrus. At 40% it has enough backbone to be sipped neat over a cube.

composition.summary: Blood orange peel and juice distilled and blended into neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sanguinello and Tarocco blood oranges, plus lemon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peel distilled, juice blended in afterwards

composition.process: Higher strength than most orange liqueurs, which is why it holds up in a stirred drink.

name: Bergamot Liqueur
description: Made from the Calabrian bergamot, a citrus grown almost nowhere else and best known for flavouring Earl Grey tea. Floral, bitter and unmistakably perfumed.
funFact: Around 80% of the world's bergamot comes from a narrow coastal strip of Calabria, and the fruit is grown almost entirely for its oil rather than to eat.

serve.how: Cold and neat after dinner, or a bar spoon in a gin sour where it does what a tea infusion would without the tannin. It is bitter enough to work as an aperitif over ice with soda.

composition.summary: Bergamot peel infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Calabrian bergamot peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated or distilled, then sweetened

composition.process: The fruit is too sour and bitter to eat, so essentially the entire crop goes to oil and liqueur.

name: Ratafia Catalana
description: A Catalan liqueur of green walnuts and dozens of herbs, macerated in the sun through summer and traditionally started on the feast of Saint John. Made at home across Catalonia to family recipes.
funFact: The jars are traditionally left outdoors for the whole of summer, so the maceration is driven by sunlight rather than heat from a still.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, at cellar temperature. Catalans serve it with dessert and at village festivals. Sweet and heavily spiced, so a small pour goes far.

composition.summary: Green walnuts and herbs sun-macerated in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or aguardiente

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green walnuts, cinnamon, nutmeg, lemon peel, dozens of herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Sun-macerated over months

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 26%

composition.process: Nou de Sant Joan — walnuts picked around 24 June, while the shell is still soft enough to cut.

name: Palo de Mallorca
description: A Mallorcan bitter of gentian root and cinchona bark, dark as treacle and originally sold as an anti-malarial when the island's wetlands still carried the disease.
funFact: It was drunk to ward off malaria in the Mallorcan marshlands, and survived the disease's eradication purely because islanders had grown to like it.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and a slice of lemon, which is the standard island serve. Neat it is thick and very sweet. Locals also drink it with orange juice.

composition.summary: Gentian and cinchona infused in spirit with caramelised sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Gentian root, cinchona bark, burnt sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

composition.process: The burnt sugar gives both the colour and most of the body.

name: Guavaberry Liqueur
description: Sint Maarten's national liqueur, made from wild guavaberries that ripen only briefly in the island's hills — a fruit unrelated to guava despite the name. Rum-based, spiced, and a Christmas tradition.
funFact: There is a traditional Christmas carol on the island whose entire subject is going house to house asking for a taste of the family's guavaberry.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or over ice. Islanders drink it at Christmas and mix it with rum punch. The wild fruit is picked from hillside trees rather than farmed, so supply is genuinely limited.

composition.summary: Wild guavaberries steeped in aged rum with spice and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aged Caribbean rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Wild guavaberry (Myrciaria floribunda), cinnamon, clove

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for months

composition.process: The berry has nothing to do with guava; it is a myrtle relative that fruits for a few weeks a year.

name: Sorrel Liqueur
description: Made from hibiscus calyces — sorrel in Caribbean usage — steeped with rum, ginger and clove. Deep crimson, tart and spiced, and inseparable from Christmas across the West Indies.
funFact: The plant is Hibiscus sabdariffa, the same species that makes agua de Jamaica in Mexico and karkade in Egypt — three continents, one calyx.

serve.how: Cold over ice, or topped with sparkling wine. It is tart enough not to need much cutting. Caribbean households make it fresh each December and the bought version is a year-round stand-in.

composition.summary: Hibiscus calyces steeped with rum, ginger and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Caribbean rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dried hibiscus calyces, ginger, clove, cinnamon, orange peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: It is the calyx that is used, not the flower — the fleshy cup left after the bloom drops.

name: Ponche Kuba
description: A Caribbean cream liqueur of rum, condensed milk, egg and spice, from Curaçao and hugely popular across Venezuela and the Dutch islands. Thicker and more cinnamon-driven than Irish cream.
funFact: It is a Christmas fixture across the southern Caribbean, where it competes directly with Venezuela's ponche crema for the same place on the table.

serve.how: Cold from the fridge, neat, in a small glass. Shake before pouring. It also goes into coffee, and over ice cream. Refrigerate once opened and finish it reasonably quickly.

composition.summary: Rum blended with condensed milk, egg and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Caribbean rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Condensed milk, egg, cinnamon, nutmeg, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended, not distilled

composition.process: Condensed milk rather than fresh cream is what makes it shelf-stable in the tropics.

name: Licor de Café
description: Costa Rican coffee liqueur, built on cane spirit and Tarrazú beans, drier and more roast-forward than the Mexican coffee liqueurs that dominate the shelf.
funFact: Tarrazú beans grow between 1,200 and 1,900 metres, and the altitude is what gives the acidity that survives into the liqueur.

serve.how: Over ice, or with milk. It is less sweet than Kahlúa, which makes it the better choice in an Espresso Martini where you want coffee rather than sugar. Costa Ricans also add it to hot coffee.

composition.summary: Costa Rican coffee extracted into cane spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Tarrazú arabica coffee, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Coffee extracted and blended

composition.process: Less sugar than the Mexican style is the whole difference, and it shows in cocktails.

name: Yuzushu
description: Japanese yuzu steeped in shochu or sake, cloudy with pulp and intensely aromatic. Yuzu is barely edible as a fruit — almost all peel and pip — which is exactly why it works as a liqueur.
funFact: Yuzu trees can take a decade to fruit, and the fruit is so pithy that a kilo yields very little juice — which is why it is priced like a spice.

serve.how: Over ice, or with soda in a highball. Shake the bottle first; the pulp settles and it is most of the flavour. Low in alcohol, so it drinks like a long aperitif rather than a digestive.

composition.summary: Yuzu fruit and peel steeped in shochu or sake and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Shochu, sake or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Whole yuzu, peel included

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened; usually unfiltered

composition.process: The peel carries the aroma, so the fruit goes in whole rather than juiced.

name: Maesil-ju
description: Korean green plum liqueur, made by steeping unripe maesil plums in soju with sugar. Sweeter and rounder than Japanese umeshu, made from the same fruit and a different tradition.
funFact: Maesil and ume are the same fruit, Prunus mume, which is neither plum nor apricot but sits somewhere between the two.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice, after a meal. Koreans also drink it with soda. It is sweeter than umeshu, so it works better as a dessert pour than an aperitif.

composition.summary: Unripe maesil plums steeped in soju with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Soju or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green maesil plums, rock sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for months

composition.process: The fruit must be unripe; ripe maesil ferments rather than infusing cleanly.

name: Lychee Liqueur
description: Lychee infused into neutral spirit, floral and perfumed to the point of tasting artificial even when it is not. Responsible for the entire 2000s vogue for the Lychee Martini.
funFact: Lychee's characteristic aroma comes partly from rose oxide, the same compound that makes roses and some Gewürztraminer wines smell as they do.

serve.how: In a Lychee Martini with vodka, or topped with sparkling wine. It needs acid — a squeeze of lime keeps it from reading as syrup. Neat it is very sweet.

composition.summary: Lychee fruit infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Lychee fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened

composition.process: The floral note is fragile and the better producers avoid heat entirely in production.

name: Ginger Liqueur
description: Fresh ginger macerated into a spirit base, often with cognac or eau-de-vie behind it. Hot, sweet and considerably more useful behind a bar than its shelf presence suggests.
funFact: Gingerol, the compound responsible for the burn, converts to the milder zingerone when heated — which is why cooked ginger is sweeter than raw.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and lime, or as a modifier in a whisky sour where it does the work of both sweetener and spice. It also improves a Moscow Mule considerably.

composition.summary: Fresh ginger macerated into a brandy or neutral spirit base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac, eau-de-vie or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Fresh ginger root, citrus, sometimes vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then blended and sweetened

composition.process: Cold maceration preserves the raw burn that heat would soften.

name: Apricot Brandy Liqueur
description: Not a brandy at all in most bottles but an apricot liqueur, which causes endless confusion with classic cocktail recipes. Sweet, stone-fruited, and essential to a great many pre-war drinks.
funFact: Old cocktail books calling for apricot brandy almost always mean the liqueur, not a true fruit distillate — substituting a dry eau-de-vie wrecks the drink.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient. It is in a Pendennis Club, a Charlie Chaplin and countless tiki builds. If a vintage recipe calls for apricot brandy, reach for this rather than a Marillenbrand.

composition.summary: Apricots and kernels infused into brandy or neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Brandy or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Apricot flesh and kernels

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: Kernels supply the almond note; flesh alone tastes flat and jammy.

name: Sea Buckthorn Liqueur
description: Made from a fiercely tart orange berry that grows on coastal dunes across northern Europe and central Asia. Sharp, oily and high in vitamin C, with a flavour somewhere between passionfruit and pine.
funFact: The berries cling so tightly that traditional harvesting involves freezing whole branches and shaking the fruit off.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or topped with sparkling wine where the acidity does real work. It is tart enough to function as the citrus element in a cocktail rather than only the sweet one.

composition.summary: Sea buckthorn berries macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Hippophae rhamnoides berries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and pressed, then sweetened

composition.process: The berries carry oil as well as juice, which gives an unusual weight on the palate.

name: Lingonberry Liqueur
description: Nordic lingonberries steeped in grain spirit — tart, faintly bitter and less sweet than most berry liqueurs. The berry is a Scandinavian staple that grows wild in forest floor across the north.
funFact: Lingonberries keep almost indefinitely without preservation because they are naturally high in benzoic acid.

serve.how: Cold and neat after a meal, or over ice with soda. The tartness makes it useful in cocktails wherever you would otherwise reach for cranberry, with far more depth.

composition.summary: Wild lingonberries macerated in grain spirit and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Wild-picked lingonberries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, pressed, sweetened

composition.process: Less sugar than most berry liqueurs, which is what keeps the tartness in front.

name: Rum Cream
description: Jamaican rum blended with dairy cream and spice, the Caribbean's answer to Irish cream. Richer and more molasses-driven, and considerably better over ice than its supermarket placement suggests.
funFact: It emerged in the 1970s as Caribbean distillers watched Irish cream take off and reasoned that aged rum would work at least as well as whiskey.

serve.how: Over ice, or in coffee. Shake before pouring. Jamaican rum cream carries more spice than the Irish style, so it works in a Mudslide or over ice cream without needing extra nutmeg.

composition.summary: Aged Jamaican rum emulsified with dairy cream and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aged Jamaican rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dairy cream, nutmeg, vanilla, sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended and homogenised

composition.process: The rum's ester content is what keeps the fruit note detectable through the dairy.

name: Dulce de Leche Liqueur
description: Argentina's caramelised milk turned into a cream liqueur, thick and sweet enough to be a dessert on its own. A relatively modern product built on the country's most beloved ingredient.
funFact: Argentina and Uruguay have argued for decades over which country invented dulce de leche, and neither has conceded an inch.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in a small glass, or poured over ice cream. It is extremely sweet, so treat it as dessert. It also goes into coffee, which cuts it usefully.

composition.summary: Dulce de leche blended with spirit and cream.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or brandy

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dulce de leche, cream, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended and homogenised

composition.process: Real dulce de leche rather than caramel syrup is what separates the good bottles from the rest.

name: Crema de Orujo
description: Galician pomace spirit blended with cream, coffee and sugar into a pale, sweet liqueur that has quietly become the region's most popular after-dinner drink — outselling the clear orujo it comes from.
funFact: Galician restaurants routinely bring a bottle to the table unasked at the end of a meal, alongside the clear orujo and the herbal one.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer or the fridge, neat, in a small glass. Cold is essential — warm it separates on the palate and the pomace shows through the cream unpleasantly.

composition.summary: Orujo blended with dairy cream, coffee and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Galician orujo

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Cream, coffee, sugar, sometimes vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: The pomace base gives a rougher edge than the Irish cream style, which Galicians consider the point.

name: Grande Champagne Cognac
description: The premier cru of Cognac, whose chalky soil gives a spirit so slow to mature that it is often unapproachable young and extraordinary old. Champagne here means open field, not the wine region.
funFact: The chalk is Campanian limestone, the same geology as the Champagne wine region hundreds of kilometres north, which is where the shared name comes from.

serve.how: Neat in a tulip that concentrates rather than disperses. Do not warm it in your hands — the fashion for heating cognac drives off exactly the delicate floral notes the cru is prized for.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc grown on chalk, twice pot-distilled, long-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc from the Grande Champagne cru

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double distillation in Charentais pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Very long; the cru rewards decades in Limousin oak

composition.process: Rancio — the nutty, mushroomy note of great old cognac — develops here more than in any other cru.

name: Petite Champagne Cognac
description: The second cru, ringing Grande Champagne on slightly less chalky soil. Finer and faster to mature than its neighbour, and the other half of what makes a Fine Champagne blend.
funFact: A cognac labelled Fine Champagne must be Grande and Petite Champagne only, with at least half from the Grande.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature. It matures faster than Grande Champagne, so a mid-aged bottling is often more expressive than an equivalent from the premier cru at the same age.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc from the second cru, double-distilled and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc from Petite Champagne

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Charentais double distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Limousin or Tronçais oak

composition.process: Slightly less chalk means slightly less structure, and a spirit that opens earlier.

name: Borderies Cognac
description: The smallest cognac cru, on clay and flint rather than chalk, producing a rounder spirit famous for violets and nuts. Only about five per cent of the region, and blenders fight over it.
funFact: At roughly 4,000 hectares it is by far the smallest of the six crus, and single-cru Borderies bottlings are correspondingly scarce.

serve.how: Neat and unwarmed. The violet note is the signature and it is fragile, so avoid ice and avoid heat. Worth tasting beside a Grande Champagne to see how much the soil does.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc on clay and flint, double-distilled and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc from the Borderies cru

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Charentais double distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Matures faster than the Champagne crus

composition.process: Clay-flint soil rather than chalk is credited with the floral, nutty profile the cru is known for.

name: Fins Bois Cognac
description: The largest cognac cru, wrapping around all the others, giving a rounder and quicker-maturing spirit with pressed grape and stone fruit. The workhorse of most house blends.
funFact: It covers more than a third of the entire Cognac appellation, which is why it forms the backbone of most VS and VSOP blends.

serve.how: Neat, or in cocktails where its fruit-forward roundness holds up better than the finer crus. This is the cognac to use in a Sidecar without feeling guilty about it.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc from the largest cru, double-distilled and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc from Fins Bois

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Charentais double distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Matures quickly; good young

composition.process: Fast maturation makes it commercially essential, since it is drinkable years before the Champagne crus.

name: Cognac Hors d'Âge
description: Beyond age — officially the same minimum as XO, but used by houses for blends far older than any category covers. Where rancio, that nutty oxidative note, becomes the point of the drink.
funFact: The oldest components in some Hors d'Âge blends predate the phylloxera louse that destroyed the region's vineyards in the 1870s.

serve.how: Neat, in a small pour, and give it twenty minutes in the glass. Never warmed, never iced, and emphatically never mixed. The whole value is in aromas that heat destroys.

composition.summary: Very old cognac eaux-de-vie blended across decades.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc, usually across several crus

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Charentais double distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Decades; officially XO minimum but in practice far older

composition.process: Above about 50 years in cask the spirit is moved to glass demijohns to stop it taking more wood.

name: Bas-Armagnac
description: The finest of the three Armagnac zones, on sandy acidic soil in the west of Gascony. Column-distilled once to a low strength, which leaves in the character that a second pass would strip out.
funFact: Armagnac is the oldest documented distilled spirit in France, with a description of its medicinal virtues written down in 1310.

serve.how: Neat, unwarmed, in a small pour. Vintage Armagnacs are common in a way vintage cognacs are not, so buying a bottle from a birth year is genuinely possible.

composition.summary: Gascon white grapes column-distilled once and long-aged in local oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Baco, Ugni Blanc, Folle Blanche, Colombard

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single pass through an alambic armagnaçais, to around 52%

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Black Gascon oak, often decades; vintages are common

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–48%, often cask strength

composition.process: Single distillation to a low strength is the defining choice — it keeps congeners cognac deliberately removes.

name: Ténarèze
description: The middle Armagnac zone, on clay and limestone, giving a firmer and more structured spirit than Bas-Armagnac. Needs longer in wood, and rewards it with real grip.
funFact: Ténarèze is the zone most associated with Folle Blanche, a delicate and disease-prone grape that nearly disappeared after phylloxera.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature. Young Ténarèze can be tough going; it is a zone that genuinely needs twenty years, and blenders often use it to give backbone to softer Bas-Armagnac.

composition.summary: Gascon grapes on clay-limestone, single-distilled and long-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc, Folle Blanche, Baco

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single pass, alambic armagnaçais

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Long ageing required; firm when young

composition.process: Clay-limestone gives structure where Bas-Armagnac's sand gives finesse.

name: Blanche Armagnac
description: Unaged Armagnac, given its own appellation only in 2005 after centuries of being drunk quietly by producers who never bottled it. Clear, floral and startlingly grape-forward.
funFact: Growers had drunk it at home for generations; it only became a legal category when the region realised there was a market for a clear, aromatic spirit.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in a small glass — treat it like an eau-de-vie rather than a brandy. It also makes an unusual and very good base for a sour, where the grape character survives citrus.

composition.summary: Gascon grapes single-distilled and rested in glass, never wood.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Folle Blanche, Ugni Blanc, Colombard, Baco

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single pass, alambic armagnaçais

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three months in inert vessels — no wood permitted

composition.process: The rule forbidding wood is what makes it a distinct appellation rather than simply young Armagnac.

name: Calvados Pays d'Auge
description: The top Calvados appellation, twice pot-distilled from cider in the heart of Normandy. Richer and more complex than standard Calvados, and the only zone where double distillation is compulsory.
funFact: The trou normand — a shot of Calvados mid-meal to reopen the appetite — is a genuine regional custom, not a tourist invention.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or mid-meal in the Norman fashion. Older bottlings develop a dried-fruit depth that surprises people expecting apple juice. Do not chill it.

composition.summary: Norman cider twice pot-distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cider from Pays d'Auge apples, at least 70% bitter and bittersweet varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double distillation in a copper pot still, compulsory in this AOC

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum two years in oak

composition.process: Cider is fermented for weeks before distilling, which is why the base is closer to wine than to juice.

name: Calvados Domfrontais
description: The pear-driven Calvados, requiring at least 30% perry in the base — and in practice often far more. Lighter, more floral and markedly different from the apple-dominated appellations.
funFact: The perry pear trees of the Domfrontais can live over two hundred years and are often far older than the orchards' apple trees.

serve.how: Neat, slightly below room temperature so the pear stays forward. It is the Calvados to give someone who thinks they do not like Calvados — lighter and more perfumed than they expect.

composition.summary: Perry and cider column-distilled once and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Minimum 30% pears; often 70% or more in practice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single column distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak

composition.process: Single distillation here, unlike Pays d'Auge, keeps the delicate pear aromatics intact.

name: Pommeau de Normandie
description: Fresh apple must stopped with Calvados before it can ferment, then aged in oak. Normandy's answer to Pineau des Charentes, and a far better aperitif than its obscurity suggests.
funFact: It was made informally by Norman farmers for centuries before receiving its own appellation in 1991.

serve.how: Cold, before the meal, in a small pour. It is exceptional with foie gras and with melon, and Normans also use it to deglaze pans for pork and chicken.

composition.summary: Unfermented apple must fortified with Calvados and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh cider apple must

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Calvados, at least one year old

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum 14 months in oak

composition.process: Because fermentation never starts, the apple's own sugar is what sweetens it.

name: Macvin du Jura
description: Jura grape must fortified with the region's own marc, to a recipe recorded in the fourteenth century. Nutty and oxidative in the way everything from the Jura is.
funFact: The recipe appears in a fourteenth-century manuscript from the Abbey of Château-Chalon, which makes it one of the oldest documented fortified drinks in France.

serve.how: Cold as an aperitif or with a fruit dessert. The Jura's characteristic walnut note makes it superb with Comté, which is the local pairing and hard to improve on.

composition.summary: Jura grape must fortified with aged marc du Jura.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Must from Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard or Trousseau

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Marc du Jura aged at least 18 months

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum 12 months in oak

composition.process: The marc must come from the same estate, which keeps it a genuinely local product.

name: Pisco Puro
description: Peruvian pisco from a single grape variety, distilled to proof with no water added and no wood contact. The purest expression of the category and the one that shows the grape most clearly.
funFact: Peruvian law forbids adding water after distillation, so the strength in the bottle is the strength that came off the still — a rule almost unique in world spirits.

serve.how: Cool and neat in a glass that holds aroma, or in a Pisco Sour. A puro made from Quebranta is the classic sour base; the aromatic varieties are better sipped.

composition.summary: A single permitted grape variety, fermented and distilled to bottling strength.

components.label: Base
components.detail: One of eight permitted varieties, single-varietal

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper falca or alembic, distilled to proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three months in inert vessels; no wood

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 38–48%, undiluted

composition.process: Distilling to proof means the cut points alone determine the final strength — there is no correcting afterwards.

name: Pisco Acholado
description: A blend of grape varieties, either co-fermented or blended after distilling. Acholado means mixed, and it is the style most Peruvian bartenders reach for in a sour.
funFact: Blending is where the distiller's skill shows most, since the aromatic and non-aromatic varieties behave very differently in the glass.

serve.glass: Coupe for a sour, copita neat
serve.how: The default choice for a Pisco Sour — it has enough aromatic lift to survive lime, egg white and bitters. Neat it is more complex than a puro and less pointed.

composition.summary: Two or more permitted varieties blended, distilled to proof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: A blend of aromatic and non-aromatic permitted grapes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, to proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three months minimum, no wood

composition.process: Blending can happen before fermentation or after distillation, and producers argue about which is better.

name: Pisco Mosto Verde
description: Distilled from must that has been stopped mid-fermentation, so sugar is still present when it hits the still. Wasteful, expensive, and produces the silkiest pisco made.
funFact: Because the must is not fully fermented, it takes substantially more grapes per bottle than any other pisco style — which is exactly why it costs more.

serve.how: Neat and cool, always. Using a mosto verde in a sour is not wrong but is close to a waste — the texture that justifies the price disappears under lime.

composition.summary: Partially fermented must distilled while sugar remains.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Permitted varieties, fermentation halted early

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, to proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three months in inert vessels

composition.process: Residual sugar does not survive distillation, but the unfermented must changes the aromatic profile and the mouthfeel.

name: Pisco Quebranta
description: Made from Peru's signature non-aromatic grape, a mutation of Criolla Negra that adapted to the coastal desert. Earthy and restrained rather than floral, and the traditional backbone of a Pisco Sour.
funFact: The grape is named for the way it breaks — quebrar — the palate of anyone who eats it fresh, being far too tannic for the table.

serve.glass: Copita neat, coupe in a sour
serve.how: The classic Pisco Sour base. Its lack of floral aromatics is a feature there: it gives body without fighting the lime. Neat it is a quieter, earthier pisco than the aromatic varieties.

composition.summary: Single-varietal Quebranta, fermented dry and distilled to proof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Quebranta grapes from the Ica valley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, single distillation to proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three months, no wood

composition.process: It is classed as non-aromatic, which in pisco terms means the spirit tastes of texture and earth rather than flowers.

name: Pisco Italia
description: Made from the Italia grape, a Muscat cross, and the most overtly perfumed of the Peruvian piscos. Intensely floral and grapey, and closer to a Muscat eau-de-vie than to a neutral brandy.
funFact: Italia is one of four grapes Peru classes as aromatic, alongside Torontel, Moscatel and Albilla.

serve.how: Neat and cool, in a glass wide enough to release the aromatics. It makes a striking Chilcano with ginger ale and lime, where the floral note lifts the whole drink.

composition.summary: Single-varietal Italia grapes distilled to proof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Italia, a Muscat-family grape

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, to proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three months in inert vessels

composition.process: Aromatic varieties need gentler distillation, since the terpenes that carry the perfume are easily cooked off.

name: Brandy de Penedès
description: Catalonia's brandy, distilled from Penedès white grapes and aged by the same solera method as Jerez but in a cooler, wetter climate that slows everything down.
funFact: It holds its own protected designation separate from Brandy de Jerez, which is unusual for two brandies made in the same country by similar methods.

serve.how: Neat after dinner. It is drier and less caramel-heavy than Jerez brandy because the casks are less often ex-sherry, which makes it the better of the two in a cocktail.

composition.summary: Penedès grapes distilled and solera-aged in Catalonia.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Parellada, Macabeo and other Penedès whites

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot and column

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera system, often in French oak rather than ex-sherry

composition.process: French oak rather than ex-sherry butts is the main reason it tastes drier than Jerez.

name: Aguardente da Lourinhã
description: Portugal's only wine-brandy appellation, from a small coastal area north of Lisbon. One of just three wine-brandy DOCs in Europe alongside Cognac and Armagnac, and by far the least known.
funFact: Cognac, Armagnac and Lourinhã are the only three demarcated wine-brandy regions in Europe, and almost nobody outside Portugal has heard of the third.

serve.how: Neat after dinner. The Atlantic climate gives high-acid base wine, which distils into something noticeably brighter than most Iberian brandy.

composition.summary: Atlantic-coast white wine distilled and oak-aged in Lourinhã.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Local white varieties from the Lourinhã DOC

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or continuous still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum two years in oak

composition.process: Cool Atlantic conditions give thin, acidic wine — poor to drink and excellent to distil.

name: Kanyak
description: Turkish grape brandy, made since the 1930s as part of the young republic's push to build domestic industry. Sweeter and softer than French brandy, and drunk in Turkey as often in coffee as neat.
funFact: The name is a Turkish rendering of cognac, adopted after French producers objected to the original spelling on Turkish labels.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or added to Turkish coffee. It is sweeter than western brandy, so it needs less warming and rewards a smaller pour.

composition.summary: Anatolian grapes distilled and oak-aged in Turkey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Turkish white grapes, largely from the Aegean

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot and column

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, three years and up

composition.process: State monopoly production shaped the style for decades before privatisation.

name: Divin
description: Moldova's brandy, made by the Charentais method in a country that has grown wine grapes for four thousand years. Renamed from konyak after independence, and genuinely good for its price.
funFact: Moldova's Cricova cellars run to more than a hundred kilometres of tunnels, enough that visitors are driven through them by car.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, and in the Moldovan manner during rather than after the meal. Older bottlings are notably soft, since local oak is milder than Limousin.

composition.summary: Moldovan white wine double-distilled and aged in local oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Moldovan white grapes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Charentais-style double distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Local Moldovan oak, three years and up

composition.process: The name was coined after independence, from divine, to break with the Soviet-era konyak label.

name: Zwetschgenwasser
description: Made from the Zwetschge, a small oval damson-type plum that grows across southern Germany and Alsace. Drier and more austere than Slivovitz, and one of the classic clear fruit brandies.
funFact: The Zwetschge is a different fruit from the round Pflaume, and using the wrong one produces a noticeably jammier, less precise spirit.

serve.how: Cool but not frozen, in a small pour after a meal. The stone note is part of the character, so let it sit in the glass a minute rather than shooting it.

composition.summary: Zwetschge plums fermented whole and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Zwetschge plums, stones often included

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, tight heart cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass, never wood

composition.process: A proportion of stones fermented with the fruit supplies the bitter-almond finish.

name: Mirabelle
description: Distilled from the small golden Mirabelle plum of Lorraine, which has protected status and a season lasting about six weeks. Delicate, honeyed and among the finest eaux-de-vie made.
funFact: Lorraine produces the overwhelming majority of the world's Mirabelles, and the harvest is short enough that the whole region organises around it.

serve.how: Cool and neat, in a narrow glass that traps the aroma. Nose it well before drinking; a good Mirabelle smells more intensely of the fruit than the fruit does.

composition.summary: Mirabelle plums fermented and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Mirabelle de Lorraine plums

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: The fruit is tiny and yields little juice, which is why good Mirabelle is priced like a fine spirit.

name: Quetsch
description: Alsatian purple plum brandy, darker and spicier in character than Mirabelle, though equally clear in the glass. Made from the same fruit family as Zwetschgenwasser across the border.
funFact: Quetsche, Zwetschge and the Slavic sliva are all the same fruit under different linguistic traditions, which is why the spirits taste like relatives.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal. Alsatian restaurants pour it alongside Mirabelle and kirsch as a trio, and tasting them side by side is the best way to learn what fruit distillation does.

composition.summary: Quetsch plums fermented and double-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Quetsch plums from Alsace

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: More stone character than Mirabelle, which is what makes it read as spicier.

name: Himbeergeist
description: Raspberry spirit made by macerating the fruit in neutral alcohol and then redistilling, because raspberries carry too little sugar to ferment usefully on their own. Geist means spirit in exactly that sense.
funFact: Any fruit too low in sugar to ferment — raspberry, elderberry, sloe — is made as a Geist rather than a Wasser, which is a legal distinction as well as a technical one.

serve.how: Chill the glass rather than the bottle and pour a small measure. The aroma is the entire product. It is also superb poured over fresh raspberries as a dessert.

composition.summary: Raspberries macerated in neutral spirit, then redistilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit plus fresh raspberries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated then redistilled — not fermented

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: Fermenting raspberries directly gives almost no alcohol, hence the maceration-and-redistill method.

name: Vieille Prune
description: Plum brandy aged in oak until it turns amber — the aged counterpart to the clear plum eaux-de-vie, and a speciality of southwest France. Softer and rounder, with the fruit turned to compote.
funFact: Souillac in the Lot has made it for centuries, and older bottlings can spend twenty years or more in cask before release.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature after dinner. Unlike clear plum brandy this one takes warmth well and behaves more like an Armagnac than an eau-de-vie.

composition.summary: Plums fermented, distilled and aged in oak for years.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ente or local plums

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak casks, often a decade or more

composition.process: Wood ageing turns the sharp stone-fruit character into something closer to dried fruit and spice.

name: Eau-de-Vie de Coing
description: Quince brandy, from a fruit that is hard, astringent and nearly inedible raw but distils into one of the most perfumed spirits in the category. Difficult to make and made in small quantities.
funFact: Quince yields very little juice for its weight and ferments slowly, which is why quince eau-de-vie is among the most expensive fruit distillates.

serve.how: Cool and neat, in a small pour, at the end of a meal. It is intensely floral and does not need help. Alsatian producers make it in tiny runs and it sells out locally.

composition.summary: Quinces fermented whole and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ripe quince

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, narrow cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: The fruit must be fully ripe and yellow; green quince gives a harsh, resinous spirit.

name: Holunderbeergeist
description: Elderberry spirit, made by maceration and redistillation like Himbeergeist because the berries carry too little sugar to ferment. Dark-fruited and faintly tannic, quite unlike elderflower.
funFact: Elderberries are mildly toxic raw and must be processed, which is one reason the spirit is far less common than the flower liqueur.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal. It is darker and more brooding than the pale fruit spirits, and works well after game or a rich stew rather than a light dessert.

composition.summary: Elderberries macerated in neutral spirit and redistilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit plus wild elderberries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated then redistilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: Distillation removes the compounds that make raw elderberries unwise to eat.

name: Eau-de-Vie de Sorbier
description: Rowan berry spirit from the Alps and central Europe, made from a fruit so bitter that it must be frosted on the tree before it is usable. One of the rarest eaux-de-vie in production.
funFact: Rowan berries need a hard frost to break down their sorbic acid, so the harvest cannot begin until the first serious cold snap.

serve.how: Cool and neat in a small pour. It is astringent and unusual, and it belongs at the end of a long meal rather than as an introduction to fruit brandy.

composition.summary: Frosted rowan berries fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rowan (Sorbus) berries, harvested after frost

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: Sorbic acid, named for this genus, is what makes the raw fruit unusable until frost breaks it down.

name: French Whisky
description: France drinks more whisky per head than almost anywhere and started making its own seriously in the 1980s. Brittany leads, often using buckwheat or local barley and finishing in wine casks the country has in abundance.
funFact: France consumes more Scotch per capita than Scotland does, which is a large part of why French distillers eventually decided to compete.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. Sauternes, Banyuls and Bordeaux cask finishes are the French signature, so expect more wine influence and less sherry than a Scotch drinker is used to.

composition.summary: Barley or buckwheat distilled and matured in France, often in wine casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, or buckwheat in Breton whiskies

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills, some using cognac-style alembics

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-wine casks — Sauternes, Banyuls, Bordeaux — as often as ex-bourbon

composition.process: Buckwheat, blé noir, is a Breton speciality and gives a distinctly nutty, spicy whisky.

name: Swedish Whisky
description: Sweden built a whisky industry from nothing in the late 1990s, using Swedish barley, juniper-smoked malt and small casks stored in disused mines. Distinctive rather than imitative.
funFact: Some Swedish malt is smoked over juniper twigs rather than peat, which gives a resinous smoke quite unlike Islay's.

serve.how: Neat with a few drops of water. The juniper-smoked expressions are the ones worth seeking out — they taste like nothing in Scotland and reward being tried beside an Islay for contrast.

composition.summary: Swedish barley, sometimes juniper-smoked, matured in small casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Swedish malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Small casks, some warehoused underground in old mines

composition.process: Wide seasonal temperature swings drive spirit in and out of the wood faster than in Scotland.

name: Danish Whisky
description: Denmark's whisky is built on floor-malted Danish barley, sometimes smoked with heather and seaweed rather than peat. A young industry that leaned into local agriculture from the start.
funFact: Several Danish distilleries floor-malt their own barley, a labour-intensive practice most Scottish distilleries abandoned decades ago.

serve.how: Neat, with water to open it. The smoked expressions use heather and local peat, which reads as sweeter and more herbal than Islay smoke.

composition.summary: Danish floor-malted barley distilled and matured in Denmark.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Danish barley, often floor-malted on site

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and ex-sherry, plus local oak experiments

composition.process: Heather and seaweed smoking is a deliberate attempt to make a smoke that is not Scottish.

name: Dutch Whisky
description: The Netherlands has distilled grain for four centuries as jenever, so whisky was a short step. Dutch single malts lean rich and sherried, made by distillers with deep column and pot experience.
funFact: Zuidam, one of the best-known producers, mills its grain using restored Dutch windmills.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. Dutch malts tend heavily toward sherry-cask maturation, so expect dried fruit and spice rather than the vanilla of ex-bourbon.

composition.summary: Dutch barley and rye distilled in pot stills and sherry-matured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, sometimes rye

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, slow runs

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Predominantly ex-sherry casks

composition.process: Centuries of jenever malt-wine production gave Dutch distillers a head start on grain handling.

name: German Whisky
description: Germany has more whisky distilleries than Ireland, most of them tiny operations attached to existing fruit-brandy or beer businesses. Wheat and spelt appear alongside barley, and the results vary wildly.
funFact: Germany's distilling licences were historically tied to fruit brandy, so many whisky makers came to it with pot-still expertise but no malt tradition at all.

serve.how: Neat with water. Expect greater variation than from any established whisky nation — some are excellent, some are fruit distillers experimenting. Spelt and wheat expressions are the most distinctive.

composition.summary: Barley, wheat or spelt distilled in small German pot stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, wheat, spelt or rye

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills, often fruit-brandy equipment

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-wine and ex-beer casks alongside standard oak

composition.process: Beer-cask and Riesling-cask finishes are a genuinely German contribution to the category.

name: Austrian Whisky
description: Austria distils whisky from rye as readily as barley, and often from spelt — a grain barely used anywhere else for the purpose. Waldviertel in the north is the centre.
funFact: Austria only legalised whisky production in 1995; before that, distilling grain rather than fruit was effectively barred.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. The rye and spelt expressions taste distinctly of dark bread, which is the signature and worth approaching on its own terms rather than as a Scotch substitute.

composition.summary: Rye, spelt or barley distilled and matured in Austrian oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rye, spelt, barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often local Manhartsberg oak rather than American or French

composition.process: Native Austrian oak is more aromatic than American white oak and marks the spirit heavily.

name: Swiss Whisky
description: Illegal in Switzerland until 1999, because grain was reserved for food. The industry that followed is small, expensive and fond of finishing in casks from the country's own wine regions.
funFact: A Swiss law dating from the 1930s forbade distilling bread grains, and it was only repealed in 1999 — which is why Swiss whisky has no history before that date.

serve.how: Neat with water. Beer-cask and wine-cask finishes dominate, and some producers use casks from Swiss vineyards you cannot buy wine from outside the country.

composition.summary: Swiss barley distilled and matured in local wine and beer casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Swiss malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills, some using fruit-brandy equipment

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-wine, ex-beer and standard oak

composition.process: A twelve-year-old Swiss whisky is by definition made after 1999, so the category has a hard start date.

name: Czech Whisky
description: Czechia has distilled single malt since the 1980s, quietly and mostly for the domestic market. Made in a country with world-class barley and brewing, which shows in the wash.
funFact: Hammer Head whisky was distilled in 1989, forgotten in a communist-era warehouse, and rediscovered and bottled two decades later as an accidental vintage single malt.

serve.how: Neat with water. Czech barley is the same crop that supplies the country's brewing industry, and the malt-forward character reflects it.

composition.summary: Czech malted barley distilled and matured domestically.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Moravian malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Czech oak as well as ex-bourbon

composition.process: Local oak is used more than imported, which gives a drier, more tannic profile.

name: Finnish Whisky
description: Finland distils whisky from rye and barley, sometimes smoked with local peat from bogs that are among the youngest in Europe. Cold maturation makes for slow, gentle development.
funFact: Finnish rye whisky uses the same grain that makes the country's dense sour rye bread, and the resemblance in the glass is not subtle.

serve.how: Neat with water. The 100% rye expressions are the distinctive ones — spicier and breadier than any Scotch, and closer in spirit to American rye than to malt.

composition.summary: Finnish rye or barley distilled and matured in the far north.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Finnish rye and malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, ex-sherry and Finnish oak

composition.process: Cold cellars slow maturation, so Finnish whisky ages more like Scotch than like Tasmanian.

name: Icelandic Whisky
description: Made from Icelandic barley — a crop that only became viable as the climate warmed — and smoked with sheep dung rather than peat, because Iceland has almost no trees and never has.
funFact: Smoking with dried sheep dung is a genuine Icelandic food tradition, used for centuries on lamb and fish because firewood was unavailable.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. The smoked expression is the point — it is nothing like peat, closer to a barnyard sweetness, and divides opinion sharply.

composition.summary: Icelandic barley distilled and matured on the island.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Icelandic-grown barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and new oak; rapid due to temperature swings

composition.process: Barley barely ripens at this latitude, which is why the crop is recent and the whisky newer still.

name: South African Whisky
description: Made at the southern tip of Africa since the 1970s, with grain and malt distilled on one site. The climate matures spirit fast, and the results have taken world awards more than once.
funFact: The James Sedgwick distillery in Wellington has been operating since 1886, though it only turned to whisky nearly a century later.

serve.how: Neat with water. Warm maturation pushes fast, so a ten-year-old carries more wood than the age suggests. Also excellent in a highball with soda, which is how much of it is drunk locally.

composition.summary: Malted barley and maize distilled and matured in the Western Cape.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley plus maize for the grain component

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot and column on one site

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak, warm-climate maturation

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 43%

composition.process: Having grain and malt distillation in one place is unusual and lets the blender work from components rather than trade.

name: Mexican Whisky
description: Made from native Oaxacan corn landraces — the ancestors of every corn whiskey elsewhere — grown by smallholders and distilled in the mountains. A whisky category that could only exist in Mexico.
funFact: The corn varieties used — Olotillo, Bolita, Yellow — are heirloom landraces that would be commercially useless as feed crops and are grown specifically for this.

serve.how: Neat, in a small glass. It tastes distinctly of masa and toasted corn in a way American corn whiskey does not, and it rewards being approached as its own thing rather than as bourbon.

composition.summary: Heirloom Oaxacan corn fermented and distilled in the Sierra Norte.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Native Oaxacan corn landraces

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper stills, mezcal-style equipment

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-whiskey and new oak, typically short

composition.process: Single-landrace bottlings exist, which makes it possible to taste one corn variety against another.

name: Chinese Whisky
description: China began building serious malt distilleries in the late 2010s, at scale and with foreign expertise, in a country whose spirits market is the largest on earth. The first releases arrived in the 2020s.
funFact: Some Chinese distilleries mature stock at high altitude in Yunnan and Sichuan, where the thin air and temperature swings accelerate cask interaction.

serve.how: Neat with water. The category is young enough that most releases are under five years old, so expect wood-forward spirit and judge it on texture rather than age.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in China.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Imported and domestic malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, largely Scottish-built

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, ex-sherry, and casks from Chinese baijiu and wine production

composition.process: Ageing in ex-baijiu vessels is a genuinely novel finish that no other country can attempt.

name: Peated Single Malt
description: Malt dried over burning peat, so the smoke's phenols bind to the grain and survive fermentation, distillation and years in wood. Measured in parts per million, and the single most divisive variable in whisky.
funFact: Phenol levels are measured in the malt, not the bottle — much is lost in production, so a 50ppm malt might yield a whisky at half that.

serve.how: Neat, then a few drops of water, which genuinely opens peated whisky more than any other style. Do not over-dilute heavily peated spirit; the smoke collapses before the malt emerges.

composition.summary: Barley malt kilned over peat smoke, then distilled and matured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley dried over peat fire

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years; peat softens with time in cask

composition.process: Peat from different regions smells different — Islay's is maritime and iodine-heavy, Highland peat is drier and more heathery.

name: Sherry Cask Single Malt
description: Matured in casks that previously held sherry, which supplies dried fruit, spice and colour no ex-bourbon barrel can. The casks are now made and seasoned specifically for whisky, since sherry itself sells too slowly.
funFact: Almost no genuine sherry-transport casks remain; distillers now pay Spanish bodegas to season new oak with sherry for a few years purely to make whisky casks.

serve.how: Neat, with water added sparingly. Sherry casks carry a lot of tannin, so heavy dilution turns them drying rather than sweeter. Oloroso gives nuts and spice; PX gives raisin and syrup.

composition.summary: Malt whisky matured in ex-sherry European or American oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-oloroso, ex-Pedro Ximénez or ex-fino casks

composition.process: European oak gives more tannin and spice; American oak seasoned with sherry is softer and sweeter.

name: Japanese Blended Whisky
description: The dominant Japanese style, built from malt and grain whiskies made in-house because Japanese distillers historically did not trade stock with each other. That isolation forced enormous variety within single companies.
funFact: Because Japanese distillers do not swap casks the way Scottish ones do, a single site may run several still shapes and yeast strains to generate the components a blend needs.

serve.how: The Japanese highball: one part whisky, three or four parts cold soda, over hard clear ice, stirred once. It is not a downgrade from neat service — the style is built for it, and most Japanese blends taste better this way.

composition.summary: In-house malt and grain whiskies blended to a house style.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley plus corn or wheat grain whisky

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills of varied shape, plus continuous column

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, ex-sherry and Japanese mizunara oak

composition.process: Mizunara oak is porous and difficult to work, and gives the sandalwood and incense note the category is known for.

name: Mizunara Cask Whisky
description: Matured in Japanese oak, a species so porous and knotted that coopers reject most of it and casks leak. What survives gives sandalwood, coconut and temple incense found nowhere else.
funFact: Mizunara trees need around two hundred years before they are large enough to make casks from, and the wood's high moisture content makes leaking casks routine.

serve.how: Neat, with the smallest amount of water. The incense note takes years to emerge and is fragile — this is a whisky to sit with rather than to mix, and the price reflects the cooperage failure rate.

composition.summary: Whisky matured in casks of Quercus crispula, Japanese oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mizunara oak, usually as a finish after ex-bourbon

composition.process: Japanese distillers turned to mizunara during the war when imported oak was unobtainable, and kept it.

name: Rye Malt Whiskey
description: Made from malted rye rather than raw rye, which is technically difficult — malted rye foams violently in the mash and gums up equipment. The result is spicier and more aromatic than standard rye.
funFact: Malted rye is so prone to foaming that distillers describe mashing it as trying to boil a pan of soap.

serve.glass: Glencairn neat, rocks in a drink
serve.how: Neat to appreciate what malting does, or in a Manhattan where the extra aromatics stand up to sweet vermouth better than standard rye. Cask-strength bottlings take water well.
