name: Whitley Neill Rhubarb & Ginger
description: Contemporary Gin from England.
funFact: One of 21 Contemporary Gin bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Build a Spanish-style gin tonic: fill a large copa glass to the top with ice, pour in two ounces of well-chilled gin, add a quality tonic slowly down a bar spoon, and garnish to match the botanicals — cucumber for fresh styles, rose petals or grapefruit for floral and citrus-led ones. The big bowl traps the aromatics, so nose the glass before each sip. Taste for what leads: in these modern gins the juniper steps back and the signature botanical should shine.

name: Smirnoff No. 21
description: Grain Vodka from Russia.
funFact: One of 13 Grain Vodka bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Store the bottle in the freezer and pour small measures into chilled shot glasses — the cold thickens the texture to a silky, almost viscous pour. Sip rather than slam it, and pay attention to the finish: good grain vodka shows faint cream, white pepper, and mineral notes instead of burn. Serve it alongside salty little bites, Eastern European style, refilling glasses in rounds.
pair: caviar or salted roe on blini

name: Chopin Potato
description: Potato Vodka from Poland.

serve.how: Chill the bottle thoroughly but not to freezer-death — a fridge-cold pour keeps the signature creamy weight on the tongue that hard freezing can dull. Sip it slowly from a chilled shot glass and roll it around; the earthy, buttery body is the whole point of choosing potato over grain. It also anchors an exceptional dirty martini, where its fuller texture stands up to the brine.

serve.how: Chill the bottle thoroughly but not to freezer-death — a fridge-cold pour keeps the signature creamy weight on the tongue that hard freezing can dull. Sip it slowly from a chilled shot glass and roll it around; the earthy, buttery body is the whole point of choosing potato over grain. It also anchors an exceptional dirty martini, where its fuller texture stands up to the brine.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube

High-proof bottlings welcome a big cube or a teaspoon of water, which softens the heat and amplifies the fruit.

name: Rhum Clément VSOP
description: Rhum Agricole from Martinique.
funFact: One of 4 Rhum Agricole bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Drink it the Martinique way: a short pour in a rocks glass at room temperature, ideally as a Ti' Punch — a squeeze of lime disc and a small spoon of cane syrup stirred right in the glass. Neat, swirl gently and breathe in the fresh-cut-grass and green-olive aromas that molasses rums never show. Skip heavy ice on aged expressions; the vegetal character is delicate and fades when over-chilled.

Skip heavy ice on aged expressions; the vegetal character is delicate and fades when over-chilled.

Fruit-cured 'pitorro curao,' steeped with tropical fruit for months, is best lightly chilled so the infusion stays bright. Around the holidays, do as Puerto Rican families do and fold it into homemade coquito, or toast with it straight at the Christmas table.

name: Del Maguey Tobalá
description: Mezcal Tobalá from Mexico.
funFact: The only Mezcal Tobalá bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour sparingly, this is scarce juice, and let the glass sit for several minutes; tobala's floral perfume needs air to bloom. Sip in small, slow draws and chase the wild fruit and wet-stone notes that float above the gentle smoke. No ice, no citrus, no mixing: at this rarity you are tasting a plant that took a decade to grow in a mountain canyon.

serve.how: Treat this like the ceremonial spirit it is: pour a small measure into a veladora, no ice, no mixing, and share it slowly with people you like. Let the glass sit between sips; it keeps evolving as it breathes.

components.detail: Agave marmorata, wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

name: Bozal Cuishe
description: Mezcal Cuishe from Mexico.
funFact: The only Mezcal Cuishe bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, small pours. Drier and more austere than Espadín, and it makes an excellent bridge between the cultivated and wild styles for someone working through a flight.

composition.summary: Wild Cuishe agave pit-roasted and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave karwinskii (Cuishe), wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Producers often distil the different karwinskii varieties separately purely to show the differences.

name: Los Amantes Joven
description: Mezcal Joven from Mexico.
funFact: One of 4 Mezcal Joven bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a wide, shallow veladora and let it breathe for a minute before nosing. Kiss it rather than gulp it: small sips held on the palate reveal tropical fruit and wet-stone minerality behind the campfire smoke. Traditional accompaniments are orange slices dusted with sal de gusano, not lime and shot glasses.
pair: orange slices with sal de gusano

composition.summary: Unaged mezcal from agave hearts roasted in earthen pits and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave hearts, most often cultivated espadín

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper or clay pot stills, typically twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None — bottled clear and straight off the still

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–52% ABV

composition.process: Days of roasting in stone-lined earth pits is the single step that makes mezcal smoky.

name: Alipús San Andrés
description: Mezcal Espadín from Mexico.
funFact: One of 3 Mezcal Espadín bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, in a wide shallow glass, sipped rather than shot. Orange slices with sal de gusano are the traditional accompaniment in Oaxaca. Never chill it.

composition.summary: Cultivated Espadín agave pit-roasted, crushed and twice pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave angustifolia (Espadín), 6–8 years to maturity

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, tahona-crushed, copper or clay pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually joven, unaged

composition.process: Earth-pit roasting over hot stones is where all the smoke comes from — nothing is added.

name: Bacanora Cielo Rojo
description: Bacanora from Mexico.
funFact: The only Bacanora bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour an ounce or two into a veladora and let it sit for a minute or two so the alcohol vapors lift off before you nose it. Sip neat in small draws, rolling the spirit across your tongue to catch the mineral edge and desert-herb notes beneath the light smoke. Skip ice entirely; dilution flattens the wild-agave character that makes bacanora worth hunting down.

composition.summary: Distilled from Sonoran agave, mostly the wild-harvested Agave angustifolia known locally as pacífico.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave angustifolia ('pacífico'), much of it still gathered wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then run through small copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Almost always bottled unaged and clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–48% ABV

composition.process: Roasting the agave hearts in earth-and-stone pits is what lays down that mountain smoke.

name: Sotol Por Siempre
description: Sotol from Mexico.
funFact: The only Sotol bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a small measure neat and give it a minute of air, then nose gently: sotol smells like the high desert after rain, all grass, pine, and mineral. Sip slowly and let it sit on the mid-palate, where the earthy, vegetal side unfolds; it is drier and greener than mezcal, so do not go looking for sweetness. Room temperature keeps those delicate herbal notes alive.

composition.summary: Distilled from the wild desert spoon plant, not agave at all.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wild Dasylirion — desert spoon — harvested across the Chihuahuan Desert

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Roasted, crushed, then run through small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Most is unaged; some producers rest it briefly in oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: The plants are gathered wild from desert hillsides, so the spirit changes with the terrain.

name: Raicilla La Venenosa
description: Raicilla from Mexico.
funFact: The only Raicilla bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve neat at room temperature in a veladora and nose it first: raicilla leads with ripe fruit and wild funk rather than smoke, so expect something closer to a natural wine's aromatics. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate, watching for the green agave brightness underneath the fermented-fruit character. Keep it away from ice and mixers until you have met it on its own terms.
pair: tropical fruit with chile and lime

composition.summary: Western Jalisco agave spirit from mountain and coastal species, cooked without heavy smoke.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Local Jalisco agaves such as maximiliana and inaequidens

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or filipino-style stills, often clay or wood-fired

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged, bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: Many producers cook the agave in above-ground ovens, which is why it reads fruity, not smoky.

name: Comiteco Balún Canán
description: Comiteco from Mexico.
funFact: The only Comiteco bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature. It is sweeter and rounder than mezcal, closer to a light rum in weight, and the aged versions drink comfortably after a meal.

composition.summary: Agave sap fermented, distilled and blended with piloncillo, then aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aguamiel from Agave americana, tapped from living plants

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, then blended with unrefined cane sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, typically one to three years

composition.process: Because the plant is tapped rather than harvested, it keeps producing sap for months before it dies.

name: Cocuy Pecayero
description: Cocuy from Venezuela.
funFact: The only Cocuy bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat and unchilled in a small wide glass, sipped rather than shot, exactly as you would treat mezcal. The wild-harvested versions carry more mineral and less sweetness.

composition.summary: Agave cocui hearts roasted, fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave cocui, largely wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The plant takes eight to ten years to mature, and overharvesting has been a genuine conservation concern.

name: Hennessy VS
description: Cognac VS from France.
funFact: One of 2 Cognac VS bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Young and grape-bright, VS is the cognac to enjoy casually: neat in a small snifter, over a single large cube, or stretched into a highball with ginger ale or tonic. If sipping neat, warm the glass briefly in your hand, swirl, and look for fresh grape and citrus over young oak. Don't overthink it — this grade was made for mixing and easy evenings, so save the ceremony for older bottles.

composition.summary: The youngest cognac grade: Charente grape brandy aged at least two years.

components.detail: Thin, acidic white wine, overwhelmingly Ugni Blanc

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice through the copper Charentais alembic

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Youngest eau-de-vie at least two years in French oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Bottled at 40% ABV

composition.process: The second pass — la bonne chauffe — is where the distiller cuts the heart of the spirit.

name: Hennessy VSOP
description: Cognac VSOP from France.
funFact: One of 6 Cognac VSOP bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour an ounce and a half into a snifter or tulip glass at room temperature — skip the flame-warming cliché, gentle hand warmth is plenty. Swirl, nose in two or three passes, and sip slowly, tracking dried apricot into vanilla and baking spice. VSOP straddles both worlds: refined enough to sip neat after dinner, sturdy enough for an elegant Sidecar or a single cube on a warm night.

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Bottled at 40% ABV

composition.process: Extra years in oak round the fruit and pull warm spice out of the wood.

name: Hennessy XO
description: Cognac XO from France.
funFact: One of 5 Cognac XO bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Reserve XO for unhurried evenings: pour a small measure into a snifter, let it breathe five to ten minutes, and resist any ice or water. Cradle the bowl, swirl slowly, and nose repeatedly — candied orange, fig, and walnut should deepen with every pass as the rancio character emerges. Sip in tiny draws and let each one sit on the palate; a single pour should comfortably last half an hour.

name: Darroze Les Grands Assemblages
description: Armagnac from France.
funFact: One of 3 Armagnac bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a modest ounce and a half into a snifter or small tulip and give it ten patient minutes to breathe — older Armagnacs unfold dramatically with air. Warm the bowl slightly with your hand, swirl slowly, and return to the nose repeatedly as prune, violet, and toffee emerge in waves. Sip in small draws with no ice and no water at first; this is a fireside spirit meant to be interrogated over an hour.

name: Boulard Grand Solage
description: Calvados from France.
funFact: One of 3 Calvados bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve an ounce and a half in a snifter at room temperature, swirl once, and breathe in the orchard — baked apple and cider aromas should leap out before you ever sip. Take small sips and note how younger bottlings stay crisp and appley while older ones drift toward butterscotch and spice. Honor the 'trou normand' by pouring a small glass mid-feast, or serve it alongside dessert in place of whisky.

serve.how: Serve slightly cool but never frozen — an over-chilled pour hides the ripe-pear perfume that makes this eau-de-vie special. Pour a small measure into a tulip glass, warm it faintly in your hand, and nose it in slow passes; a fully ripe Williams pear should materialize before you sip. Take tiny sips as a digestif, letting the clean spice and white-fruit sweetness linger between them.

name: Massenez Kirsch
description: Kirschwasser from France.
funFact: The only Kirschwasser bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a small measure into a tulip glass at cellar temperature — freezing it, as some bars do, kills the delicate sour-cherry perfume. Nose gently for the signature whisper of bitter almond from the distilled pits, then sip slowly and let the clean heat carry the stone fruit across your palate. Serve it as a digestif after a rich meal, the traditional Black Forest role it was born for.

funFact: One of 2 Peach Schnapps bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Keep it in the fridge and embrace the fun: build a Fuzzy Navel with orange juice over ice in a highball, or lengthen it with soda water and a squeeze of lemon to trim the candy sweetness. A frozen blend with fresh peaches is its summer party trick. Sip and enjoy the unapologetic ripe-peach juiciness — this is sunshine, not subtlety.

composition.summary: A sweet American peach liqueur, flavoured and sugared rather than distilled from fruit.

components.label: Base

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Flavoured after distillation — no fruit brandy involved

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 15–24% ABV

composition.process: Sweetening is the whole point, and it's what separates it from unsweetened German schnaps.

name: Midori
description: Melon Liqueur from Japan.
funFact: The only Melon Liqueur bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: With soda and lime over ice, which is far better than its reputation. In cocktails it makes a Midori Sour or a Japanese Slipper. Cut it with acid; the sugar needs something to push against.

composition.summary: Muskmelon infused into neutral spirit, sweetened and coloured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Yubari and muskmelon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened; colour added

composition.process: Two melon varieties are used, one for aroma and one for body.

name: Cointreau Blood Orange
description: Triple Sec from France.
funFact: One of 3 Triple Sec bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Triple sec is a workhorse, so let it work: keep it cool and reach for it in margaritas, cosmopolitans, and sidecars, where its clean orange brightness does the heavy lifting. To assess a bottle, sip a small chilled pour from a rocks glass — better versions taste of real orange peel, not candy. A splash in chilled prosecco with a twist makes an effortless aperitif.

composition.summary: A clear orange liqueur made by distilling neutral spirit with orange peel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sweet and bitter orange peel, sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with the peels, which keeps it clear and bright

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: A wide 15–40% ABV depending on quality

composition.process: Redistilling with the peel — rather than just infusing — is what makes it clean enough to disappear into a margarita.

name: Sheridan's
description: Irish Cream from Ireland.
funFact: One of 3 Irish Cream bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Keep the bottle in the fridge and pour it well chilled over ice in a rocks glass, or spike your coffee and crown it with whipped cream. Steer clear of citrus-heavy mixers — the cream will curdle — and refrigerate after opening. Sip slowly and notice the order of arrival: silky cream, then chocolate and vanilla, with the whiskey warmth surfacing only at the finish.

composition.summary: Irish whiskey emulsified with fresh dairy cream, sugar and chocolate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Irish whiskey, fresh dairy cream, sugar and cocoa

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Not distilled as a liqueur — the whiskey is blended in

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; the cream sets a real shelf life

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 17% ABV

composition.process: Homogenising the cream with the spirit is the trick that stops it curdling or separating.

name: Bénédictine D.O.M.
description: Bénédictine from France.
funFact: The only Bénédictine bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour an ounce or two into a snifter at room temperature, cup the bowl in your palm, and give it a slow swirl to release the honey and herb aromatics. Sip it neat as an after-dinner drink, or go classic with a B&B — equal parts Bénédictine and brandy in the same glass. As it warms, count the layers: honey first, then baking spice, then a long herbal finish that hints at the 27 botanicals.

composition.summary: A honeyed French liqueur of twenty-seven herbs and spices on a spirit base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral and brandy spirit carrying twenty-seven herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals distilled in separate batches, then blended to recipe

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak before the final blend and sweetening

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40% ABV

composition.process: Distilling the botanical groups separately lets the blender assemble the flavour like an orchestra.

name: Izarra Verte
description: Izarra from France.
funFact: The only Izarra bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight and cold after a meal, or poured over crushed ice as they do in Bayonne. The yellow is the gentler of the two and the better introduction; the green is stronger and more aggressively herbal.

composition.summary: Armagnac and plant distillates blended with honey and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Armagnac

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Reportedly 32 Pyrenean plants for the yellow, 48 for the green

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Plants macerated and distilled, then blended and sweetened with honey

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak

composition.process: Honey rather than sugar syrup gives it the weight that separates it from its Alpine cousins.

name: Génépi Le Chamois
description: Génépi from France.
funFact: The only Génépi bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Do as the ski lodges do: keep the bottle cold and pour a small measure into a cordial glass after a rich meal. It also takes well to a single small cube or a splash of tonic if the wormwood bite runs hot. Sip in small doses and notice the progression from meadow herbs and chamomile to the bittersweet, alpine-scree finish that makes it such a bracing digestif.

composition.summary: An Alpine liqueur made from tiny high-altitude artemisia flowers.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit steeped with génépi (Artemisia) flowers and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditionally a maceration; some producers distil the herb

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; often the flower stalks sit right in the bottle

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 30–40% ABV

composition.process: The wormwood-family flowers only grow on high scree, which is why the bite tastes so alpine.

name: Mastiha Skinos
description: Mastiha from Greece.
funFact: The only Mastiha bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass after dinner. It also works over ice with soda and a strip of lemon, and Greek bartenders use it in place of a herbal liqueur in gin drinks.

composition.summary: Mastic tree resin distilled or infused into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or tsipouro

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mastiha resin from Pistacia lentiscus var. Chia

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Resin distilled or macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: The trees only weep usable mastic on Chios, an agricultural mystery nobody has fully explained.

name: Beerenburg Sonnema
description: Beerenburg from Netherlands.
funFact: The only Beerenburg bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass, taken before or after food rather than with it. In Friesland it is also drunk with hot water and sugar as a cure for whatever is going around.

composition.summary: Jenever or neutral spirit steeped with a fixed herb blend.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Juniper spirit or jenever

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, bay, juniper berry, laurel and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated rather than redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 30%

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation keeps the herbs tasting green and raw instead of polished.

name: Zirbenz Stone Pine
description: Zirbenschnaps from Austria.
funFact: The only Zirbenschnaps bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: After a long walk, at room temperature, in a small glass. Cold flattens the resin note that is the entire reason to drink it. Austrians pour it into hut coffee when the weather turns.

composition.summary: Young stone pine cones macerated in spirit and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or clear fruit brandy

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green cones of Pinus cembra, the Swiss stone pine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks; colour and flavour extract together

composition.process: The pink colour leaches out of the cone resin and deepens the longer the maceration runs.

name: Enzian Grassl
description: Enzian from Germany.
funFact: The only Enzian bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cool, neat, in a very small pour after a heavy meal. It is not a beginner's spirit and does not reward gulping. Give it time in the glass, since the earthiness settles into something closer to celery and honey.

composition.summary: Fermented gentian root distilled to a clear, dry spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Gentiana lutea or punctata root, fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still; the root itself is the fermentable

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Unlike gentian liqueurs, the root is fermented and distilled rather than steeped, so there is no sugar to hide behind.

name: Hierbas Ibicencas
description: Hierbas from Spain.
funFact: The only Hierbas bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after eating, or over ice in summer. The dulce version is thick and sweet; the seca is drier and closer to a straight herbal anise.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Anise-flavoured spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Rosemary, thyme, fennel, lemon verbena, juniper, orange leaf

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated; sprigs often left in the bottle

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 20–40% depending on style

composition.process: Leaving the herbs in means the liqueur keeps changing on the shelf, which producers treat as a feature.

name: Travarica Badel
description: Travarica from Croatia.
funFact: The only Travarica bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, poured on arrival with dried figs or cheese. The herbs are usually left in the bottle, so the last glass is noticeably more medicinal than the first.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lozovača or fruit rakija

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Sage, rosemary, juniper, mint, wormwood, St John's wort

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, sometimes redistilled

composition.process: Herbs are picked in early summer when the oils are highest and steeped for weeks in the sun.

name: Branca Menta
description: Fernet-Branca from Italy.
funFact: One of 2 Fernet-Branca bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Shot glass or small chilled rocks glass
serve.how: Pour a small measure neat as a digestif after a heavy meal; the menthol-and-bitter-herb blast is the point, so take it in confident sips rather than nervous ones. A light chill softens the eucalyptus edge for newcomers, but true believers drink it room temperature. For the Argentine experience, pour an ounce or two over ice and top generously with cola for a fernet con coca.

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 39% ABV

composition.process: Myrrh, saffron and menthol-heavy botanicals are steeped until the result tastes like medicine that won.

description: Amaro from Italy.
funFact: One of 6 Amaro bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat after a meal at room temperature, which is how Italy drinks it. Lighter amari take ice and soda well; heavy ones do not. In cocktails they swap in for vermouth to add bitterness without more alcohol.

name: Ricard
description: Pastis from France.
funFact: One of 3 Pastis bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour one part pastis into a tall or small tumbler and top with about five parts very cold water — the drink blooms milky yellow on contact. Add an ice cube after diluting if you like, but never drop ice into neat pastis or the oils will clump. Sip unhurried, aperitif-style, noticing star anise and licorice mellowing into gentle sweet herbs; it should taste like a Marseille terrace at golden hour.

name: Ouzo 12

funFact: One of 2 Ouzo bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour two fingers into a small tumbler and add cold water or an ice cube to taste, watching it cloud ghostly white as the anise oils louche. Greeks sip it slowly over a long afternoon, never as a shot, always with a little food on the table. Take small sips and notice the licorice sweetness up front giving way to fennel and a faint citrus lift.

name: Yeni Rakı
description: Rakı from Turkey.
funFact: One of 2 Rakı bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a couple fingers into a tall narrow rakı glass, add an equal measure of cool water to summon the milky 'lion's milk' cloud, then a cube of ice if you wish. Keep a second glass of plain water alongside, Turkish-style, and alternate sips. Drink it slowly across a long meze table — rakı is a conversation spirit — noticing the raisin sweetness beneath the anise and the warm spice on the finish.

name: Arak Touma
description: Arak from Lebanon.
funFact: One of 2 Arak bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: 38-45°F, well chilled with water and ice
serve.how: Mix roughly one part arak with two parts cool water in a small tumbler, then add ice — always in that order, since ice added first can crystallize the anise oils into a film. Watch it swirl milky white, the classic louche of the Levant. Sip it alongside food rather than alone, letting small sips reset your palate between bites of mezze; notice the grape sweetness underneath the licorice.

composition.process: Adding aniseed only to the last distillation keeps the perfume clean rather than heavy.

description: Chinchón from Spain.
funFact: The only Chinchón bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Dry over ice as an aperitif, sweet after a meal, and the 74% version with considerable respect and a great deal of water. Spaniards also add it to coffee as a carajillo.

composition.summary: Locally grown anise distilled in copper alembics.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Anise grown around Chinchón

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, distilled with the seed

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 35% to 74% depending on style

composition.process: Distilling with the seed rather than adding oil afterwards is what earns it protected status.

name: Zibib Sudanese
description: Zibib from Sudan.
funFact: The only Zibib bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Poured over ice or cut with two parts water, which turns it milky white. Egyptians drink it with mezze rather than after a meal, and it stands up well to strongly spiced food.

composition.summary: Grape or raisin spirit redistilled with aniseed.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grapes, raisins or dates

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Aniseed, sometimes mastic

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the anise, usually twice

composition.process: Anethole precipitating out of solution when water is added is what produces the cloud.

name: Mastika Peshtera
description: Mastika from Bulgaria.
funFact: The only Mastika bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or with a splash of water, which turns it cloudy. It is a before-dinner drink in the Balkans, taken with salty meze rather than at the end of a meal.

composition.summary: Grape or grain spirit distilled with anise and mastic resin.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape or grain spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mastic resin, anise, sometimes fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with botanicals, then sweetened

composition.process: The resin gives a pine-and-cedar note that separates it immediately from a plain anise spirit.

name: Aalborg Taffel Akvavit
description: Taffel Akvavit from Denmark.
funFact: The only Taffel Akvavit bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Freezer cold, in small measures, with the meal. Danish tradition is a beer alongside and a toast before each glass, with eye contact — skipping the eye contact is the part visitors get wrong.

composition.summary: Grain spirit redistilled with caraway and citrus, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Caraway dominant, plus citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Bottling unaged and clear is what distinguishes it from the oak-rested Norwegian styles.

name: O.P. Anderson
description: Dill Aquavit from Sweden.
funFact: The only Dill Aquavit bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: From the freezer, in small measures, with food rather than before it. Dill aquavit belongs with crayfish and new potatoes in a way the caraway styles do not — it is a summer spirit.

composition.summary: Grain or potato spirit redistilled with dill as the lead botanical.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain or potato neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dill leading, with fennel, coriander and citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Dill's aromatics are fragile, so it goes in later and gentler than caraway would.

name: Moutai
description: Sauce-Aroma Baijiu from China. China's most famous baijiu.
funFact: Moutai: China's most famous baijiu

serve.how: Room temperature in a very small cup, with food, and shared. Chinese banquet custom is to toast rather than sip. The umami depth needs food alongside it; drunk alone it can be overwhelming.

composition.summary: Sorghum solid-state fermented with wheat qu in stone pits, distilled seven times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Red sorghum and wheat qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Seven distillations across a year-long cycle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware jars, then blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 53%

composition.process: 53% is considered the point where water and ethanol molecules bind most tightly, and the style is bottled there deliberately.

name: Wuliangye
description: Strong-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: One of 2 Strong-Aroma Baijiu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with food. The fruit-and-funk profile is intense on its own but cuts through rich, oily Sichuan food remarkably well. Toast rather than sip.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in aged mud pits, distilled and blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with rice, wheat, corn and glutinous rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation in steamer stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The older the mud pit, the more complex the microbial population, and the higher the value of the spirit.

name: Luzhou Laojiao
description: Strong-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: One of 2 Strong-Aroma Baijiu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with food. The fruit-and-funk profile is intense on its own but cuts through rich, oily Sichuan food remarkably well. Toast rather than sip.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in aged mud pits, distilled and blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with rice, wheat, corn and glutinous rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation in steamer stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The older the mud pit, the more complex the microbial population, and the higher the value of the spirit.

name: Fenjiu
description: Light-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Light-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food, or lightly chilled if it is your first baijiu. Its cleaner profile also makes it the style most usable in cocktails, where it behaves a little like a funky gin.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in stone jars with barley and pea qu.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, with a barley and pea qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, two fermentations

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware, typically shorter than other styles

composition.process: Stone jars keep the ferment isolated from soil microbes, which is why the style stays clean.

name: Erguotou Red Star
description: Erguotou from China.
glassware: Small cup or straight from the bottle
funFact: The only Erguotou bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with street food. It is a working drink and treated as one; nobody in Beijing contemplates their erguotou. It also mixes surprisingly well with sour or citrus flavours.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented and distilled, with only the middle cut kept.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation, middle fraction only

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimal

composition.process: Discarding the head and tail of the run is exactly what the name describes, and why it is cleaner than its price suggests.

name: Kinmen Kaoliang
description: Kaoliang from Taiwan.
funFact: The only Kaoliang bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. At 58% it is not a sipping spirit; Taiwanese custom is to drain the cup on a toast and refill.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented with wheat qu and solid-state distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum grown on Kinmen

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Stored in granite tunnels cut into the island

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 38–63%, with 58% the signature

composition.process: The granite tunnels hold a stable cool temperature year-round, which is why they are still used.

name: Xifeng
description: Feng-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Feng-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. It is a good bridge for anyone who finds strong-aroma too pungent and light-aroma too plain.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in annually rebuilt earth pits, then basket-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with barley and pea qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Wax-sealed wicker baskets rather than earthenware jars

composition.process: Rebuilding the pits each year is the opposite of the strong-aroma approach and deliberately so.

name: Jinmailang Sesame
description: Sesame-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Sesame-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food. The sesame note is genuinely reminiscent of the oil, and it pairs remarkably well with northern Chinese dishes that already use it.

composition.summary: Sorghum, wheat and bran fermented in brick-lined pits.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with wheat, bran and barley qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, in brick and mud pits

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The sesame note comes from the fermentation, not from any sesame — none is used.

name: Iichiko
description: Mugi Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Mugi Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with cold water
serve.how: On the rocks, or mizuwari with cold water at about one to one. Barrel-aged versions drink comfortably neat and are often mistaken for a light whisky in a blind pour.

composition.summary: Barley fermented with barley koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barley

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Barley or rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, often under vacuum for a lighter result

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point and produces a markedly cleaner, fruitier spirit.

name: Kurokirishima
description: Imo Shochu from Japan.
funFact: One of 2 Imo Shochu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%, sometimes 20%

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

name: Satsuma Shiranami
description: Imo Shochu from Japan.
funFact: One of 2 Imo Shochu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%, sometimes 20%

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

name: Takara Jun
description: Kome Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Kome Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp, warm or on the rocks
serve.glass: Wine glass, or warmed in a choku
serve.how: Warmed gently in winter, on the rocks in summer, or neat at room temperature. Kuma shochu is traditionally pre-mixed with water and warmed in a ceramic flask overnight before serving.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Both the base and the koji are rice, which is why it sits so close to sake on the palate.

name: Lento Kokuto
description: Kokuto Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Kokuto Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with water
serve.how: On the rocks, or with cold water. Despite the base it is not sweet, since the sugar ferments out entirely. It sits somewhere between a light rum and a shochu, which is exactly what it is.

composition.summary: Brown sugar fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Amami kokuto, unrefined brown sugar

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji, which is legally required

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

composition.process: The rice koji requirement is what keeps it classified as shochu rather than as rum.

name: Zuisen Awamori
description: Awamori Kusu from Japan.
funFact: The only Awamori Kusu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.how: Neat at room temperature in a small cup, or on the rocks. Okinawans traditionally cut it with water and let it sit overnight before serving, which softens it noticeably.

composition.summary: Awamori aged three years or more in clay pots by fractional topping.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Long-grain Thai rice with black koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware; traditional systems run far longer

composition.process: Clay is slightly porous, so the spirit oxidises slowly in a way glass or steel would not allow.

name: Jinro Chamisul
description: Andong Soju from South Korea. The world's best-selling spirit by volume.
funFact: Jinro Chamisul: The world's best-selling spirit by volume

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with nuruk and distilled in a traditional soju gori.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nuruk, a Korean wild-culture starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in an earthenware soju gori

composition.process: Nuruk carries a wilder mix of moulds and yeasts than Japanese koji, which gives a more rustic result.

name: Chum Churum
description: Andong Soju from South Korea.
funFact: One of 3 Andong Soju bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with nuruk and distilled in a traditional soju gori.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nuruk, a Korean wild-culture starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in an earthenware soju gori

composition.process: Nuruk carries a wilder mix of moulds and yeasts than Japanese koji, which gives a more rustic result.

name: Korn Berentzen
description: Korn from Germany.
funFact: The only Korn bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a tiny glass, drunk in one go with a beer to follow. In the north it is called Herrengedeck when paired with a pilsner. Ageing it in oak makes something closer to a light whisky, but that is no longer Korn.

composition.summary: Rye, wheat, barley or oats distilled to a modest strength with nothing added.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rye, wheat, barley or oats, or a blend

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, but not to full neutrality

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None permitted for the Korn designation

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 32% minimum, 38% for Doppelkorn

composition.process: Distilling below neutrality is deliberate: the grain character is the product, so stripping it out would defeat the purpose.

name: Brännvin Skåne
description: Brännvin from Sweden.
funFact: The only Brännvin bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Freezer cold in a small stemmed glass, drunk with food rather than before it. At a Swedish table it is taken in measured shots between courses, each one preceded by a song, which is not optional.

composition.summary: Grain or potato spirit, rectified and cut with water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wheat or potato

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Continuous column, to near neutrality

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Flavoured versions are steeped after distillation, which is where snaps and aquavit branch off.

name: Palm Wine Ogogoro
description: Ogogoro from Nigeria.
funFact: The only Ogogoro bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, or infused with herbs and roots as it often is locally. The new craft bottlings are clean enough to drink like a rhum agricole and mix well with citrus.

composition.summary: Fermented palm sap distilled in pot stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap of raffia or oil palm, fermented in the tree

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills, traditionally improvised

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none

composition.process: The sap begins fermenting the moment it is tapped, so distilling has to happen within a day or two.

name: Toddy Arrack
description: Ceylon Arrack from Sri Lanka.
funFact: The only Ceylon Arrack bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: With ginger beer and lime, which is the Sri Lankan standard, or over ice with soda. The premium aged bottlings are worth drinking neat, where the halmilla wood shows as a soft spice.

composition.summary: Coconut flower sap fermented and distilled, then aged in halmilla casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Toddy from coconut palm flower stalks

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Halmilla wood vats, six months to fifteen years

composition.process: The sap must be distilled within a day of tapping, since it ferments almost immediately in the heat.

name: Viche del Pacífico
description: Viche from Colombia.
funFact: The only Viche bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or in one of its infused forms. Arrechón, blended with milk, honey and herbs, is the best-known preparation and considerably easier going than the raw spirit.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and distilled in artisanal stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed Pacific coast sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Handmade copper or improvised stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; infused versions are common

composition.process: The 2021 law recognising viche was written to protect it as ancestral knowledge, not just as a product.

name: Chirrinchi Wayuu
description: Chirrinchi from Colombia.
funFact: The only Chirrinchi bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. It is a ceremonial and social spirit within Wayúu communities rather than a bar product, and the commercial bottlings that exist are recent.

composition.summary: Panela fermented and distilled in the Guajira desert.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Panela, unrefined cane sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper or improvised stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Water is scarce in La Guajira, which shapes both the fermentation and the scale of production.

name: Ron Ligero Havana
description: Ron Ligero from Cuba.
funFact: The only Ron Ligero bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: This is a mixing rum by design. A daiquiri with lime and sugar, or a mojito, is what it was built for. Neat, the aged expressions are dry and elegant, but the white is not meant to be sipped.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented, column-distilled, aged and charcoal-filtered.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cuban sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, to a light spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years even for white, then filtered clear

composition.process: Filtering after ageing removes the colour but leaves the softness, which is the whole trick of the Cuban style.

name: Belizean One Barrel
description: Belizean Rum from Belize.
funFact: The only Belizean Rum bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Over ice, or long with soda and lime. The one-barrel style is light and vanilla-forward, which makes it a good daiquiri rum and an easy sipper over a single cube.

composition.summary: Belizean molasses fermented and column-distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses from Belizean sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: One year and upward in oak

composition.process: Belize's sugar industry is concentrated in the north, and the distilleries sit alongside the mills.

name: Coteaux de Mascara Ghriss
description: A AOG red wine from Aïn Témouchent, Algeria. Made from Carignan.
funFact: Once the world's largest wine exporter under French rule; a fraction of that today.

serve.how: Pour into a large bowl and give it air — most reds are built to open up rather than to be drunk the moment the cork is out. Serve cooler than the room actually is; at true room temperature the alcohol comes forward and the fruit flattens.

components.detail: Fermented on the skins for colour and tannin, then aged in oak or steel depending on the house.

composition.process: Protected as AOG, made in Aïn Témouchent and bottled to the local rules for red wine.

name: Brown Derby
description: Bourbon, grapefruit and honey — three ingredients from a Hollywood hat-shaped restaurant, and one of the cleanest sours ever written.
funFact: Named for the Brown Derby restaurant on Wilshire Boulevard, which was built in the shape of a hat; the drink itself was reportedly first mixed at the Vendôme Club nearby.

steps: Loosen honey with an equal part of warm water to make a pourable syrup.
Shake the bourbon, grapefruit juice and honey syrup hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.

name: Blinker
description: Rye, grapefruit and raspberry syrup. A Prohibition-era oddity that only works once you replace the grenadine most books wrongly call for.
funFact: The original 1934 recipe calls for grenadine, but modern bartenders almost universally swap in raspberry syrup — the drink is markedly better for it, and the substitution has effectively become the recipe.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Cameron's Kick
description: Scotch and Irish whiskey together, with lemon and orgeat. Two whiskies that should not share a glass, and somehow do.
funFact: It appears in Harry MacElhone's 1922 book, and its trick is that orgeat's almond richness bridges the gap between smoky Scotch and soft Irish whiskey — neither works alone in this shape.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.
Serve very cold.

name: Chancellor
description: Scotch, tawny port and dry vermouth. Nutty, dried-fruited and considerably older-tasting than its ingredients suggest.
funFact: Port and Scotch is an unfashionable pairing that the sherry-cask whisky trade quietly proves every day: oxidative fortified wine and malt have been sharing a barrel for two centuries.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Algonquin
description: Rye, dry vermouth and pineapple juice — named for the hotel whose Round Table drank through the 1920s.
funFact: The Algonquin Hotel's Round Table met daily for a decade and produced more quotable insults than cocktails; the drink named for it is gentler than its namesakes were.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice — fresh pineapple juice needs aeration.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a pineapple leaf, or nothing at all.
Serve immediately.

name: Monte Carlo Cocktail
description: A Manhattan with Bénédictine in place of the vermouth. Honeyed herbs against rye, and shorter than either parent.
funFact: Bénédictine's recipe is held by three people at a time at Fécamp in Normandy, and its 27 herbs and spices make it one of the few liqueurs that can replace vermouth without unbalancing a drink.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve very cold.

name: Preakness
description: A Manhattan with Bénédictine added rather than substituted, named for the second leg of the Triple Crown.
funFact: The Preakness Stakes has been run at Pimlico since 1873, and the winning horse is traditionally draped in black-eyed Susans — which are not in season and are usually painted daisies.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Palmetto
description: A Manhattan built on aged rum instead of whiskey. Older than the Cuba Libre and considerably more serious.
funFact: It appears in bar books from the 1890s onward, from the era when rum and whiskey were treated as interchangeable bases rather than as separate worlds.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
Serve very cold.

name: Pegu Club
description: Gin, orange curaçao and lime with two bitters — the house drink of a British officers' club in colonial Burma.
funFact: The Pegu Club in Rangoon was a British colonial institution; the drink outlived the club entirely and later gave its name to Audrey Saunders' influential New York bar.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Saratoga
description: Equal parts rye, cognac and sweet vermouth. Jerry Thomas printed it in 1887 and nobody has improved on the ratio since.
funFact: Saratoga Springs was America's first great resort town, and its racetrack and mineral springs put its name on drinks, chips and a whole style of trunk.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry or a lemon twist.
Serve cold.

name: Journalist
description: Gin with both vermouths, curaçao, lemon and bitters — six ingredients, and a Savoy recipe that rewards precision.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book is full of six-ingredient gin drinks in tiny measures; most collapse under modern pours, and the Journalist is one of the few that holds together.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds — the citrus is a seasoning here, not a sour base.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.

name: Twentieth Century
description: Gin, Lillet, lemon and crème de cacao. Chocolate and citrus in the same glass, named for a luxury train.
funFact: Named for the 20th Century Limited, the express that ran New York to Chicago overnight and gave us the phrase 'red carpet treatment' — the carpet was literal.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and discard it.
Serve very cold — this one falls apart warm.

name: Corpse Reviver No. 1
description: Cognac, calvados and sweet vermouth — the forgotten sibling, all brown spirit where the famous one is all citrus.
funFact: The Savoy notes that No. 1 is 'to be taken before 11am, or whenever steam and energy are needed' — a prescription it declines to explain further.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an apple slice or a lemon twist.
Serve cold.

name: Satan's Whiskers
description: Gin, both vermouths, orange juice, curaçao and orange bitters. 'Straight' uses Grand Marnier, 'curled' uses curaçao.
funFact: The Savoy lists both versions side by side — straight with Grand Marnier, curled with orange curaçao — and declines to say which is better, which has kept the argument alive for ninety years.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Maiden's Prayer
description: Gin, Cointreau and equal lemon and orange juice. A White Lady that let some orange in.
funFact: It belongs to a whole family of interwar gin-and-orange-liqueur sours whose names — Maiden's Prayer, Maiden's Blush, Leap Year — say more about the era than the drinks do.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve cold.

name: Leap Year
description: Gin, sweet vermouth, Grand Marnier and lemon — created at the Savoy for the leap-year party of 29 February 1928.
funFact: Harry Craddock created it for the Savoy's leap-year celebration in 1928, and the book claims it 'is responsible for more proposals than any other cocktail ever mixed'.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve very cold.

name: Lucien Gaudin
description: Gin, Campari, dry vermouth and Cointreau — a Negroni that swapped half its sweetness for orange and got sharper.
funFact: Named for the French fencer who took two golds at the 1928 Olympics — one of very few cocktails named after an Olympic athlete rather than a bar or a film.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Millionaire
description: Rye, orange curaçao, grenadine and egg white — a foamy pink sour with far more backbone than its colour suggests.
funFact: At least four unrelated drinks have carried the name Millionaire across the last century, which is what happens when a name sounds better than it describes.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate a little nutmeg over the foam.

name: Ampersand
description: Old Tom gin, cognac, sweet vermouth and curaçao in equal parts. A Martinez that took brandy along.
funFact: Equal-parts drinks were the default before jiggers were common — four ingredients in the same measure is a recipe you can pour accurately in a dark bar.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top.
Serve cold.

name: Colonial
description: Gin, grapefruit and maraschino — a pre-Prohibition sour built on grapefruit before grapefruit was a bar staple.
funFact: Grapefruit was a novelty crop in America until the 1900s; its arrival in bar books marks the point at which Florida citrus started shipping north by rail.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Nuclear Daiquiri
description: Overproof Jamaican rum, green Chartreuse, falernum and lime. A Daiquiri with the safety catch removed.
funFact: Gregor de Gruyther created it at LAB in London in the mid-2000s; Wray & Nephew at 63% and Chartreuse at 55% in the same short glass is the reason for the name.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve one, and think carefully about a second.

name: Vieux Mot
description: Gin, elderflower, lemon and sugar — the Last Word's floral cousin, and the drink that put St-Germain on every back bar.
funFact: Don Lee created it at PDT in 2007, the year St-Germain launched; the name puns on the Last Word, since 'vieux mot' is French for old word.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve very cold.

name: The Business
description: Gin, honey and lime. Three ingredients, no garnish, nothing to hide behind.
funFact: It is a Bee's Knees with lime in place of lemon, and the swap matters more than it should — lime's sharper acidity keeps the honey from turning the drink syrupy.

steps: Loosen honey with warm water at three parts honey to one of water.
Shake the gin, honey syrup and lime juice hard with ice.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish.

name: Weeski
description: Irish whiskey, Lillet Blanc and Cointreau with orange bitters. Light, aromatic and unusually easy for a stirred drink.
funFact: Created at Milk & Honey in New York; the name is a phonetic joke on 'whiskey' delivered in the accent the drink is built around.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve very cold.

name: Ford Cocktail
description: Old Tom gin, dry vermouth and Bénédictine with orange bitters — a pre-Prohibition stirred drink that reads modern.
funFact: It appears in Hugo Ensslin's 1916 book, named for a bartender rather than the carmaker — the two were contemporaries and the confusion is permanent.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Bywater
description: Rye, Averna, green Chartreuse and falernum — a modern New Orleans drink with a Vieux Carré's density and none of its vermouth.
funFact: Chris Hannah created it at Arnaud's French 75 Bar and named it for the New Orleans neighbourhood downriver of the Marigny.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Elder Fashion
description: An Old Fashioned with elderflower liqueur where the sugar goes, built on gin rather than whiskey.
funFact: It belongs to a wave of drinks from around 2007 that treated St-Germain as a sweetener rather than a flavour, which is the only way it works in a spirit-forward build.

steps: Stir the gin, St-Germain and bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over one large cube in a rocks glass.
Express a grapefruit twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve immediately.

name: Silver Monk
description: Tequila, green Chartreuse, cucumber, mint and lime — herbal, cooling and considerably more complex than a Margarita.
funFact: Created at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco; cucumber and Chartreuse is an unlikely pairing that works because both are green in completely different registers.

steps: Muddle the cucumber slices gently in the shaker.
Add the mint and press once — do not shred it.
Add the tequila, Chartreuse, lime and syrup with ice, then shake hard.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a cucumber slice and a mint leaf.

name: Vaina
description: Port or pisco shaken with egg yolk, cocoa and sugar — a Chilean dessert drink poured at every Fiestas Patrias.
funFact: The name means 'sheath' or, colloquially, a nuisance — Chileans have several competing explanations and none of them are flattering to the drink.

steps: Whisk the cocoa powder and sugar into the port until fully dissolved.
Add the pisco and egg yolk to a shaker with the port mixture.
Dry-shake without ice for 15 seconds, then add ice and shake hard again.
Double-strain into a small wine glass.
Dust with cinnamon and serve cold.

name: Sucumbé
description: Hot milk whipped with egg, singani and cinnamon — Bolivian Christmas Eve, drunk at midnight after mass.
funFact: In Santa Cruz it is served in the small hours of 25 December, and families judge it on how much foam sits on top — under-whipped sucumbé is considered a failure of effort.

steps: Heat the milk with the cinnamon stick and sugar until steaming, not boiling.
Beat the egg hard in a separate bowl until pale and frothy.
Pour the hot milk slowly onto the egg while whisking constantly, or it scrambles.
Stir in the singani off the heat.
Pour into mugs with the foam on top and dust with cinnamon.

name: Crema de Vie
description: Cuba's Christmas cream: rum, egg yolk and condensed milk cooked into something thicker and sweeter than eggnog.
funFact: Cuban households make it in December and keep it refrigerated for weeks; the alcohol and sugar together do the preserving, which is why the recipe survived decades of scarce ingredients.

steps: Blend the egg yolks with both milks until completely smooth.
Warm gently over low heat, stirring, until slightly thickened — do not boil.
Cool completely to room temperature.
Stir in the rum, vanilla and lime zest.
Bottle and refrigerate at least overnight; serve cold in small glasses.

name: Guavaberry Colada
description: The island's guavaberry liqueur blended with coconut and pineapple — a Piña Colada with a wild-berry backbone.
funFact: Guavaberries are not guavas — they are a small wild fruit that ripens once a year, and islanders pick them for a folk liqueur celebrated in Sint Maarten's unofficial anthem.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with the ice.
Blend until smooth and thick.
Pour into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and, if you can get them, a few guavaberries.

name: Clericot
description: Red or white wine loaded with chopped summer fruit and served by the jug — Mexico's answer to sangria, lighter and fruitier.
funFact: Clericot descends from the English claret cup by way of Spain, and the same drink surfaces as clericó in Paraguay and Argentina with the fruit changed to whatever is in season.

ingredients.item: Apple, orange, strawberry and grape, diced

steps: Toss the diced fruit with the sugar and let it sit for an hour.
Pour over the wine and orange liqueur, then refrigerate for at least four hours.
Top with soda water just before serving.
Serve very cold over ice, spooning plenty of fruit into each glass.

name: Té con Té
description: Black tea with singani, lemon and sugar, served scalding at altitude. La Paz's answer to a cold night at 3,600 metres.
funFact: The name literally means 'tea with tea', which is the joke — the second 'té' stands in for the singani nobody wanted to name out loud.

steps: Brew the black tea strong and keep it hot.
Put the sugar and lemon juice in a warmed glass mug and stir to dissolve.
Add the hot tea and stir again.
Pour in the singani last, off the heat.
Garnish with a lemon slice and drink hot.

name: Blue Moon Cocktail
description: Gin, dry vermouth and crème de violette — pale lilac, floral and the reason violette came back into production.
funFact: Crème de violette vanished from the American market for most of the twentieth century, and the drinks that needed it — Blue Moon, Aviation — were unmakeable until it returned in 2007.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve very cold — the floral note fades as it warms.

name: Bronx Terrace
description: The Bronx with the orange juice swapped for lime and the sweet vermouth dropped. Drier, sharper and largely forgotten.
funFact: It appears in the Savoy directly after the Bronx itself, which is how the book handles variations — no cross-reference, just the next entry along.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime twist or a cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Clover Leaf
description: The Clover Club with a mint leaf on the foam. One garnish separates the two, and the mint changes the whole nose.
funFact: The only difference from a Clover Club is the mint leaf floated on the foam — an unusually small distinction to earn a separate name, and both appear in the same books.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a single mint leaf on the foam.

name: Dempsey
description: Gin and calvados with grenadine and absinthe — named for the heavyweight champion, and it hits about as hard.
funFact: Jack Dempsey held the world heavyweight title from 1919 to 1926, exactly the window in which London bartenders were naming drinks after American celebrities.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top.
Serve very cold.

name: Knickerbocker
description: Rum, raspberry, curaçao and lime over crushed ice — a mid-nineteenth-century drink that predates most of the canon.
funFact: Jerry Thomas printed it in 1862, which makes it older than the Manhattan, the Martini and almost everything else still ordered by name.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a goblet.
Garnish with berries and a slice of orange.
Serve with a straw.

name: Merry Widow
description: Gin and dry vermouth in equal parts with Bénédictine, absinthe and bitters. Low-proof by Savoy standards and unusually aromatic.
funFact: At least six unrelated drinks carry the name Merry Widow, after the operetta that was the biggest theatrical hit of the 1900s — bartenders named drinks after whatever was selling tickets.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Old Etonian
description: Gin, Lillet, orange bitters and crème de noyaux — almond and quinine, and about as English as a drink name gets.
funFact: Crème de noyaux is made from apricot and peach kernels rather than almonds, which is why it tastes of marzipan without containing any.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and discard it.
Serve very cold.

name: Opera
description: Gin, Dubonnet and maraschino with orange bitters. Bittersweet, cherry-scented and considerably drier than Dubonnet suggests.
funFact: Dubonnet was created in 1846 to make quinine palatable to French Foreign Legionnaires in North Africa — the same problem that produced tonic water.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Orange Blossom
description: Gin and orange juice, sweetened. A Prohibition drink whose whole job was hiding what the gin tasted like.
funFact: Bathtub gin was frequently undrinkable, and the Orange Blossom exists as a solution to that problem — which is why it fell out of favour the moment good gin was legal again.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve very cold.

name: Poet's Dream
description: Gin, dry vermouth and Bénédictine with a lemon twist. Three ingredients, and the Bénédictine does all the talking.
funFact: Bénédictine's label carries the letters D.O.M. — Deo Optimo Maximo, 'to God, most good, most great' — a monastic dedication that survived the liqueur going fully commercial in 1863.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Red Snapper
description: The Bloody Mary's gin original. Fernand Petiot rebuilt it with gin at the St. Regis, and the name was a euphemism.
funFact: Petiot brought the drink from Harry's Bar in Paris to the St. Regis in New York, where management thought 'Bloody Mary' too coarse for the King Cole Bar — so it became the Red Snapper.

steps: Combine everything in a shaker with ice.
Roll the drink between two tins rather than shaking, so it does not froth.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with a celery stalk and a lemon wedge.
Season further at the table.

name: Royal Bermuda Yacht Club
description: Rum, lime, falernum and curaçao — the club's own drink, and a sharper alternative to its Rum Swizzle.
funFact: The Royal Bermuda Yacht Club received its royal warrant in 1845 from Prince Albert, and the drink named for it appears in Trader Vic's book a century later.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve immediately.

name: Seventh Heaven
description: Gin, maraschino and grapefruit with a mint sprig. Bright, cherry-scented and one of the Savoy's better short sours.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book contains roughly 750 recipes, most of them gin, and the ones that survived are almost all the ones with fresh citrus in them.

steps: Shake the gin, maraschino and grapefruit juice hard with ice.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Slap a mint sprig between your palms and float it on top.
Serve very cold.

name: Tipperary
description: Irish whiskey, sweet vermouth and green Chartreuse in equal parts. Herbal, sweet and much heavier than the name suggests.
funFact: Named for the marching song rather than the county; 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary' was written in 1912 and became the defining British song of the First World War.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface.
Modern versions cut the Chartreuse back; the equal-parts original is the historic one.

name: Waldorf
description: A Manhattan rinsed with absinthe. The hotel that gave us the Bronx and the Rob Roy produced this too.
funFact: The original Waldorf-Astoria stood where the Empire State Building now is; its bar produced a remarkable share of the American canon before it was demolished in 1929.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Stir the rye, vermouth and bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into the rinsed coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.

name: Yale
description: A Martini turned blue with a dash of crème de violette, and stiffened with orange bitters.
funFact: American universities each acquired a cocktail in the early 1900s — Yale, Princeton, Harvard — in a fashion that says more about who was drinking in hotel bars than about the colleges.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a thoroughly chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.
Serve very cold.

name: Fallen Angel
description: Gin, lime and crème de menthe with bitters. Mint and juniper together, which sounds wrong and drinks clean.
funFact: White crème de menthe is the same liqueur as the green one without the colouring, which is why a Fallen Angel looks like a Gimlet and tastes nothing like one.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a mint leaf.
Serve very cold.

name: Napoleon
description: Gin with three dashes each of Dubonnet, curaçao and Fernet. Almost neat gin, seasoned rather than mixed.
funFact: Fernet in dashes rather than measures is a nineteenth-century habit that modern bartenders rediscovered — a quarter-teaspoon changes a drink that an ounce would destroy.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.
Serve extremely cold.

name: Wassail
description: Hot spiced ale with roasted apples bobbing in it, carried house to house at midwinter. Older than the word cocktail by centuries.
funFact: 'Wassail' comes from the Old Norse ves heill, 'be in good health', and in cider counties the bowl is still carried into the orchards in January to toast the trees themselves.
