steps: Core the apples, fill them with brown sugar and roast at 180°C until soft and foaming, about 40 minutes.
Warm the ale and sherry with the spices and remaining sugar — steaming, never boiling.
Float the roasted apples in the bowl; the pulp bursting into the ale is where 'lamb's wool' gets its name.
Ladle into cups, making sure everyone gets some apple.
Serve hot, and pass the bowl rather than pouring individual drinks.

name: Smoking Bishop
description: Port and roasted oranges mulled together — the drink Scrooge promises Bob Cratchit on the last page of A Christmas Carol.
funFact: Dickens gave it the last line of dialogue in A Christmas Carol — 'a bowl of Smoking Bishop' — and the drink was already old enough by 1843 that he needed no footnote.

steps: Stud each orange with five cloves and roast at 180°C until browned, about an hour.
Quarter the roasted oranges and steep them in the red wine with the sugar and spices overnight.
Strain, pressing the fruit, then add the port.
Heat gently to steaming — never boil, or the port turns harsh.
Ladle into mugs and serve hot.

name: Lamb's Wool
description: Hot ale poured over roasted apple pulp until it froths white — the froth is the wool, and the drink is medieval.
funFact: The name describes the appearance: burst roasted apple whipped into hot ale forms a woolly white foam, and the drink belongs to Twelfth Night rather than Christmas.

steps: Roast the apples whole at 180°C until they split and collapse, about 45 minutes.
Scoop out the pulp and beat it smooth with the sugar and spices.
Warm the ale to steaming, then whisk it into the apple pulp a little at a time.
Keep whisking until the surface turns white and woolly.
Serve hot in tankards.

name: Syllabub
description: Cream whipped with sweet wine, sugar and lemon until it holds its shape. Tudor England's dessert, eaten with a spoon.
funFact: The earliest version was made by milking a cow directly into a bowl of spiced wine, so the froth formed on impact — a technique that limits where you can make it.

steps: Steep the lemon zest and juice in the wine and sherry with the sugar for several hours.
Strain out the zest and stir until the sugar has fully dissolved.
Pour the cream in slowly while whisking, until it holds soft peaks.
Spoon into small glasses and chill for at least two hours.
Grate nutmeg over just before serving, with a spoon.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and lemon zest

name: Negus
description: Port with hot water, lemon, sugar and nutmeg. Served to children at Victorian parties, which says something about the era.
funFact: Named for Colonel Francis Negus, who reportedly diluted the port at a heated gathering to calm the argument down; Dickens has it served at children's parties in more than one novel.

steps: Rub the sugar over the lemon zest to draw out the oil, then put both in a warmed jug.
Add the lemon juice and the port.
Pour in hot but not boiling water and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Ladle into warmed glasses.
Grate nutmeg over each serving.

name: Posset
description: Hot milk curdled deliberately with ale or wine, spiced and sweetened. Medicinal, medieval, and eaten as much as drunk.
funFact: Posset pots had a spout so the drinker could take the liquid from beneath while the curds sat on top; the modern lemon posset dessert kept the name and dropped the alcohol entirely.

steps: Warm the milk with the cinnamon and nutmeg until steaming; do not boil.
Warm the ale or wine separately with the sugar.
Pour the hot ale into the hot milk — it will curdle immediately, which is correct.
Let it stand a minute so the curd rises and the liquid settles below.
Serve hot, with a spoon.

name: Brandy Sour
description: Cyprus's national cocktail: local brandy, lemon squash, bitters and soda. Invented, by tradition, to disguise a king's drinking.
funFact: The story holds that it was created in the 1930s for King Farouk of Egypt, so a visiting Muslim monarch could be served something that looked like iced tea.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the brandy and lemon squash.
Dash the Angostura generously over the top.
Top with soda water and stir once.
Garnish with a lemon slice.

name: Kinnie and Gin
description: Malta's bitter-orange soda lengthening a measure of gin — wormwood and bitter orange over juniper.
funFact: Kinnie has been bottled in Malta since 1952 from bitter oranges and a mix of aromatic herbs including wormwood, and Maltese abroad have it shipped to them.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the gin.
Top with cold Kinnie.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice.

name: Rum and Raspberry
description: White rum with raspberry cordial and soda — 'R&R' across southern Africa, and a staple of Mozambican beach bars.
funFact: Ordered simply as 'R and R' from Maputo to Johannesburg, it is one of very few mixed drinks with genuine regional currency across southern Africa.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum, raspberry cordial and lime juice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Fort Point
description: Rye, Punt e Mes, Bénédictine and maraschino — a Manhattan with the bitterness turned up and the sweetness pulled back.
funFact: Sam Ross created it at Milk & Honey; Punt e Mes is a vermouth with an extra measure of bitterness stirred in, and its name means 'point and a half' from an old Turin trading term.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Kentucky Maid
description: Bourbon with muddled cucumber and mint over lime. A Southside that went south, and better in summer than either parent.
funFact: Sam Ross built it at Milk & Honey as a bourbon answer to the gin Southside; cucumber and bourbon is an unlikely pairing that the mint holds together.

steps: Muddle two cucumber slices with the syrup in the shaker.
Add the mint and press once, gently.
Add the bourbon, lime juice and ice, then shake hard for 10 seconds.
Double-strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a cucumber slice and a mint sprig.

name: Death Flip
description: Tequila, yellow Chartreuse, Jägermeister and a whole egg. It should be undrinkable. It is one of the best modern cocktails made.
funFact: Chris Hysted created it at Black Pearl in Melbourne around 2010; the combination reads as a dare on paper and converts almost everyone who is talked into ordering one.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate nutmeg over the foam.
Serve immediately.

name: Gordon's Breakfast
description: Gin with lime, Worcestershire, Tabasco and muddled cucumber. A savoury gin sour that behaves like a Bloody Mary without the tomato.
funFact: Sam Ross named it for Gordon's gin and for the fact that it is, structurally, a breakfast drink — savoury, saline and built to be drunk before noon.

steps: Muddle the cucumber slices in the bottom of the shaker.
Add the gin, lime, syrup, Worcestershire, Tabasco and seasoning.
Add ice and shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a cucumber slice and a crack of black pepper.

name: Bermuda Rose
description: Gin with apricot brandy and grenadine, sharpened with lemon. Pink, stone-fruited and entirely of its decade.
funFact: Apricot brandy in interwar bar books means an apricot liqueur, not a distilled eau-de-vie — buying the wrong bottle turns half the Savoy unmakeable.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Blackthorn
description: Irish whiskey, dry vermouth and absinthe with Angostura. Softer than a Sazerac and sharper than a Manhattan.
funFact: A second, unrelated Blackthorn made with sloe gin exists in the same books — the name attaches to the blackthorn shrub, which gives both sloes and shillelaghs.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Charlie Chaplin
description: Equal parts sloe gin, apricot brandy and lime. Invented at the Waldorf while Chaplin was the most famous man alive.
funFact: The Waldorf-Astoria named it during Chaplin's peak, when he was arguably the most recognisable person on earth — an equal-parts drink for a man who needed no introduction.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Claridge
description: Gin and dry vermouth cut with apricot and triple sec — a Martini that let the fruit in.
funFact: Named for the Hôtel Claridge on the Champs-Élysées rather than the London hotel, which spells its name with an apostrophe and served different drinks entirely.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Cornell
description: Gin, maraschino and egg white shaken to a pale foam — the quietest of the American college cocktails.
funFact: Cornell, Yale, Princeton and Harvard all acquired cocktails in the 1900s; the drinks have nothing in common beyond the hotel bars that named them.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before serving.

name: Deep Sea
description: Gin and dry vermouth with absinthe and orange bitters. A Martini pulled toward anise and further out to sea.
funFact: Absinthe in dashes rather than measures is the interwar house style: enough to perfume a drink, never enough to lead it.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Delmonico
description: Gin, brandy and both vermouths with orange bitters — named for the restaurant that invented American fine dining.
funFact: Delmonico's opened in 1837 and is credited with the first à la carte menu in America, along with eggs Benedict and lobster Newberg.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Dubonnet Cocktail
description: Gin and Dubonnet, two to one, with a lemon twist. The Queen's drink, reportedly taken daily before lunch.
funFact: Queen Elizabeth II's preference for gin and Dubonnet was well enough known that a 1950s note in her own hand requesting one was later sold at auction.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Emerald
description: A Manhattan made with Irish whiskey. Lighter, grassier and unaccountably rare on menus.
funFact: Irish whiskey outsold Scotch worldwide before Prohibition and the Irish War of Independence between them destroyed its export trade; the category took eighty years to recover.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Fine and Dandy
description: Gin, triple sec and lemon with a dash of Angostura — a White Lady with bitters and no egg.
funFact: The gin sour with orange liqueur is the single most repeated shape in the Savoy, appearing under at least a dozen names with only the garnish or a dash separating them.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Flying Dutchman
description: Gin with a dash of triple sec, stirred hard and served cold. Barely a cocktail, and better for it.
funFact: Named for the ghost ship of North Sea legend, a story Dutch and English sailors traded for centuries before Wagner set it to music.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Golden Dawn
description: Gin, calvados, apricot and orange, with grenadine dropped through so it bleeds a sunrise up the glass.
funFact: It won a London hotel competition in 1930, and the grenadine sunrise it is named for predates the Tequila Sunrise by four decades.

steps: Shake the gin, calvados, apricot brandy and orange juice hard with ice.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Drop a dash of grenadine through the centre and let it settle.
Do not stir — the sunrise is the drink.
recipe.garnish: A grenadine sunrise through the glass

name: Green Dragon
description: Gin, kümmel, green crème de menthe and lemon with peach bitters. Caraway and mint, which is stranger than it sounds.
funFact: Kümmel is a caraway and fennel liqueur that survives in Britain almost entirely because golf clubs kept ordering it as a cure for the shakes on the first tee.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Hula-Hula
description: Gin, orange juice and a dash of curaçao. A Bronx without the vermouth, named a decade before tiki existed.
funFact: It predates the American tiki craze by twenty years; the interwar fashion for Polynesian names ran well ahead of any Polynesian drinks.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Jockey Club
description: Gin, crème de noyaux, lemon and two bitters. Almond and juniper in a short, dry glass.
funFact: Almond notes in cocktails come from three unrelated places — noyaux from stone fruit kernels, orgeat from real almonds, and amaretto from either.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Judge Jr.
description: Gin, rum, lemon and grenadine. A Prohibition drink named for a humour magazine that ran cocktail recipes illegally.
funFact: Judge magazine printed cocktail recipes throughout Prohibition, when publishing them was legally dubious and commercially irresistible.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Leave It To Me
description: Gin, apricot, lemon and grenadine. One of several Savoy drinks whose name is a complete sentence.
funFact: The Savoy is full of imperative titles — Leave It To Me, Between the Sheets, Hanky Panky — which reads as a house voice rather than coincidence.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Lone Tree
description: Gin with both vermouths and orange bitters — a Perfect Martini under a different name.
funFact: Half the interwar canon is a Martini with the vermouth ratio moved and a new name attached; the Lone Tree is the perfect split.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Moulin Rouge
description: Sloe gin, apricot and Angostura, shaken cold. Deep red and named for the windmill on Boulevard de Clichy.
funFact: The Moulin Rouge opened in 1889 and its windmill has burned down and been rebuilt more than once; the sails still turn over Pigalle.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Obituary
description: A Martini with absinthe in place of most of the vermouth. Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop has poured it for decades.
funFact: Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop on Bourbon Street claims to be among the oldest structures used as a bar in the United States, built in the 1720s and still lit largely by candle.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Palm Beach
description: Gin, sweet vermouth and grapefruit. Three ingredients, bitter and dry, and it drinks like Florida in February.
funFact: Grapefruit was still a novelty when this was written — Florida's groves only reached the northern market once refrigerated rail cars made the trip viable.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Pall Mall
description: Gin, both vermouths, white crème de menthe and orange bitters. Mint through a Perfect Martini.
funFact: Pall Mall is named for pall-mall, a croquet-like game played on the street in the seventeenth century before it became London's clubland.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Park Avenue
description: Gin, sweet vermouth, pineapple and a dash of curaçao. Softer and more tropical than its address suggests.
funFact: Tinned pineapple juice reached British bars in the 1920s and appears all over the Savoy — one of the first industrially processed ingredients the cocktail canon absorbed.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Perfect Lady
description: Gin, peach brandy, lemon and egg white — a competition winner from 1936 and a White Lady with stone fruit.
funFact: It won the 1936 British Empire Cocktail Competition, an annual contest that shaped London drinking more than any single bar did.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve once the foam has set.

name: Prince's Smile
description: Gin, calvados and apricot with lemon. Apple and stone fruit over juniper, and drier than the fruit list suggests.
funFact: Calvados appears throughout the interwar books because Normandy apple brandy was cheap and plentiful in London; it went scarce after the war and the drinks went with it.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Princeton
description: Gin and port, layered rather than mixed, with orange bitters. The port sits underneath and stays there.
funFact: The original instruction is to pour the port carefully so it settles below the gin — a layered Martini, and one of very few stirred drinks meant to be served unmixed.

steps: Stir the gin and orange bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Pour the port slowly down the side so it settles beneath the gin.
Serve without stirring; the layers are the point.

name: Racquet Club
description: Gin and dry vermouth with orange bitters — a club Martini, and the bitters are not optional.
funFact: Orange bitters were standard in Martinis until the 1940s and then vanished for fifty years; nearly every pre-war Martini variant assumes them.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Rolls-Royce
description: Gin, both vermouths and a dash of Bénédictine. Smooth, herbal and named to sell itself.
funFact: Naming a cocktail after a luxury marque was standard interwar practice — the Rolls-Royce, the Hispano-Suiza and the Bentley all have drinks.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Royal Smile
description: Gin, calvados, grenadine and lemon. Pink, appley and one of the better Savoy fruit sours.
funFact: Real grenadine is pomegranate, not cherry — the artificially flavoured red syrup that replaced it in the 1950s is responsible for a generation dismissing these drinks.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Silver Bullet
description: Gin, kümmel and lemon, stirred cold. Caraway against juniper, and much drier than it reads.
funFact: Kümmel has been made in the Low Countries since the sixteenth century, and the same caraway-and-fennel formula turns up in Scandinavian aquavit under a different name.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Straits Sling
description: The Singapore Sling's older, drier ancestor: gin, Bénédictine, cherry brandy, lemon and soda.
funFact: Printed in the 1920s as the Straits Sling, it is markedly less sweet than the pineapple-heavy Singapore Sling that Raffles serves today.

steps: Shake everything except the soda hard with ice.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish.

name: Sunshine Cocktail
description: Gin, sweet vermouth and a dash of grenadine, strained cold. Pink, short and sweeter than a Martini by a hair.
funFact: There are at least three unrelated Sunshine Cocktails in print between 1900 and 1940, which is roughly the base rate for optimistic cocktail names.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Tango Cocktail
description: Gin, both vermouths, curaçao and orange juice. Six things in a small glass, and it holds together.
funFact: The tango reached London around 1913 and caused enough moral panic that some hotels banned it — the cocktail arrived with the dance.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Ulanda
description: Gin, triple sec and a dash of absinthe. Two parts gin to one of orange, and the absinthe does the rest.
funFact: Nobody has established what Ulanda refers to — it is one of a handful of Savoy names with no traceable origin at all.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Union Jack
description: Gin and sloe gin with a dash of grenadine — red and blue in one glass, which is the whole joke.
funFact: Sloe gin is made by steeping blackthorn sloes in gin and sugar, traditionally after the first frost splits their skins.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Wembley
description: Gin, dry vermouth and apricot with a dash of calvados. Named for the 1924 British Empire Exhibition.
funFact: The British Empire Exhibition at Wembley drew 27 million visitors across 1924 and 1925, and left behind the stadium and a handful of cocktails.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: White Rose
description: Gin, maraschino, orange and lemon with egg white. A Clover Club that swapped raspberry for citrus.
funFact: Egg white in a sour is doing structural work rather than adding flavour — it emulsifies the citrus oils and holds the aromatics at the surface.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve once the foam has settled.

name: Whizz Bang
description: Scotch, dry vermouth, absinthe and grenadine with orange bitters. Named for a First World War shell.
funFact: A whizz-bang was a German field shell whose shriek arrived barely before the explosion; soldiers' slang moved straight onto interwar drinks lists.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Yellow Daisy
description: Gin, dry vermouth and Grand Marnier in equal-ish measure. Orange-heavy, aromatic and easy to like.
funFact: The daisy family — spirit, citrus liqueur and lemon over ice — is one of the oldest cocktail templates, and the Margarita is a tequila daisy by another name.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Zaza
description: Gin and Dubonnet with orange bitters — the Dubonnet Cocktail under a stage name, from a 1898 French play.
funFact: Zaza was a hit French play of 1898 about a music-hall singer, adapted into three separate Hollywood films; the drink outlived all of them.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Kon-Tiki
description: Aged rum with orange curaçao, lemon and orgeat over crushed ice — a Trader Vic build named for Heyerdahl's raft.
funFact: Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft crossed 4,300 miles of Pacific in 1947; the name was attached to restaurants, drinks and a whole aesthetic within a decade.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and a lemon wheel

name: Mariner's Grog
description: Three rums with grapefruit, honey and cinnamon. Grog in the naval sense — rum, water, citrus and something to stop scurvy.
funFact: The Royal Navy issued grog — rum cut with water and citrus — from 1740 until 1970, and the last daily ration was poured on 31 July, still called Black Tot Day.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.

name: Outrigger
description: Light rum with passionfruit, lime and a float of dark rum — named for the canoe hull that made Pacific voyaging possible.
funFact: The outrigger float is what let Polynesian voyagers sail thousands of miles of open ocean in canoes; it is the single most consequential piece of Pacific technology.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: A dark rum float and a lime wheel

name: Pi Yi
description: Rum, passionfruit and lime blended and served in a hollowed pineapple. Beachcomber's fruit-vessel showpiece.
funFact: Serving in the hollowed fruit was practical marketing: the vessel cost nothing, could not be stolen easily, and photographed better than any glass.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Served in a hollowed pineapple with a mint sprig

name: Port au Prince
description: Haitian rum with pineapple, lime, falernum and grenadine — one of the few tiki drinks that names its rum's actual origin.
funFact: Haitian rhum is distilled from cane juice rather than molasses, which is why it tastes grassy and vegetal where Jamaican rum tastes of treacle.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.

name: Tortuga
description: Two rums with orange, lime and a sweet vermouth backbone — unusual for tiki, which almost never uses vermouth.
funFact: Tortuga, off northern Haiti, was the buccaneers' base in the seventeenth century — the actual pirate island the tiki aesthetic was borrowing from.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.

name: Tropical Itch
description: Bourbon and two rums with passionfruit, served with a backscratcher in the glass. The garnish is not optional.
funFact: The bamboo backscratcher is the drink — Hawaiian bars have served it that way since the 1950s, and ordering one without is considered a failure of nerve.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: A bamboo backscratcher and an orchid

name: Coconut Grog
description: Rum with coconut cream, honey, cinnamon and citrus — a grog that went through the tropics rather than the North Atlantic.
funFact: Beachcomber layered spice syrups the way a perfumer layers base notes — cinnamon, vanilla and allspice recur across dozens of his recipes in different proportions.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Toasted coconut and a cinnamon stick

name: Demerara Dry Float
description: A short rum sour under a float of overproof Demerara. The float is the drink's whole architecture.
funFact: A float sits on top because it is less dense; you get the overproof rum on the nose and the first sip, then the drink beneath softens as it mixes.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: An overproof float and a lime wheel

name: Japanese Cocktail
description: Cognac, orgeat and bitters. No Japanese ingredient at all — named for a diplomatic delegation that visited New York in 1860.
funFact: Jerry Thomas named it for the first Japanese embassy to the United States, which arrived in 1860 and was received with enormous public curiosity.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Brandy Smash
description: Brandy, sugar and mint pounded over crushed ice. Jerry Thomas called the smash a julep on a small plan, and meant it literally.
funFact: The 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide is the first cocktail book published anywhere, and the smash is one of the six families it organises everything around.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in the bottom of a rocks glass.
Add the brandy and fill with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the glass frosts.
Top with more crushed ice and crown with a mint bouquet.

name: Gin Sling
description: Gin, lemon, sugar and water, with nutmeg over the top. The sling predates the cocktail and was originally served hot.
funFact: A sling in the eighteenth century was spirit, water, sugar and nutmeg — the cocktail was defined in 1806 specifically as a sling with bitters added.

steps: Shake the gin, lemon juice, syrup and water with ice.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface.
Serve with a straw.

name: Locomotive
description: Hot red wine with honey, egg yolk and curaçao, whisked smooth. A Victorian hot drink with a custard's texture.
funFact: Nineteenth-century bar books are full of hot egg drinks; central heating and refrigeration between them killed off almost the entire category.

steps: Whisk the egg yolk with the honey until pale and smooth.
Warm the wine with the cloves until steaming — never boiling.
Pour the hot wine slowly onto the egg mixture while whisking hard.
Return briefly to low heat to thicken, then stir in the curaçao.
Serve hot with cinnamon grated over.

name: Golden Slipper
description: Yellow Chartreuse, apricot brandy and an egg yolk floated whole between them. A Victorian layered drink that takes a steady hand.
funFact: The unbroken yolk suspended between two liqueurs is the point — layered pousse-café drinks were a display of bartending skill as much as anything to drink.

steps: Pour the yellow Chartreuse into a small wine glass.
Float the apricot brandy over the back of a barspoon so it layers cleanly.
Slide a whole unbroken egg yolk gently into the centre.
Serve immediately, without stirring.

name: Bishop
description: Port mulled with a clove-studded roasted orange and sugar. The parent of the Smoking Bishop and older than it.
funFact: The whole family is named for ecclesiastical ranks by strength and ingredient — Bishop is port, Cardinal is claret, Pope is champagne, Archbishop is claret with ginger.

steps: Stud an orange with cloves and roast at 180°C until browned, about 45 minutes.
Quarter the roasted orange and add it to the port with the sugar and cinnamon.
Heat gently to steaming for 20 minutes; do not boil.
Strain into warmed mugs and serve hot.

name: Arrack Punch
description: Batavia arrack with lemon, sugar, tea and water. The original punch, brought back from the Indies by the East India Company.
funFact: Punch reached England from India in the seventeenth century and the word probably comes from panch, Hindi for five — spirit, citrus, sugar, water and spice.

steps: Rub the sugar into the lemon peel and leave for an hour to draw out the oil.
Add the lemon juice and stir until the sugar dissolves, then strain out the peel.
Add the arrack and the hot tea, and stir well.
Chill thoroughly, or serve warm in winter.
Ladle into cups over a block of ice, with nutmeg grated on top.

name: Cambridge Milk Punch
description: Brandy and rum in hot milk with sugar, lemon and egg, whisked to a froth. A university drink from before the cocktail existed.
funFact: Distinct from clarified milk punch, where the milk is curdled and strained out — here the milk stays in, and the drink is served hot and foaming.

steps: Warm the milk with the lemon peel and sugar until steaming, then discard the peel.
Beat the egg hard in a separate bowl.
Pour the hot milk slowly onto the egg while whisking, or it will scramble.
Stir in the brandy and rum off the heat and whisk until foaming.
Serve hot with nutmeg grated over.

name: Regent's Punch
description: Champagne, brandy, rum, arrack and tea over citrus — the Prince Regent's punch, and about as extravagant as it sounds.
funFact: Named for the future George IV, whose household spent so freely on entertaining that Parliament twice had to settle his debts.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the cooled tea and citrus juice.
Add the brandy, rum and arrack and stir well.
Chill for several hours with a large block of ice in the bowl.
Top with champagne only at the moment of serving.
Ladle into cups, giving each a wheel of citrus.
recipe.garnish: Citrus wheels and a block of ice

name: Stone Wall
description: Aged rum over hard cider with bitters. Colonial New England drank it before the word cocktail was written down.
funFact: New England distilled rum from Caribbean molasses and pressed cider from its own orchards, so a drink combining the two was the cheapest thing on the table.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum and the bitters.
Top with cold hard cider.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice.

name: Green Beast
description: Absinthe, lime, sugar and water with cucumber — a low-proof absinthe punch that converts people who think they hate absinthe.
funFact: Charles Vexenat built it as equal parts absinthe, lime, sugar and water — the classic punch ratio — which dilutes absinthe to about the strength of wine.

steps: Combine the absinthe, lime juice and syrup in a tall glass.
Add the cold water and stir — it will louche to opaque green.
Fill with ice and stir again briefly.
Float cucumber wheels on the surface and serve.

name: Newark
description: Applejack, sweet vermouth, Fernet and maraschino — a Brooklyn built on apple brandy, and named across the river.
funFact: Jim Meehan and Toby Maloney built it as a Brooklyn variation; Laird's in New Jersey has been distilling applejack since 1780 and holds America's oldest distilling licence.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Marconi Wireless
description: Applejack and sweet vermouth with orange bitters — a Manhattan made with apple brandy, named for the radio.
funFact: Marconi sent the first transatlantic wireless signal in 1901, and American bars named drinks after the technology the way they later would after aviation.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Rattlesnake
description: Rye, lemon, sugar and egg white with an absinthe rinse. The Savoy says it will 'either cure a rattlesnake bite, kill rattlesnakes, or make you see them'.
funFact: That three-part claim is printed verbatim in the Savoy Cocktail Book, which is unusually candid for a drinks list of any era.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Dry-shake the rye, lemon, syrup and egg white without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into the rinsed coupe and let the foam settle.

name: Tia Mia
description: A Mai Tai split between mezcal and Jamaican rum. Smoke where the second rum was, and it changes the whole drink.
funFact: Ivy Mix created it at Leyenda in Brooklyn; the name is an anagram of Mai Tai, which is also exactly what the drink is.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 10 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig and the spent lime shell.
Serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and a spent lime shell

name: Chrysanthemum Royale
description: The Chrysanthemum lengthened with champagne — vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe under bubbles.
funFact: Adding champagne to an existing cocktail and calling it 'Royale' is a French convention that produced the Kir Royale, the French 75 and a dozen lesser drinks.

steps: Stir the vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express an orange twist over the surface and serve.

name: Bitter Elder
description: Elderflower, Campari and grapefruit over soda. Bitter and floral at once, and low enough proof for an afternoon.
funFact: Elderflower and Campari share a register that most bartenders miss — both are simultaneously perfumed and bitter, which is why they layer rather than fight.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add the St-Germain, Campari and grapefruit juice and stir.
Top with soda water and stir once more.
Express a grapefruit twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Chartreuse Daisy
description: Green Chartreuse with lemon, grenadine and soda over crushed ice. A daisy built on a liqueur rather than a spirit.
funFact: The daisy is spirit, citrus and a sweetener topped with soda; swapping the base spirit for Chartreuse is the kind of substitution nineteenth-century books made freely.

steps: Shake the Chartreuse, lemon juice and grenadine with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a mint sprig.

name: Bensonhurst Fizz
description: The Bensonhurst lengthened with soda over ice — rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and Cynar made long.
funFact: Lengthening a stirred drink with soda is the simplest way to make a spirit-forward recipe drinkable in summer, and Brooklyn bars did it to most of the neighbourhood series.

steps: Stir the rye, vermouth, maraschino and Cynar over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water and stir once.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Oaxaca Sour
description: Mezcal, lime and agave under an egg-white foam with a chilli-salt dusting. A smoky sour with heat on the finish.
funFact: Sal de gusano — salt ground with toasted agave worm and chilli — is the traditional Oaxacan accompaniment to mezcal, and works as a dusting where a rim would be too much.

steps: Dry-shake the mezcal, lime, agave and egg white without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dust the foam lightly with chilli salt and serve.

name: Harvard
description: Brandy, sweet vermouth and bitters with a splash of soda — a Manhattan built on cognac, and the oldest of the college cocktails.
funFact: Brandy was America's default spirit until phylloxera destroyed the French vineyards in the 1870s and whiskey took its place — most brandy cocktails date from before that shift.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Duplex
description: Both vermouths in equal measure with orange bitters. No base spirit at all, and a staple order before Prohibition.
funFact: Vermouth-only cocktails filled American afternoon drinking until Prohibition killed the habit; the category had to be rediscovered from books eighty years later.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Vermouth Cocktail
description: Sweet vermouth with bitters and a cherry, stirred cold. The simplest drink in the nineteenth-century canon.
funFact: Jerry Thomas lists it in 1862 with no base spirit — proof that a cocktail was originally defined by structure, spirit plus sugar plus bitters, rather than by strength.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Absinthe Frappé
description: Absinthe, anisette and mint shaken over crushed ice until the glass frosts white. New Orleans in the heat.
funFact: The Old Absinthe House on Bourbon Street has served it since the 1870s, and a song was written about it in 1904 — decades before absinthe was banned in America.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in a shaker.
Add the absinthe, anisette and crushed ice and shake hard until the tin frosts.
Pour unstrained into a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda and crown with mint.

name: Absinthe Suissesse
description: Absinthe with orgeat, cream and egg white, blended pale green. A New Orleans breakfast drink, and served as one.
funFact: It is served in the French Quarter as a morning drink, and Brennan's has poured it at breakfast for decades alongside eggs and turtle soup.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with crushed ice.
Blend until pale green, smooth and frothy.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a mint sprig and serve immediately.

name: Roffignac
description: Cognac with raspberry shrub and soda over ice — named for a New Orleans mayor of the 1820s.
funFact: Count Louis Philippe de Roffignac was mayor of New Orleans from 1820 to 1828 and is credited with the city's first street lighting and paved roads.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the cognac and raspberry shrub and stir.
Top with cold soda water.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Alabazam
description: Cognac, curaçao, lemon and a heavy hand of Angostura. Named by a Victorian barman for no reason anyone recorded.
funFact: The bitters measure is unusually large for the era — a full two teaspoons where most recipes call for dashes, which is what gives the drink its name-worthy kick.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Fanciulli
description: A Manhattan with Fernet-Branca in place of the bitters. Minty, medicinal and considerably more assertive.
funFact: Fernet-Branca has been made in Milan since 1845 and contains around 27 botanicals; its recipe is held by the Branca family and has never been published.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Star Cocktail
description: Applejack and sweet vermouth with bitters — the apple-brandy Manhattan, and older than most whiskey ones.
funFact: Applejack was made in colonial America by freezing cider and removing the ice — a method called jacking, which is where the spirit gets its name.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Bombay Cocktail
description: Brandy, both vermouths, curaçao and absinthe. Five ingredients, all of them aromatic, and no citrus anywhere.
funFact: It has nothing to do with Bombay — interwar bar books attached imperial place names to drinks with no connection to them, which is most of the Savoy's geography.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Metropole
description: Brandy and dry vermouth with Peychaud's and orange bitters. The Metropolitan's drier twin, from the hotel of the same name.
funFact: The Hotel Metropole stood on Broadway and was notorious enough that gambler Herman Rosenthal was shot outside it in 1912, in a case that brought down a police lieutenant.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Metropolitan
description: Brandy and sweet vermouth with bitters and a little sugar. The sweeter half of a Victorian pair.
funFact: Not to be confused with the 1990s vodka-and-cranberry Metropolitan, which shares the name and nothing else — the collision is a century apart.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Third Rail
description: Rum, brandy and applejack in equal measure with an absinthe rinse. Named for the electrified rail, and appropriately.
funFact: Three base spirits at equal measure with no dilution beyond stirring — this is among the strongest drinks in the classic canon by design rather than accident.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Stir the rum, brandy and applejack over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into the rinsed coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and serve.

name: Honeymoon
description: Calvados, Bénédictine, curaçao and lemon — from a Berkshires restaurant, and one of the better applejack sours.
funFact: It comes from the Hotel Wentworth's Honeymoon Cocktail via a 1930s Massachusetts restaurant, and is sometimes printed as the Farmer's Daughter.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Bosom Caresser
description: Brandy, curaçao and grenadine shaken with a whole egg yolk. Rich, orange-red and named with Victorian directness.
funFact: Nineteenth-century drink names were startlingly frank — the Bosom Caresser sits in the same books as the Corpse Reviver and the Maiden's Blush.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate nutmeg over the surface.

name: Deauville
description: Calvados and cognac with Cointreau and lemon — a Sidecar split between grape and apple brandy.
funFact: Deauville on the Normandy coast was the fashionable summer resort of interwar Paris, close enough to the calvados orchards to explain the recipe.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Depth Bomb
description: Calvados and cognac with lemon and grenadine — a First World War name for a drink of apple and grape.
funFact: Depth charges were new technology in 1916, and the drink joined a wave of cocktails named after weapons that also gave us the Whizz Bang and the French 75.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Chicago Cocktail
description: Brandy and curaçao with bitters, topped with champagne in a sugar-rimmed glass.
funFact: The sugared rim is the tell of a whole family of nineteenth-century 'crusta'-influenced drinks, of which the Brandy Crusta is the best-known survivor.

steps: Rim a chilled coupe with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the brandy, curaçao and bitters with ice.
Strain into the rimmed coupe.
Top slowly with champagne and serve.
recipe.garnish: A sugared rim and a lemon twist

name: Brandy Champarelle
description: Curaçao, yellow Chartreuse, anisette and brandy, layered in that order. A New Orleans pousse-café.
funFact: Layering works on sugar density: the sweetest liqueur goes first and the driest spirit last, which is why the brandy floats on top rather than sinking.

steps: Pour the curaçao into a pony glass.
Float the yellow Chartreuse over the back of a barspoon.
Float the anisette the same way, then the brandy last.
Serve immediately without stirring.
recipe.garnish: None — the layers are the presentation

name: Silver Fizz
description: A Gin Fizz with egg white shaken through it. The silver is the foam, and it is the whole difference.
funFact: The fizz family is graded by egg: silver takes the white, golden the yolk, and royal the whole egg — three named drinks from one recipe.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam and serve at once.

name: Golden Fizz
description: A Gin Fizz built on the yolk instead of the white — richer, rounder and pale gold rather than white.
funFact: The yolk emulsifies rather than foams, so a Golden Fizz has body where a Silver Fizz has head — the same trick that separates a flip from a sour.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam and serve at once.

name: Royal Fizz
description: The whole egg, white and yolk together. Foam and body at once, and the richest member of the family.
funFact: A whole egg needs a longer dry shake than either half alone — twenty seconds minimum, or the white and yolk never properly combine.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam and serve at once.

name: Diamond Fizz
description: A Gin Fizz topped with champagne instead of soda. Also sold as a French 75 with the ratio moved.
funFact: The line between a Diamond Fizz and a French 75 is almost entirely a matter of which book you are reading and how much gin is in it.

steps: Shake the gin, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled highball glass with no ice.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and serve.

name: Gin Daisy
description: Gin, lemon and grenadine over crushed ice with a splash of soda. The daisy is the template the Margarita descends from.
funFact: Margarita is Spanish for daisy, and a Margarita is structurally a tequila daisy — spirit, citrus and a sweetener, served the same way.

steps: Shake the gin, lemon juice and grenadine hard with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a mint sprig.

name: Brandy Daisy
description: The daisy built on cognac, with yellow Chartreuse standing in for part of the sweetener.
funFact: Nineteenth-century books print the daisy separately for every base spirit — gin, brandy, whiskey, rum — as four entries rather than one recipe with a note.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice, Chartreuse and grenadine with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.

name: Whiskey Daisy
description: Rye, lemon and grenadine over crushed ice. The American branch of the daisy family.
funFact: The daisy, the fix, the fizz and the cobbler are all the same idea at different dilutions — the nineteenth century organised drinks by structure rather than by base.

steps: Shake the rye, lemon juice and grenadine hard with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and seasonal berries.

name: Gin Fix
description: Gin, lemon, sugar and a little water over crushed ice, fruit piled on top. A sour served long and cold.
funFact: A fix differs from a sour only in being built over crushed ice in the glass rather than shaken and strained — the fruit garnish is doing the work of the presentation.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the lemon juice and water in the glass.
Add the gin and stir once.
Fill with crushed ice and churn with a barspoon until frosted.
Cap with more crushed ice and pile fruit on top.
recipe.garnish: Seasonal fruit piled on the ice

name: Whiskey Fix
description: Bourbon over crushed ice with lemon and sugar, fruit heaped over. The fix, in its most-ordered form.
funFact: Crushed ice was a luxury before mechanical refrigeration — a fix or a julep was a display of a bar's ice supply as much as its bartending.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the lemon juice and water in the glass.
Add the bourbon and stir.
Fill with crushed ice and churn until the glass frosts.
Top with more ice and heap fruit over it.
recipe.garnish: Seasonal fruit and a lemon wheel

name: Whiskey Cobbler
description: Bourbon over crushed ice with sugar and fruit, churned until frosted. The cobbler that made the straw famous.
funFact: The Sherry Cobbler popularised the drinking straw in the 1840s — before it, straws were literal rye stalks, and the cobbler is what made them a bar fixture.

steps: Muddle the orange slices with the sugar in a goblet.
Add the bourbon and fill with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the glass frosts.
Cap with more ice, heap the berries on top and add a straw.
recipe.garnish: Orange slices, berries and a mint sprig

name: Brandy Cobbler
description: Cognac, sugar and orange over crushed ice — the cobbler with brandy in place of sherry or whiskey.
funFact: Cobblers were among the first American drinks to reach Europe; Dickens wrote about encountering one on his 1842 American tour and being impressed by the straw.

steps: Muddle the orange with the sugar in a goblet.
Add the cognac and fill with crushed ice.
Churn until the outside of the glass frosts.
Top with more ice and pile fruit over it.

name: Whiskey Rickey
description: Bourbon, lime and soda with no sugar at all. The rickey's defining feature is what it leaves out.
funFact: The rickey was created for lobbyist Joe Rickey in Washington in the 1880s with whiskey; the gin version came later and took the name with it.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Squeeze half a lime in and drop the spent shell into the glass.
Add the bourbon and top with cold soda water.
Stir once and serve with no sugar — that is the point of a rickey.

name: Pierre Collins
description: The Collins built on cognac. Same lemon, sugar and soda; a rounder, fruitier result.
funFact: The Collins family names by base spirit — Tom for Old Tom gin, John for whiskey, Pierre for cognac, Pedro for rum, Mike for Irish whiskey.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

name: Pedro Collins
description: The rum Collins. Lighter than the whiskey version and sharper than the gin one.
funFact: Collins glasses are named after the drink rather than the other way round — the tall, narrow shape exists to keep a long soda drink carbonated.

steps: Shake the rum, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

name: Bamboo Royale
description: The Bamboo lengthened with champagne — sherry and vermouth under bubbles, and lower proof than almost anything.
funFact: The Bamboo was created at Yokohama's Grand Hotel in the 1890s; adding champagne follows the French 'Royale' convention applied to a Japanese-invented drink.

steps: Stir the sherry, vermouth and bitters over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and serve.

name: Port Sangaree
description: Port with sugar over ice and a heavy grate of nutmeg. The nutmeg is not a garnish here — it is what makes the drink a sangaree.
funFact: Sangaree and sangria share a root in the Spanish sangre, for blood, and both describe a wine lengthened and spiced rather than a cocktail.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in a little water in the glass.
Add the wine or spirit and stir.
Fill with ice and stir until chilled.
Grate nutmeg over the top — the nutmeg is what makes it a sangaree.

name: Sherry Sangaree
description: Sherry, sugar and nutmeg over ice. Lighter and drier than the port version, and the one Victorian bars actually poured most.
funFact: Sherry was the most-drunk wine in nineteenth-century Britain and America, which is why so many drinks in the old books simply assume a bottle is already open.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in a little water in the glass.
Add the wine or spirit and stir.
Fill with ice and stir until chilled.
Grate nutmeg over the top — the nutmeg is what makes it a sangaree.

name: Brandy Sangaree
description: Brandy over ice with sugar and nutmeg, and a float of port on top in the fuller version.
funFact: Jerry Thomas prints the sangaree once per base — port, sherry, brandy, gin, ale and porter — treating it as a template rather than a single drink.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in a little water in the glass.
Add the wine or spirit and stir.
Fill with ice and stir until chilled.
Grate nutmeg over the top — the nutmeg is what makes it a sangaree.

name: Rum Flip
description: Dark rum with a whole egg and sugar, shaken to a custard. Colonial New England drank this by the tankard.
funFact: The original colonial flip was ale, rum and sugar heated with a red-hot iron called a loggerhead — which is where the phrase at loggerheads comes from.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface and serve.

name: Sherry Flip
description: Sherry, whole egg and sugar. The lightest flip in the family and the easiest to drink two of.
funFact: A flip is defined by the whole egg — white for foam, yolk for body. Drop the white and it becomes a sangaree; drop the spirit and it is eggnog.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface and serve.

name: Whiskey Flip
description: Bourbon with a whole egg and sugar, shaken cold and dusted with nutmeg.
funFact: Flips were considered restorative rather than indulgent, and nineteenth-century bar books recommend them to the convalescent with a straight face.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface and serve.

name: Ale Flip
description: Hot ale beaten with egg, sugar and spice until it foams. The ancestor of every flip, and originally heated by plunging an iron from the fire straight into the tankard.
funFact: The loggerhead was a poker kept in the fire specifically for this; plunging it into the tankard both heated and foamed the drink in one motion.

steps: Beat the eggs hard with the sugar and nutmeg until pale.
Heat the ale to steaming without letting it boil.
Pour the hot ale slowly onto the eggs, whisking constantly so they do not scramble.
Pour back and forth between two jugs from a height until thick and foaming.
Serve immediately in a warmed tankard.

name: Whiskey Toddy
description: Bourbon, sugar and hot water. Three ingredients and no lemon — the American toddy leaves the citrus out.
funFact: American bar books separate the toddy from the sling by a single ingredient: a sling takes nutmeg, a toddy does not.

steps: Put the sugar in a warmed heatproof glass and add a splash of hot water to dissolve it.
Add the spirit and stir once.
Top with hot water and stir again.
Garnish and drink while hot.

name: Brandy Toddy
description: Cognac with sugar and hot water, served in a warmed glass with a spoon left standing in it.
funFact: The metal spoon is a genuine precaution rather than a flourish — it conducts heat away and stops boiling water cracking the glass.

steps: Put the sugar in a warmed heatproof glass and add a splash of hot water to dissolve it.
Add the spirit and stir once.
Top with hot water and stir again.
Garnish and drink while hot.

name: Rum Toddy
description: Dark rum, sugar and hot water with nutmeg. The winter drink of colonial New England, made from whatever was cheapest, which was rum.
funFact: New England imported Caribbean molasses and distilled it locally, so rum was cheaper than beer in eighteenth-century Massachusetts.

steps: Put the sugar in a warmed heatproof glass and add a splash of hot water to dissolve it.
Add the spirit and stir once.
Top with hot water and stir again.
Garnish and drink while hot.

name: Whiskey Sling
description: Bourbon, lemon, sugar and water with nutmeg over the top. A toddy served cold, which is all a sling has ever been.
funFact: The 1806 newspaper definition of a cocktail — spirits, sugar, water and bitters — describes it explicitly as a bittered sling, which makes the sling the parent form.

steps: Shake the bourbon, lemon juice, syrup and water with ice.
Strain into a tumbler over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface.
Serve without a straw.

name: Brandy Sling
description: Cognac with lemon, sugar and water, nutmeg grated over the top. The sling in its brandy form.
funFact: Slings were drunk hot in winter and cold in summer from the same recipe, which is why the old books often print no temperature at all.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice, syrup and water with ice.
Strain into a tumbler over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg over the top.
Serve cold, or build the same measures with hot water in winter.

name: Gin Sour
description: Gin, lemon and sugar. The plainest sour there is, and the shape almost every gin drink in the canon is built on.
funFact: Two of spirit, three-quarters of citrus, half of sugar is the ratio nearly every sour resolves to — the Daiquiri, the Sidecar and the Margarita are the same arithmetic in different bottles.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Rum Sour
description: Aged rum with lemon and sugar. Sits between a Daiquiri and a Whiskey Sour, and lands closer to the whiskey than you would expect.
funFact: The only difference from a Daiquiri is lemon in place of lime, which sounds trivial and changes the drink completely — lemon reads richer, lime reads sharper.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

name: Applejack Sour
description: Apple brandy with lemon and sugar. A Jack Rose without the grenadine, and considerably drier for it.
funFact: Laird's has distilled applejack in New Jersey since the 1700s and holds licence number one, the oldest commercial distilling permit in the United States.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Gin Crusta
description: Gin, maraschino, lemon and bitters in a sugar-rimmed glass lined with a single whole lemon peel.
glassware: Small wine glass with a sugared rim
funFact: The crusta is defined by the peel — one lemon rind cut in a single piece and pressed inside the glass, which is where the name comes from.

steps: Peel a lemon in one continuous spiral and press it inside a small wine glass.
Rim the glass with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the gin, maraschino, curacao, lemon juice and bitters with ice.
Strain into the prepared glass and serve.
recipe.garnish: A whole lemon peel inside a sugared rim

name: Whiskey Crusta
description: The crusta built on rye. Same lemon-lined glass, same sugared rim, a heavier drink underneath it.
glassware: Small wine glass with a sugared rim
funFact: Joseph Santini created the original Brandy Crusta in New Orleans around 1850, and it is the drink the Sidecar and the Margarita both descend from.

steps: Line a small wine glass with a single long lemon peel.
Rim it with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the rye, maraschino, lemon juice and bitters with ice.
Strain into the prepared glass and serve.
recipe.garnish: A whole lemon peel inside a sugared rim

name: Brandy Julep
description: Cognac, sugar and mint churned through crushed ice. The julep as it was made before bourbon claimed it.
funFact: The julep was originally made with cognac or peach brandy; bourbon only became standard after phylloxera cut off the French supply in the 1870s.

steps: Press the mint gently with the sugar in a julep tin — bruise it, do not tear it.
Add the cognac and pack the tin with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the outside of the tin frosts.
Cap with more crushed ice and crown with a dense mint bouquet.

name: Champagne Julep
description: Mint and sugar under champagne over crushed ice. Lighter than any julep has a right to be.
funFact: Jerry Thomas prints it in 1862, which puts champagne juleps in American bars decades before the Kentucky Derby made the bourbon version a fixture.

steps: Press the mint with the sugar in a julep tin.
Fill the tin with crushed ice.
Pour the champagne slowly over the ice so it does not foam over the rim.
Stir once, gently, and crown with mint.

name: Remsen Cooler
description: Scotch and soda over a long unbroken spiral of lemon peel. Named for a whisky brand nobody drinks any more.
funFact: The cooler is defined by the continuous citrus spiral hung inside the glass — the same construction as a Horse's Neck, which is a cooler under another name.

steps: Peel a lemon in one continuous spiral and hang it inside a Collins glass.
Fill the glass carefully with ice, holding the spiral against the side.
Add the Scotch and top with cold soda water.
Stir once and serve.

name: Klondike Cooler
description: Rye with orange peel and ginger ale over ice — a cooler named for the gold rush of 1897.
funFact: The Klondike rush drew a hundred thousand prospectors north in two years; barely a few hundred struck it rich, and the drink outlasted almost all of them.

steps: Hang a continuous orange peel spiral inside a Collins glass.
Fill with ice, keeping the spiral pressed against the side.
Add the rye and top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and serve.

name: Harvard Cooler
description: Applejack, lemon and sugar lengthened with soda. The Harvard's long, cold cousin.
funFact: Cooler, rickey, fizz and Collins are separated by fine distinctions of sweetener, citrus and garnish that Victorian bar books took entirely seriously.

steps: Shake the applejack, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wheel.

name: Bombo
description: Rum, water, sugar and nutmeg. The plainest rum drink in the colonial Atlantic, and the one sailors actually drank.
funFact: Bombo, sometimes bumbo, was the currency of colonial election campaigns — George Washington's agents handed out gallons of it during his 1758 run for the Virginia House of Burgesses.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in a little of the water in the bottom of the vessel.
Add the rum and the remaining water and stir.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface.
Serve at ambient temperature, or over ice in the heat.

name: Blackstrap
description: Dark rum with molasses and hot water. Colonial, cheap and unapologetically heavy.
funFact: Blackstrap molasses is the third boiling of cane syrup with nearly all the sugar removed, which is why it tastes bitter and mineral rather than sweet.

steps: Stir the molasses into a little hot water until it has fully dissolved.
Add the rum and stir again.
Top with the remaining hot water.
Serve hot, in a warmed mug.

name: Shandygaff
description: Ale and ginger beer, half and half. The Victorian ancestor of the shandy, and sharper than the lemonade version that replaced it.
funFact: Dickens uses the word in 1868 and Wodehouse never stopped; the ginger-beer version predates the lemonade shandy by a good half-century.

steps: Chill both the ale and the ginger beer thoroughly.
Pour the ginger beer into a pint glass first.
Add the ale slowly, down the side of the tilted glass, to control the foam.
Do not stir — the pour does the mixing.

name: Green Swizzle
description: Rum, lime and falernum swizzled green with a wormwood bitters, and immortalised by a Wodehouse character who claimed it changed his life.
funFact: The original green came from a Barbadian wormwood bitters that is now effectively lost, which is why every modern version reaches for Chartreuse instead.

steps: Fill a tall glass with crushed ice.
Add the rum, lime juice, falernum, Chartreuse and bitters.
Spin a swizzle stick between your palms until the outside of the glass frosts over.
Top with more crushed ice and crown with mint.

name: Zoom
description: Spirit, honey and cream shaken cold. Three ingredients, and it works with brandy, whisky or gin equally well.
funFact: The Savoy prints it as a template rather than a fixed recipe — the base spirit is left to the drinker, which is unusual for a book that specifies everything else.

steps: Loosen the honey with a splash of warm water so it will combine.
Add the cognac, honey syrup and cream to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe and grate nutmeg over the top.

name: Scaffa
description: Layered liqueurs and spirit served at room temperature, with no ice and no dilution whatsoever.
funFact: The scaffa is the only classical drink category defined by being served warm and undiluted — a deliberate refusal of everything ice brought to bartending.

steps: Pour the maraschino into a small glass.
Float the green Chartreuse over the back of a barspoon.
Float the brandy last and add a dash of bitters on top.
Serve at room temperature, without ice and without stirring.
recipe.garnish: None — the layers are the presentation
